Why Rwanda's deal for F1 race remains controversial
- Published
Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in a generation after Rwanda agreed a 10-year contract to stage a race, with the sport's governing body (FIA) keen to create a "lasting legacy".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, with the first edition in the "early 2030s".
For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the ambition is to "pave the way" for other F1 races on the continent.
However, the announcement has drawn criticism from some quarters amid allegations of sportswashing and questions around the East African country's human rights record.
Why is this big news?
Africa has not hosted an F1 race since 1993, and the clamour to return to the continent has been growing in recent years - with seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton among those leading the calls.
Morocco was the first African nation to host a Grand Prix in 1958 and 23 races were then held in South Africa between 1962 and 1993.
President Kagame said it was "an honour and privilege" for Rwanda to be chosen for its return.
"This partnership is long overdue but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent - especially for African fans," he added.
South Africa had been keen to secure its own F1 race, and sports minister Gayton McKenzie remains bullish about his country's hopes of emulating Rwanda.
"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it," he posted on X.
"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two [F1 races] a year, and some react like a continent of [54] countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030."
- Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993 
  - Published1 day ago
- A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1? 
  - Published1 day ago
What is still to be decided?
The year of the first African Grand Prix in the 2030s, and its timing in the calendar, are yet to be announced.
F1 is likely to want to avoid holding the race in Rwanda's main rainy season of March to May, while there is a shorter, less disruptive, rainy season from October to November.
The sport is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Former F1 driver Alex Wurz will be involved in the design of the circuit, which is due to use the undulating Rwandan landscape to produce a track with a natural flow and elevation changes of nearly 200m to challenge drivers.
Could the race boost African participation?
Jody Sheckter remains the only African to win the F1 Drivers' Championship, triumphing in 1979 with Ferrari.
"It's so expensive to get in," the South African told Newsday on the BBC World Service when discussing whether or not the race in Rwanda could open the door to more drivers from the continent.
"I built my own cars at the beginning. You can't do that anymore."
Africans hoping for a career in motorsport have previously had to chase their dream overseas, according to fellow driver Axcil Jefferies, who has previously competed in Formula 2.
But the Zimbabwean believes that could now change.
"F1 coming to Africa will highlight to everyone what a big industry motorsport is," he said.
"All the elements will inspire the youth, whether that's to come in as an engineer, as a mechanic, as drivers, as team coordinators."
South African presenter Kriya Gangiah, who hosts SuperSport's F1 Extra Africa Trackside podcast, is also hopeful of a boost in the number of female fans and drivers in Africa.
"The more you see something and the more that is present in your world, the more you take interest in it," she said.
"Being in paddocks in South Africa, you're seeing the amount of women that are making it into the sport and are actually doing really well. A lot of the girls are giving the guys a proper run for their money."
Why is the deal controversial?
Allegations of sportswashing - hosting sporting events to improve a country's international reputation - have long been levelled against Rwanda.
Securing an F1 race is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment.
The country has hosted the Basketball Africa League finals in all but one year since 2021 and staged cycling's World Road Championships last year, the first time the event had been held in Africa.
Visit Rwanda has either sponsored or had partnerships with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain, although its sleeve sponsorship of the Gunners ended this year after drawing criticism from supporter groups.
However, the tourism brand then became the front-of-shirt sponsor of fellow Premier League club Aston Villa.
Meanwhile, Rwanda's central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
Human Rights Watch previously said that "the space for freedom of expression" and "political autonomy" is shrinking in the country.
"Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record," said Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns Felix Jakens.
"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."
The Rwandan government has dismissed such accusations, with chief tourism officer Irene Murerwa calling them "a distraction' from the "amazing and outstanding achievements the country has made" when previously challenged by BBC Sport Africa.
"The benefits trickle down to every Rwandan," she said in December 2024. "Hosting F1 would be another step in our journey to becoming a world-class destination."
What has F1 said?
F1 is not blind to issues around sportswashing, with several countries on the calendar accused of utilising the strategy - not least Saudi Arabia.
F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders.
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
However, it has still drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International's Jakens believing the organisation's words "ring hollow".
"It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise," he said.
When asked about the sportswashing accusations levelled against Rwanda when it was bidding to host a race, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa: "When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.
"I honestly don't care about what they say."

Ulster's Augustus enjoying South Africa homecoming
- Published
Ulster back row Juarno Augustus says he is "enjoying his rugby again" after recovering from the ankle surgery he underwent in the summer.
This weekend the 28-year-old is preparing to go back to where it all began in terms of his professional playing career as the Irish province face the Stormers in a United Rugby Championship encounter.
Augustus, who played for the Cape Town-based side between 2017 and 2021, is relishing the prospect of coming up against his former team while also spending some precious time with his family.
"It's nice just to be at home. I'll probably need a lot of tickets, everyone's been asking me!" said the former Northampton Saints forward.
"It's always nice to play against the team you grew up playing for. I'll just try to play my game to the best of my ability.
"I had surgery and I was struggling a bit in pre-season to put it behind me but it's all gone now and I've had a run of games. That's the main thing - to keep training and being fit again. "
- Four games, no wins - Ulster aim for URC turnaround 
  - Published5 days ago
Ulster remain without a victory in their URC campaign to date, their 34-26 defeat by the Bulls in Pretoria extending their winless run in the competition this season to four games.
"I don't think huge things need to change. It's just a bounce of the ball, just small things that we need to work on and get right," added Augustus.
Ulster and the Stormers played out a pulsating 38-38 draw in Belfast last term but the number eight is hoping Richie Murphy's side can go one better on Saturday (12:45 GMT) against a Stormers outfit who have won three and lost one of their four URC matches.
"It's at their home this time so we need to be sharper, need to be ready for what they're going to bring. From minute one to minute 80, we need to give it our best. That's what we are going after.
"They have a lot of dangerous players who can make anything happen in a second. We need to be aware of it.
"Richie and his coaching staff gave us some detail on how they play and it's up to us now to go out and execute.
"We just need to be on our game every single moment."

Ryder Cup: Lee Westwood has 'no regrets' about turning down chance to captain Team Europe to play on LIV Golf
Lee Westwood was one of the candidates to captain Team Europe at the 2023 Ryder Cup before he joined LIV Golf; Westwood is yet to sign with LIV 2.0 and says the breakaway league are yet to present him with "anything agreeable"
Tuesday 3 November 2026 15:49, UK
Lee Westwood has "no regrets" about turning down the chance to captain Team Europe at the 2023 Ryder Cup to join LIV Golf, as the former world No 1 revealed he is yet to sign with LIV 2.0.
During a wide-ranging interview on The Chipping Forecast podcast, the 53-year-old said he was currently "unemployed" and added LIV 2.0 had not presented him with "anything agreeable" for the league's proposed relaunch in 2027.
Westwood has represented Team Europe at the Ryder Cup on 11 occasions, having tied Sir Nick Faldo for the most appearances at the biennial tournament during his last outing at Whistling Straits in 2021.

Having worked as a vice-captain under Thomas Bjørn at the 2018 Ryder Cup in France, the Englishman was one of the DP World Tour's leading candidates to be appointed captain for the tournament in Rome in 2023.
"Whistling Straights had happened and then quite shortly after that I had a conversation with [DP World Tour chief executive] Guy Kinnings, where he talked about the Ryder Cup captaincy and the captain in Italy," Westwood, who joined LIV Golf in 2022, said.
"It was put to me whether I'd like to be Ryder Cup captain, and I had started discussions with LIV. I think I asked: 'If I did go to LIV, could I still be Ryder Cup captain?'
"They didn't say no, but it was made clear that there would be very little chance of it, and I made the decision to go to LIV.
"You make calls in life, don't you?" Westwood added. "You make a choice, and I have no regrets over the choice I made."
The DP World Tour dictates a player cannot be a European Ryder Cup captain or vice-captain if they decline membership to the tour or fail to fulfil their minimum event obligations.
Henrik Stenson was later named captain for 2023 before he also joined LIV Golf, with the baton ultimately being handed to Luke Donald.
Westwood, who jointly holds the record for the most appearances for Europe at a Ryder Cup, was asked whether he would consider being captain in the future.
"I don't know, I get asked that question a lot," Westwood said. "I've always just wanted to play, I love playing golf.
"When I was vice captain, everybody has a little say in the team room, and I said to the guys: 'You better enjoy it as much as you can because when it's gone, you really miss it, and I'll tell you one thing worse than playing practice rounds in a Ryder Cup is watching other people playing practice rounds in a Ryder Cup.'
"I loved being a Ryder Cup player and getting in that environment. I don't know whether I'd have been a good Ryder Cup captain, because of what I said in France. I don't know whether I would have liked watching."
Delving further, Westwood said: "I'm not good at really pushing control.
"That's one of the reasons I started playing golf, I played a lot of football and rugby and cricket before taking up golf. The reason I enjoy playing golf is because the buck stops with me.
"I didn't want to have to rely on other people and that probably goes back to a little bit of the reason why the Ryder Cup captaincy wasn't really that higher priority.
"When push came to shove, it wasn't the be-all and end-all for me. I'm not sure I wanted it enough."
'I haven't made a decision on anything'
LIV Golfers have a deadline of November 16 to reapply for their DP World Tour memberships, and Westwood says he is deliberating whether to do so.
Should he reapply, he would face a 10-tournament suspension for his decision to resign his DP World Tour membership.
"I haven't signed up to anything anywhere, I haven't made a decision on anything yet," Westwood said.
"I am yet to have everything put in front of me and I have not really had any dialogue with the DP World Tour.
"I know if I sign up, I've then got to serve a 10-tournament suspension. I've looked at the schedule, and I feel like the first event I could play in on the DP World Tour will be the Turkish Airlines Open, which is the first week in May, so I haven't looked any further.
"There's nothing that's been presented to me that was agreeable for LIV 2.0. There are still a lot of things that would need fine-tuning; deadlines have come and gone, and I've heard nothing on whether I have to sign or not.
"I haven't signed [for] 2.0. So, I literally am unemployed."

A cancer medicine supplied to a retailer for ₹2,700 carries a maximum retail price (MRP) of ₹27,000. Who accounts for this tenfold difference? This was among the examples highlighted by the Supreme Court in September 2026, when it questioned the gap between the prices paid for medicines and what patients ultimately pay.
Subsequently, on October 17, the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) announced a 30% cap on trade margins for 137 anti-cancer drugs, effective from November 9. This intervention could reduce prices substantially for some products. It also raises a broader question: how does India decide what medicines should cost?

Starting Tuesday, Mexican schools will ban cellphones from classrooms as part of a federal government effort to limit children's and teenagers' use of electronic devices, following similar measures taken by over a hundred countries in the last decade.
The initiative, spearheaded by Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum, has been supported by experts who see it as an opportunity to reduce young Mexicans' exposure to technology and the resulting attention deficit, stress and anxiety.
Mexican authorities are also preparing to implement regulations this month that will require digital platforms to remove posts containing hate speech, abuse, sexual violence, harassment, cyberbullying and other illegal content.
However, the cellphone ban, which will take effect on November 3, is already facing resistance in some parts of the country. Some parents fear being unable to communicate with their children amid ongoing violence, from which children and adolescents are not spared.
According to the civil society coalition Network for Children's Rights in Mexico (REDIM), in the first half of this year, one in 10 Mexicans between the ages of 0 and 17 were victims of crimes involving organised crime.
“I don't think parents will accept not giving their children a means of digital communication, especially when those children … are spending so much time at home instead of at school,” said Francisco Ortiz, state representative of the National Union of Parents in Sinaloa, accusing the government of ignoring parents and approving regulations that “go against parental authority, against the rights of parents.”
The decree issued by Sheinbaum prohibits the use of cellphones and electronic devices inside elementary and middle schools throughout the school day, and only allows their use for educational purposes under the guidance of teachers or for personal emergencies, disability and health needs. Students can take their phones with them on the way to school.
Benigno Gomez, a father from Reynosa in the northern state of Tamaulipas, said that while he understood the educational authorities' need to reduce students' time on cellphones, he found it “a little difficult” that they weren't allowed to have a cellphone to deal with a potential risk situation.
Mexican authorities have not commented on these concerns and have instead focused on the harm caused by cellphones.
During a recent address to the Chamber of Deputies, Mexico's Secretary of Public Education, Mario Delgado, stated that the Sheinbaum administration seeks to “prevent addiction to digital platforms and the disorders they cause in minors.”
Parents seek reassurance
Just as the sun was beginning to rise, the residents of Escuinapa, the capital of the municipality of the same name located in southern Sinaloa, awoke on the morning of October 22 to alarming news. A bus that regularly travels through the small town -- which relies on mango and shrimp production -- was shot at by a man on a motorcycle.
More than a dozen high school students were on board. A video recorded by one of the passengers circulated on social media, showing children on the floor and others hiding among the seats while one teenager asks another, “Do you have any credit (on your cellphone)?”
In the attack, only the bus driver was injured, suffering cuts from shards of glass shattered by the gunfire.
Upon learning of the shooting, one Escuinapa resident immediately called her teenage daughter, who had left early for high school in a car driven by her aunt.
“Just hearing my daughter's voice and knowing she was OK calmed me down,” said the woman, who asked to remain anonymous for fear of the criminals plaguing her community -- admitting that she didn't hesitate to interrupt her daughter's class to check on her.
The mother expressed doubts that parents will comply with the cellphone ban, fearing that violence could now reach schools in Escuinapa, and insisted that “the safety of our children comes first.”
In defence of the regulation
For Israel Sanchez, president of the National Union of Parents, the Mexican government's decision represents progress after years of struggle by the civil organisation, which brings together hundreds of parents from public and private schools, mostly Catholic.
Sanchez argued that authorities must undertake an awareness campaign for parents and provide training for teachers to achieve the effective implementation of the regulation.
Lucía Magis-Weinberg, a neurodevelopmental researcher at the University of Washington who has studied the effects of technology on children and adolescents for years, said Mexico is joining the international movement to regulate cellphones at a very opportune moment.
Magis-Weinberg acknowledged the benefits of technology for socialisation and accessing information but said it is “a double-edged sword.”
Regulations are needed to avoid cognitive damage, digital conflicts, and the risks of platforms that “are designed to maintain, to maximise our attention.”
The ban on cellphones in schools is already in place in 114 countries, according to UNESCO data. In Europe, restrictions have gained increasing traction, especially in France, where the ban was extended to secondary schools in August. Controls have also been implemented in some countries in Latin America, such as Ecuador, Brazil, Chile, Bolivia and Costa Rica. In the United States, bans are only maintained in some states.

Morocco's first female prime minister caught between the king, clerics, and feminists
- Published
The Islamic saying "a people who entrust their affairs to a woman will never succeed" has resurfaced in Morocco since King Mohammed VI named Fatima Zahra El Mansouri as the country's first female prime minister.
Mustafa Ramid, a former justice minister in an Islamist-led government, cited the saying earlier this month, in a lengthy Facebook post questioning whether a woman should hold the country's highest political office.
He argued that Morocco, a Muslim majority country, had found a balance between equality and the responsibilities of state leadership, as the highest office - that of the king - continued to be reserved for men.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy. Yet executive power remains in the hands of the 63-year-old monarch.
El Mansouri's Authenticity and Modernity Party (Pam) won the most seats in September's parliamentary election and has since announced a coalition with three other parties. Together, they hold 207 of the 395 seats in parliament.
El Mansouri's royal appointment was historic but it exposed persistent reservations about women in positions of power.
The day after her appointment, local broadcaster Chouf TV took to the streets to ask Moroccan men "what they thought" of a woman heading the government.
Several men, mostly middle-aged or older, hesitated before answering. Some said they accepted the decision because it was the king's choice.
One grey-haired man, who did not give his name or age, said: "It feels strange to have a woman as head of government. I'm not sure if it sits well with me."
Criticism of the monarchy carries legal risks in Morocco. The penal code criminalises certain forms of offence or insult against the king, the royal family and the monarchy.
Online, the appointment became fodder for political satire.
A video showing two women pulling each other's hair was widely shared, with captions suggesting that this is what parliamentary disagreements between El Mansouri and her colleagues might look like.
However many younger Moroccans, especially women, welcomed her appointment.
While attitudes are changing in Morocco, conservative, religious views still hold great weight.
Some of the country's most contentious debates over gender equality centre on family law, including inheritance, marriage and divorce.
Under existing inheritance rules, a daughter typically receives half the share of a son in comparable circumstances.
The Higher Council of Ulemas, the country's body of religious scholars, has resisted calls for equal inheritance, citing Islamic jurisprudence.
It has also rejected proposals to abolish taasib, a rule that can require female orphans without brothers to share their inheritance with male relatives, including distant ones.
In a 2022 report, Morocco's National Human Rights Council said unequal inheritance rules contributed to poverty among women.
Polygamy is also legal under certain conditions. Proposed changes to the family code have included allowing women to stipulate in their marriage contracts that their husbands cannot take another wife.
But exceptions remain, including provisions relating to a first wife's infertility or illness, which women's rights groups have criticised on grounds of privacy and medical confidentiality.
These issues are at the heart of proposals to reform the Moudawana, Morocco's family code, which governs marriage, divorce and child custody.
A package of changes was announced in 2024, but the reforms have yet to become law.
As well as family law, some young women hope the new prime minister will try to improve education for girls.
Morocco's High Commission for Planning, the country's official national statistics agency, found in 2025 that just 55% of girls aged 15–17 were going to school in rural areas, where poverty, early marriage and dropping out of school remain key barriers. In urban areas, it was 100%.
"Many girls in rural Morocco drop out of school early because schools are far away, transport is unsafe or unavailable, and families with limited means often keep their daughters at home," Chifae Laazouzi, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
She says one reason is that many girls in poor and rural areas cannot afford menstrual sanitary products.
"Menstrual health is still treated as a taboo... I would like to see free menstrual products in schools," Laazouzi says.
El Mansouri is no newcomer to politics. Over more than two decades in public life, she has served as mayor of Marrakech, held government posts and sat in parliament.
For the past five years, she served as minister for national territory planning, urban planning, housing and city policy under the previous Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
After her appointment, El Mansouri presented the moment as a milestone for Moroccan women.
"Being the first female head of government is not just a source of pride for me, but for all the women of the kingdom," she said.
Since her appointment, she has not indicated whether she plans to try and push through the reforms to the family code.
In her political career so far, she has not made any prominent public statements about women's rights, even while changes to inheritance rules, polygamy and the family code were being widely debated.
Dr Irene Fernandez-Molina, an expert on the Global South at the University of Exeter in the UK, sees the appointment in the context of the monarchy's broader political interests.
"Two headlines have dominated coverage of [September's] parliamentary election in Morocco: a two-decade low turnout and King Mohammed VI's appointment of a woman as prime minister for the first time in this country's history," she tells the BBC.
"The latter cannot be understood without the former."
Official figures put turnout at just 38% of registered voters, while the proportion of all eligible voters who cast a ballot was even lower.
Fernandez-Molina describes the appointment as an example of "authoritarian state feminism, a top-down, selective instrumentalisation of the struggle for women's rights for regime legitimation purposes".
She argues that promoting a woman to the highest government office might be intended to project an image of modernisation and progress, even when the political system and the pace of social reform remain largely unchanged.
For Moroccan women's rights advocate Yasmina Benslimane, the appointment breaks a longstanding barrier, but says El Mansouri's background is also important.
"It does challenge stereotypes, because it finally breaks a ceiling that was never broken," she says. "But it matters how she got there."
El Mansouri's late father was a pasha, a senior local official, and a diplomat. Benslimane argues that her privileged background and access to political networks distinguish her from many Moroccan women who have fewer opportunities to enter public life.
For Benslimane, like many women's rights groups in the country, reform of the Moudawana remains a key test of the new government.
However, El Mansouri's room for manoeuvre is shaped by the country's political system.
The king retains extensive powers over key areas, including defence and foreign affairs, while the head of government operates within a system where authority is shared.
When it comes to Moudawana reform, she would have to face the country's religious scholars, who are mostly men.
While some Moroccan women welcome her appointment, they say it is what she does as prime minister that really counts.
"I don't think El Mansouri should be judged by the fact that she is a woman. Being a woman in power doesn't automatically make someone a champion of women's rights," Sara Zouiten, a young Moroccan woman, tells the BBC.
"Her party presents itself as a modernising political force, so I want to see whether that translates into actual change."

All countries can start to break their dependence on fossil fuels now without needing to wait for new technologies or economic changes, Brazil’s government has said ahead of a global climate summit.
Brazil, the host of last year’s UN climate conference, set out the world’s first global “roadmap” for phasing out fossil fuels on Tuesday, showing that countries could boost their economies and pull people out of poverty while breaking the link with coal, oil and gas.
But Joeri Rogelj, a professor of climate science and policy at Imperial College London, said that although the Brazilian roadmaps represented a step forward, they were limited. “The roadmaps are valuable but fall short of clearly indicating the pace of change needed by including no timeline or key benchmarks,” he said.
“Because of this omission, they still leave much to be imagined about what is needed to achieve the Paris agreement’s ultimate goal: limiting global warming to well below 2C, and preferably to 1.5C, to avoid dangerous climate harm.”
André Corrêa do Lago, Brazil’s president of the Cop30 summit, said the roadmaps were intended to help move the annual UN Cops away from their previous focus on negotiating global agreements to tackle the climate crisis, and on to implementing the targets that had already been agreed. Cop31 takes place in Antalya, Turkey, this month.
“They are documents of implementation,” Corrêa do Lago told the Guardian in an interview. “There is a different group of people that negotiate and that implement. The problem we’ve had at many Cops is to think that the same people who negotiate might also need to coordinate the implementation – this is not the case.”
He said the roadmaps should be taken up by ministries of finance, transportation, energy and infrastructure to work on how they could be implemented in each country.
Brazil hosted the Cop30 summit last November in the coastal city of Belém, in the Amazon rainforest, where a bitter dispute broke out over whether the final set of resolutions should include pledges on fossil fuels. As a compromise, the presidency agreed to produce two roadmaps, one on “transitioning away from fossil fuels in energy systems in a just orderly and equitable manner” and the other on halting and reversing deforestation.
These roadmaps are separate from similarly named plans from governments that met after Cop30 at a conference in Santa Marta, Colombia, in April, to discuss the transition away from fossil fuels. At that conference, nearly 60 countries formed a new “coalition of the willing”, separate to Cops, to set out their own national roadmaps to phase out fossil fuels. Several countries have since produced national plans, including Germany, France and the Netherlands.
The roadmaps produced by governments under the Santa Marta initiative are much more specific and prescriptive than Brazil’s, as each of those is written by the national government responsible for implementing the policies recommended.
The Brazilian roadmaps only set out steps that are possible. They are not binding, they contain no deadlines or milestones for actions, and they leave it to countries themselves to “diagnose” their degree of dependence on fossil fuels and select steps to reduce it.
“Every country will have a different rhythm [for moving away from fossil fuels] – it’s very important to concentrate on the diagnoses of countries’ circumstances,” Corrêa do Lago said. “Based on these diagnoses, they can choose their levers [of policy] and implement the transition.”
Among the steps Brazil suggests is for oil and gas producers to urgently cut the flaring and venting of gas from extraction sites. Methane is a greenhouse gas 80 times more powerful than carbon dioxide, so this would have an immediate impact. Other steps are for countries to reduce their subsidies to fossil fuel use or production, and building up renewable generation.
The roadmap on deforestation notes the large sums that are expected to be needed to help poor countries with heavily forested areas such as the Amazon, the Congo rainforests and south-east Asian tropical forests that are under threat from fires and palm oil exploitation.
About $300bn is likely to be needed every year for forests by 2030, and $500bn a year by 2050, according to the roadmap, citing UN figures. The current amounts available fall far short at about $85bn a year.
At Cop30 last year, Brazil set up the tropical forests forever facility, a fund aiming to preserve forests, to which the UK contributed £400m and other countries combined contributed about $7bn.
The deforestation roadmap also notes the importance of regulating trade between forested countries and consumer countries. At present, there are few trade checks to stop unscrupulous companies from selling goods from deforested areas.
In some cases, deforestation has appeared to be condoned or encouraged by local or even national administrations. Indonesia is being sued by civil society groups for “gross negligence” over the record-breaking fires over the last few months that have cleared swathes of forest and destroyed wildlife habitats, most likely to be replaced by palm oil plantations.
Brazil was able to publish the roadmaps after its president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, won a fourth election term just over a week ago. In the last four years under Lula, deforestation rates have fallen by about 70%. His defeated opponent Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed ex-president Jair Bolsonaro, had been expected if elected to return to his father’s policies of rampant exploitation of the Amazon rainforest.

Indian navy rescues 20 crew from Iranian fishing boat hijacked off Somalia
MOGADISHU, Somalia — Indian naval forces freed an Iranian fishing boat and its crew of 20 hijacked off Somalia after an operation lasting more than 48 hours, India's Defense Ministry said Tuesday.
The rescue of the Azini was completed Monday in the Arabian Sea, more than 3,000 kilometers (1,865 miles) from Mumbai, Indian Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said.
An official with the Puntland Maritime Police Force told The Associated Press that Indian forces disarmed 12 suspected Somali pirates, confiscated their mobile phones and released them. He spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
The suspects and two Somali security guards later came ashore at Bandar Bayla in northeastern Somalia, the official said. Three of those who came ashore had minor injuries, but he did not specify whether they were suspects or guards, or how they were hurt.
India's ministry said the operation ended without casualties or injuries. It did not specify whether that account covered everyone aboard or only the rescued crew. It was unclear whether the crew remained on the vessel or were moved elsewhere.
The operation involved a warship, a maritime surveillance aircraft and marine commandos. An Indian Air Force C-17 aircraft airdropped additional commandos, the ministry said.
The Azini was hijacked Oct. 29 between Bandar Bayla and Hafun. A Puntland maritime police officer said on Sunday that it carried 21 Iranian crew members and two Somali security guards. The difference between that crew count and India's rescue figure could not immediately be explained.
Indian forces tracked the vessel by sea and air before securing it, the ministry said. It said there had been concern that pirates could use the boat as a floating base for attacks on commercial ships.
The Puntland official said regional authorities learned of the rescue only after it had taken place.
The hijacking followed a resurgence of Somali piracy across the Gulf of Aden and western Indian Ocean. By August, pirates had hijacked six commercial vessels since April, some far from Somalia's coast. They included the oil products tanker Sibu 1, seized about 252 kilometers (136 nautical miles) east of al-Mukalla, Yemen.
In September, Puntland authorities said pirates killed five crew members of the tanker MT Honour 25 before security forces recovered it. The tanker had been held since April. Authorities said they detained 16 suspected pirates.
The renewed piracy adds to shipping risks in a region already disrupted by the Iran war. Attacks in the Strait of Hormuz and threats by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels against Saudi-linked shipping through Bab el-Mandeb have complicated oil transport routes.
Those disruptions have lengthened voyages and driven up tanker costs. Some oil shipments diverted around Africa face journeys up to a month longer.
International naval patrols and improved maritime security have sharply reduced Somali piracy over the past decade, but recent hijackings have renewed concerns about the threat.

The Indian actor Nana Patekar, who has died of a heart attack aged 75, first broke through in Mira Nair’s Salaam Bombay! (1988), and the Bollywood hits Parinda (1989) and Krantiveer (1994). These early credits established Patekar as a performer of rare versatility: he and Irrfan Khan remain the only performers to have won Filmfare’s best actor, best supporting actor and best villain awards (considered India’s “oscars”). Yet the question of whether Patekar was better suited to heroism or villainy lingered unresolved: allegations of sexual harassment and intimidation first made by his former co-star Tanushree Dutta in 2008 kickstarted India’s #MeToo movement when she raised them again in 2018.
Until that point, Patekar’s rougher edges had mostly been celebrated. As an actor, he demonstrated a baggy-eyed naturalism that spoke more to Bombay streetlife than Bollywood fantasy. He was given to writing out his dialogue until he had internalised it, and his growling line readings were both idiosyncratic and much imitated. Satyajit Ray counted among the actor’s most illustrious admirers, but apparently could not find a suitable project for him; Patekar instead had Nair to thank for launching him to international prominence in Salaam Bombay! as Baba Golub, the brutal pimp and drug dealer lording over an army of street children.
Yet the Bollywood studios also made good use of his grouchy grit. He was commanding as the kingpin Anna in Parinda, Vidhu Vinod Chopra’s inventive relocation of On the Waterfront, for which Patekar won two best supporting actor awards; he was appointed an honorary captain in the Indian territorial army after undergoing three years of army training for Prahaar: The Final Attack (1991), a film he also ended up directing. He crossed paths with the emergent megastar Shah Rukh Khan in Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (1992) and was momentarily in the running for Subhash Ghai’s blockbuster Khalnayak (1993), losing out to Sanjay Dutt.
Relations between Patekar and Dutt deteriorated further after the latter was linked to the 1993 Bombay bus bombings in which Patekar’s brother was killed. (Patekar’s wife, the Marathi actor Neelakanti, was also due to board one of the targeted vehicles.) Even after Dutt’s comeback, Patekar remained defiant: “I have not worked with [Dutt] in 22 years of my career. I will not work with him in the future.”
A comparable rage powered Krantiveer, in which Patekar played a dissolute gambler reviving his fortunes via social activism. Heart problems meant he shot his final scenes with a doctor on standby; while distributors thought Patekar a commercial risk, the film struck a chord, becoming one of that year’s biggest Hindi hits.
Born Vishwanath Patekar in Murud-Janjira, Maharashtra, Nana was one of the three sons of Dinkar Patekar, a textile painter and businessman, and his wife, Nirmala. He was educated at the Samarth Vidyalaya and the Bandra School of Arts in Bombay (now Mumbai), supporting his family after his father’s business collapsed by painting zebra crossings and cinema posters. He went on to the Sir JJ Institute of Applied Art, where he also joined the drama society.
After graduation, he briefly worked as a police sketch artist before joining the Marathi theatre group Rangayan. Switched on to films by his friend the celebrated Indian actor Smita Patil (“I was happy doing theatre, but she insisted”), he made his screen debut in the 1978 social drama Gaman, starring Patil.
A string of supporting roles followed: two years before Salaam Bombay!, he played Gandhi’s assassin Nathuram Godse in the Emmy-winning TV miniseries Lord Mountbatten: The Last Viceroy.
Despite his success in Krantiveer, for which he won several best actor awards, Patekar was not always the easiest fit with the studio system. He was replaced on Raja (1995) after spending two days hectoring his co-stars Madhuri Dixit and Mukesh Khanna with acting notes. And he paused his career during the Kargil war of 1999 to enlist with the Maratha Light infantry, serving 60 days and earning a promotion to the rank of major.
Back on civvy street, he landed a signature role as Inspector Sadhu, the dirty cop who becomes the hero of Ab Tak Chhappan (2004), and swept India’s best villain prizes as the underworld don Tabrez Alam in Apaharan (2005). He then switched into a lighter mode for the knockabout comedies Welcome (2007) and Welcome Back (2015).
Elder statesman status beckoned: he played Mumbai’s police commissioner in The Attacks of 26/11 (2013), voiced Shere Khan in the Hindi dub of Disney’s The Jungle Book (2016) and enjoyed a major success with the Marathi film Natsamrat (2016), playing an acclaimed actor unravelling in retirement. He was awarded the Padma Shri and the Raj Kapoor special contribution award in 2013; in 2015, he set up the Naam Foundation with fellow actor Makarand Anaspure to help drought-hit farmers.
Then came Dutta’s 2018 interview with the Hindu, where she repeated an earlier accusation that Patekar had first sexually harassed her while shooting a dance sequence for Horn “OK” Pleassss (2009), then, when she fled the set, sent hired thugs after her. Footage of the incident aired on Indian TV showed a mob surrounding her car, her windscreen smashed and tyres being flattened. Patekar denied the allegations. The Mumbai police opened an investigation; while no formal charges were brought, the incident sparked renewed concern about the treatment of women in Bollywood.
After a spell in industry purdah, Patekar recently attempted a comeback. There were supporting turns in the propagandistic The Vaccine War (2023), limp comedy Housefull 5 (2025) and the streaming-bound Subedaar (2026), though the actor did lend a wry centre to Vishal Bhardwaj’s Shakespeare riff O’Romeo (2026).
He married Neelakanti in 1978, and they had two sons, the first of whom, Durvasa, died in 1980, aged two. Patekar is survived by his wife and his second son, Malhar.

With World of Warcraft: Forever, Blizzard had to reconnect with what made WoW great in the first place
A lot of the team had to "unlearn" design habits they picked over the years.
After 13 years at Blizzard, Michael Nuthals faces what might just be the toughest challenge of his career yet: working on a familiar but different and highly anticipated version of World of Warcraft. As lead encounter designer, he's part of the team working on WoW: Forever. Announced at BlizzCon earlier this year, Forever is a sort of remaster of WoW designed to expand on the game's "Classic" era. It takes players back to Azeroth, the setting of the original 2004 game, before Blizzard over the course of 11 expansions took the game in the direction that it did. In the process, it imagines a "what if" scenario.
What if Blizzard had continued to expand Azeroth, instead of sending players to the Orc homeworld of Draenor and beyond with The Burning Crusade and later expansions? In Forever, there are more than 1,000 new quests for players to complete, many of them designed to continue story threads that were left unresolved in the original game. Additionally, there are new areas within Azeroth for players to explore — including Mount Hyjal, the site of one of Warcraft III's pivotal battles — in addition to fresh dungeons and raids. Blizzard has also rebalanced the game's classes and items, and built an entirely new global illumination lighting pipeline to make the game feel more atmospheric. Controversially, Forever will also feature a new race, the Skyborne Elves, who weren't in the original game.
The challenge Nuthals and his colleagues face is one of expectations. Nearly right from the moment Blizzard rereleased the original World of Warcraft in 2019, players have been asking the studio for a "Classic+" experience that expands the original game. The tricky thing is that, before Forever's announcement, every player had a different opinion on what an expanded rerelease should look like. Seemingly the only consensus was that the game shouldn't play anything like modern "retail" WoW. Realistically, there was never going to be a way Blizzard would find a way to please everyone with Forever, but it's still trying to create something fans both old and new can appreciate.
"I see it more as an opportunity — an opportunity to engage, to listen and show that we're listening," Nuthals says when asked about the weight of those expectations. With Forever, Blizzard recently concluded the largest beta in World of Warcraft's history. This is despite the fact players had to purchase one of Forever's premium bundles, which start at $60, to take part in the experience. Nuthals says Blizzard received "a lot of feedback" during the beta. He later admits one of the challenges of making Forever has been letting go of habits he learned working on the current version of WoW.
"Some of us had worked on the modern game for a long time, myself included. I come from modern, and it's almost like unlearning what you have learned," said Nuthals, who began working full-time on WoW ahead of 2014's Warlords of Draenor expansion. "We needed to understand what the DNA was [of WoW Classic], what the philosophies were, and to do that you just had to put it under your fingers and play." One way Nuthals and his colleagues did that was by revisiting the original game each week. Every Thursday morning, he and the rest of the encounter team would replay a classic dungeon like The Deadmines before jumping into one of the new dungeons they've created for Forever, such as Ruins of Lordaeron. Afterwards, they would ask themselves if those two dungeons felt like "they could live hand in glove?" and were connected.
"That was the development process," explains Nuthals. "We thought about what we want Forever to feel like, and we wanted it to feel like you wouldn't even know — like it was made in 2004. That was the vibe we were going for." Nuthals also credits the work Blizzard did with Season of Discovery, which was an offshoot of WoW Classic that saw the studio experiment with new class abilities, progression systems and dungeons within the confines of the original game.
"With Season of Discovery, we were pushing boundaries, exploring what Classic encounters could be. For Forever, we really looked back at the original Classic encounters and wanted to capture those, so we could provide a really authentic and nostalgic experience as players do these new raids," Nuthals said. As part of that process, the one thing he and the team kept coming back to is something Nuthals describes as the "strength, dexterity and intelligence" triangle of encounter design. Strength encounters reward the player for all the gear they've accumulated and their skill with their class, while dexterity ones test how well they can move and avoid hazards. Finally, intelligence-focused encounters test your understanding of a fight's mechanics and how much planning you've done.
"What we're trying to do with raids and dungeons is move toward gearing and planning, because Classic players really love that," said Nuthals. "'I overprepare, then I come in and crush the content.' That was the vibe we really wanted to hit." Part of how that philosophy will play out involves Forever's much advertised "horizontal" progression. With the new game, the studio has said it plans to keep the level cap at 60, meaning there won't be massive jumps in player power when the studio drops major new content. On paper at least, Blizzard appears committed to rewarding those who engage with and explore the game deeply.
"We're seeding the world with all these new items and things to chase, and in the future, having one of those items might pay off," said Nuthals. "We're thinking about those opportunities as we architect future raids and decide what bosses to introduce: making sure you feel smart for having pocketed something that comes in handy later. It feels good to use all that cool gear you went out and got."
Nuthals also said in the future Blizzard hopes to add new dungeons and zones, and that "not all of them will be max level." He added "there are areas players know about and want to explore, and there are opportunities for us to tell new stories in this space — taking what might have been a one-off quest name or something you found on a piece of paper and developing that story."
One question I didn't get a chance to ask Nuthals is what Blizzard will do if players, upon reaching 60, drop Forever and move onto other games. It's one thing for a studio to say it's committed to doing things differently with an MMO that doesn't take prey on player FOMO, and an entirely different thing to actually stick to that philosophy. We'll see how the future of Forever starts to unfold when the game arrives on November 4.

Dhinidhi Desinghu won the bronze medal in the women’s 100m freestyle at the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games on Monday, finishing in a record time of 56.27 seconds, the best by an Indian woman in the discipline.
It is India’s first ever swimming medal at the Youth Olympic Games, and the 16-year-old became the first Indian swimmer to win a medal at an Olympic event, across the senior and youth editions.
Croatia’s Ana Bobanovic took gold in 55.89 seconds and New Zealand’s Alyssa Lawson won silver in 56.13. Dhinidhi was fifth at the halfway mark, with a first 50m split of 27.31 seconds, before moving up to third in the second half.
She was only 14 when she became India’s youngest athlete at the Paris 2024 Olympics, finishing 23rd in the women’s 200m freestyle. Two years on, she has added a Youth Olympics medal to her name.
Dhinidhi also topped the women’s 200m freestyle at the 76th Senior National Aquatic Championships in July 2023. Months later, in March 2024, she claimed another 200m freestyle gold at the 54th Singapore National Age Group Championships.

Good morning! We’ve got something a little different for you today – an amazing new story from Megan Molteni, and also a peek at the story behind the story.
And speaking of peeks — I’d recommend this new episode of Commons Healthcare, which examines STAT’s investigative prowess and features interviews with Executive Editor Rick Berke and the late, inimitable Helen Branswell.
Inside the global fertility industry using women as ‘guinea pigs’
Heidy Willis was struggling to get pregnant. And after several rounds of failed IVF, she was willing to try anything.
So Willis flew to Albania for a process known as mitochondrial replacement therapy, or MRT. Willis’ genetic material was inserted into another woman’s egg cells. The idea is that the donor’s healthy mitochondria power the embryo into a healthy fetus and, eventually, a baby.
MRT is not legal in the U.S. But medical tourism agencies charge thousands of dollars to connect women to clinics around the world. Many of these companies target women over 40, even though there’s scant evidence the procedure can help unwind age-related infertility.
“You’re paying for the privilege of being a guinea pig,” a John Hopkins bioethicist told STAT’s Megan Molteni.
Megan has spent the last eight months doggedly investigating the companies connecting women to MRT treatments, talking to dozens of patients, employees and researchers. Some of her findings are, quite frankly, shocking. There’s a coda to Willis’s story, for example, that made me gasp out loud.
Set aside some time today or this week to dive into the story. And below, Megan took the time to answer some of my questions about this remarkable piece of journalism.
How did the idea for this story come about?
Back in 2019, I’d reported on the results of a small pilot study of MRT for infertility and since then have continued to cover developments.
In February of this year, I was contacted by a couple in the U.K. who wanted to tell me about an experience they had with a reproductive tourism company called IFG that was marketing MRT as a sort of miracle treatment for age-related infertility. The woman in this couple was a doctor in her 40s and she’d been taken in by the hope that was being offered for her to have a genetically related child of her own, despite there being scant evidence that it improves the odds of pregnancy for older women.
Ultimately, she didn’t go through with MRT because of some bad experiences she had leading up to it. But she was in touch with a number of other women who were actively in the process and she helped me get connected to them to hear more about their stories.
What was the biggest reporting challenge?
Reproductive tourism is the business of breaking procreation into distinct components that can be routed around regulations and assembled at the end to result in a baby. It is, by design, a complex chain of events often facilitated by multiple companies across multiple jurisdictions to circumvent local laws and so is a pretty opaque process.
With MRT, you’re adding even more layers of scientific and legal maneuvering to make it possible. So getting inside required actually going to the places that patients were going, including a clinic in Albania, where the laws are more amenable to technologies like MRT.
What was the most surprising thing you learned?
One of the things that was most surprising was that we were able to get our hands on this long-awaited data from a clinic in Ukraine that had been at one time the most prolific provider of MRT, before the full-scale Russian invasion of 2022.
I had been aware of them for years, thanks to reporting by NPR and this Netflix documentary.
Scientists I know in this space have been awaiting this publication of data, but with the war breaking out, things had gone rather silent. I reached out to their former embryologist, Pavlo Mazur, to ask him what he thought about these commercial clinics offering MRT for age-related infertility, not really expecting to hear back.
Instead, that started months of conversations. He had data he wanted in the world but hadn’t been able to publish, for some reasons that make a lot of sense, and for some others that have to do with biases against science coming out of countries like Ukraine without a long history of evidence-based medicine and well-regulated biomedical research. Their results are the strongest refutation of the idea that MRT can be a silver bullet remedy for age-related infertility.
The health policies that could be transformed after the election
No matter what happens tomorrow, health care policy could be in for a shakeup. That’s the message from more than two dozen policymakers, lobbyists, and experts STAT’s Daniel Payne spoke with.
Of course, control of Congress will shape what happens next. But some of Daniel’s sources said the anger with the health care status quo runs deep. One health policy consultant said they’re telling insurance leaders that they predict “significant” changes to the fundamentals of American health care, and that they should “be afraid.”
If you prefer your election predictions via video, check out our new “STATus Report”. And if you haven’t yet checked out our midterms page, do it today! Who knows what it will hold after tomorrow!
Elections may be bad for your heart
Did Daniel’s story about the stakes of tomorrow’s election get your heart racing? It turns out, you’re not alone.
As STAT’s Liz Cooney reports, “studies have found a significantly higher chance of arrhythmias in the weeks just before and after elections, and an increased rate of hospitalizations for heart attacks right after voting day.”
The issue is stress. A deluge of news can raise your adrenaline and amp up your sympathetic nervous system, which can in turn alter the heart’s electrical activity. This makes abnormal rhythms more likely in someone already prone to them. Interested to learn about what researchers found when they looked at heart health around the 2020 and 2016 elections? Read more.
What doctors need to know about cancer and pregnancy
Years ago, maternal fetal medicine doctor Elyce Cardonick met two pregnant women, both suffering from ovarian cancer. The women became friends, meeting up with their newborns and comparing wigs after hair loss.
One of those mothers is thriving, alongside her 28-year-old twins. The other didn’t live to see her child turn three.
Why did one die and the other survive? Read this new First Opinion for answers.
