Days before his retirement as Chief of Air Staff, Air Chief Marshal AP Singh wrote to Defence Minister Rajnath Singh, urging him to intervene in the sealing of the Indian Air Force's (IAF) sports complex at the Race Course Air Force Station in New Delhi.
In a letter dated October 26, Singh sought to ensure that the approximately 40-acre land parcel housing the Air Force Sports Complex (AFSC) remained under the IAF's control, citing operational requirements and the facilities located within the premises, Hindustan Times reported, quoting officials familiar with the matter.
The former Air Chief Marshal also raised the issue during an in-person meeting with Rajnath Singh on October 29, two days before his retirement on October 31, as per the HT report.
He reportedly urged the defence minister to direct the concerned authorities to reconsider the decision and hand over the land to the Air Force.
The intervention came after the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs (MoHUA) reclaimed the sports complex, triggering concerns within defence circles.
The closure also led to the cancellation of a farewell event planned for the outgoing Air Chief, as per reports.
In his communication, AP Singh argued that it would be prudent for the land housing the AFSC to remain under the Air Force's control, citing its importance to the overall functioning of the Race Course Air Force Station, according to officials cited by PTI.
He also referred to a joint survey of the land conducted in 2014 by the then Ministry of Urban Development, the Defence Estates Department and the Air Force.
The IAF has separately conveyed its objections to the Defence Ministry and sought the cancellation of the sealing process, officials said.
A key concern relates to the strategic location of the air station, which lies in the high-security zone surrounding the Prime Minister's residence at Lok Kalyan Marg. The Air Force has highlighted the station's role in addressing potential aerial security threats in the area.
Singh also referred to the station's history and existing land arrangements, stressing that its various facilities should continue to function without disruption.
According to officials cited in the report, the station provides administrative support to Air Headquarters and more than 5,000 Air Force personnel.
Its premises house accommodation for married and unmarried personnel, training facilities for airmen and Agniveervayus, security infrastructure, recreational facilities, a medical centre, a school and a unit-run canteen.
The Air Force Sports Complex itself includes a golf course, guest cottages, a swimming pool, a fitness centre and restaurants.
The facility's closure reportedly disrupted regular activities and forced the cancellation of a farewell golf event scheduled for October 28 for the outgoing Air Chief Marshal.
The development also drew attention because of the timing of the reclamation, coming days before AP Singh's retirement.
The sealing of the Air Force Sports Complex is part of a wider exercise by the Centre to reclaim high-value land parcels in the vicinity of Lok Kalyan Marg.
The Land and Development Office (L&DO), which functions under MoHUA, has been reviewing land parcels used for defence-related golf courses and sports facilities in the area.
The ministry had earlier reportedly asked the authorities concerned to hand over the land housing the Air Force Golf Course.
The L&DO subsequently issued eviction notices to the sports complex's management, seeking the return of the property.
Other prominent establishments have also faced action as part of the reclamation drive.
In August this year, the government evicted the Delhi Race Club from its 53-acre premises on Lok Kalyan Marg, citing the requirement of the land for an unspecified public purpose.
The Centre also reclaimed the Jaipur Polo Ground from the India Polo Association, citing broader public purposes, governance and defence infrastructure projects.
The government has not publicly specified the exact purpose for reclaiming the approximately 40-acre Air Force Sports Complex land parcel.
The controversy also triggered a political response, with the Congress criticising the Centre over the reclamation of the Air Force Sports Complex.
Congress general secretary in-charge of communications Jairam Ramesh shared a media report about AP Singh's letter to Rajnath Singh on X, accusing the government of showing "utter disrespect" to the IAF community.
Ramesh said the sports complex had a long history and had served several public purposes over the decades, while also remaining an integral part of the Indian Air Force's social infrastructure.

'We grew up around this historic Delhi mosque - now we have been forced out'
- Published
In the heart of Delhi, a short distance from the Indian prime minister's residence, a small mosque stands amid piles of rubble. Its pale walls and pointed arches remain intact, its courtyard still lined with green-and-white tiles.
But the people who gave life to the place are gone.
Mohammad Wasim, 50, points across the rubble to the spot where his house once stood.
"My father was married there, and, decades later, so was my daughter," says Wasim, a driver.
Wasim and his family were among hundreds of people who lived around the mosque in a patchwork of modest homes tucked between military compounds, exclusive clubs and sprawling bungalows in Race Course, one of the Indian capital's wealthiest and most heavily guarded neighbourhoods. Many of them had lived here for generations, working as drivers, cleaners and gardeners in the wealthy houses around them.
On 7 October, the authorities demolished their houses across three settlements, saying they had been built illegally on government land. They also raised security concerns because of the houses' proximity to military installations. Some 717 families were relocated to Savda Ghevra, a colony nearly 31 miles away, on the city's outskirts.
Residents had challenged the evictions in the Delhi High Court, arguing that moving so far from their jobs, schools and communities would upend their lives. But in August, the court allowed the relocation, accepting the government's security concerns and noting that alternative housing had been provided.
Only the mosque and a nearby Hindu temple were left standing. But their water and electricity supplies were cut off that day, and access to the compound has since been restricted. Worshippers are generally turned away at the gates, though some are occasionally allowed through after pleading with guards.
The government says it owns the land on which the mosque stands, but mosque authorities say it was registered in 1977 as waqf property - land or buildings set aside under Islamic law for religious or charitable purposes - and is listed, external as a heritage structure. The Delhi Waqf Board says it is nearly 300 years old, though other estimates put its age at 125-150 years.
The board has written to the authorities seeking restoration of the mosque's water and electricity and raising concerns about its future. Separately, a worshipper has petitioned the high court over restrictions on prayers and fears that the mosque could be demolished.
1 of 5
On 29 October, the government told the court it would take no action against the mosque for four weeks while considering the board's objections. It opposed restoring access for prayers, citing safety concerns during demolition work, a position disputed by the worshippers' lawyer. The court declined to intervene and scheduled another hearing for 16 December.
While the mosque's future remains uncertain, for those who once lived around it, the question now is what can be salvaged of the lives they built there.
Wasim still returns to the mosque to pray when he can, though guards sometimes turn him away. On a recent afternoon, he was among just four or five worshippers inside. A generator chugged loudly outside, supplying electricity after the power had been cut off.
"Our hearts and entire lives are tied to this place," he says. "How can we let it go, when our childhood was spent playing here?"
Rekha, a widow, remembers the colony with longing. She washed dishes in nearby homes, raised her family and performed seva (voluntary service) at the local temple.
To her, the word rehabilitation seems painfully inadequate: "How can a life built over decades be uprooted and planted somewhere else?" she asks.
Since the move, she has lost the work she depended on. Her 19-year-old son is struggling to find a job. She has been allotted a third-floor apartment but climbing stairs is painful because of a metal rod in her leg after an operation.
"I may have a house but my home was snatched away."
Critics say these experiences are part of a longer history of displacement in Delhi, where working-class communities have repeatedly been pushed, external to the city's distant edges because they lack documents proving legal ownership of land they have lived on for decades.
"Relocation disconnects them from both jobs and networks, resulting in livelihood and income loss," urban researcher Mukta Naik told the BBC.
As families scatter in search of work, she says, the informal support systems they once relied on become harder to rebuild.
"This leaves families to fend for themselves," she says.
The Delhi government's housing agency, the local municipal council and the central government's land office did not respond to requests for comment.
Savda Ghevra was established in 2006 on farmland near Delhi's border with Haryana state, to house families displaced from elsewhere in the city.
The first arrivals found little more than bare plots, without roads, running water or electricity. Over time, they built homes, opened shops and fought for basic services. By the early 2020s, an estimated 50,000 people lived here, external, having made a neighbourhood out of a place they had little choice but to inhabit.
Now the families from Race Course have begun the same slow work.
They have traded the lush tree-lined avenues of central Delhi for rows of nearly identical concrete blocks, with open fields stretching beyond. Life is going on, but much of what sustained these families remains on the other side of the city.
Every day, Babloo leaves home at 5am to take his children by metro to their old school in central Delhi, changing trains three times along the way. He waits out the six hours until classes finish at a tea stall outside his former neighbourhood. When he has work his wife makes the journey.
Their new home is too far away, he says, to return between the school runs. By the time the family reaches Savda Ghevra, it is around 4pm.
Babloo once worked at a club in Race Course. He has now found work in Meerut, a town to the north-east of Delhi. Residents knew they might have to leave, he says, but they hoped they would be relocated somewhere close enough to continue their jobs and their children's schooling.
The government says suitable apartments were unavailable closer to Race Course. In court, it cited Savda Ghevra's schools, dispensaries and transport links as evidence that the area could accommodate the displaced families.
But the presence of these facilities offers little reassurance to Naeem Khan, 63. His two grandsons have hearing and speech disabilities and need specialised care and schooling that he says are unavailable in the area.
The move has also scattered Naeem's family. One son and a divorced daughter share his tiny one-room apartment, while his two other sons had to move elsewhere due to lack of space.
"We have been thrown 20 years backward," he says.
The distance has been especially costly for women. Naik says childcare responsibilities, transport costs and safety concerns make long commutes to work particularly difficult for them.
At Race Course, the wealth surrounding the settlements offered small but vital ways to earn money - dishes to wash, gardens to tend, discarded bottles to collect and sell.
Akhtari, an elderly widow, collected mineral-water bottles for about 100 rupees (about $1.05; £0.80) a day and dried leftover rotis, or flatbreads, to sell as cattle feed.
Now even these modest sources of income have disappeared.
"Everyone living here was evicted; everyone is poor, broken, and struggling themselves," Akhtari says. "Who will hire someone else for housework?"
At Race Course, when she had nothing, the mosque's imam or a neighbour might give her money for flour. Her neighbours checked on her. In the new apartment, she has a roof over her head, but few people to fall back on.
She has begun to worry about what will happen if she falls ill.
"If I collapse and die inside, no one will even know," she says. " Hopefully someone will break down the door and find me."

Two of them are Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, who arrived in deals that could reach a combined £241m. But the jury is still out on both of them. Isak has only just started delivering his highly-anticipated goal numbers, while many believe Wirtz is yet to get going on Merseyside.

After making the move, Barcola failed to get a goal or an assist in his first 10 games for club and country this season. But then came some encouraging signs.
A hat-trick in Liverpool's thumping Champions League over LASK was backed up by back-to-back assists in wins over the tricky Brighton and Brentford.
While Barcola fired a blank against Arsenal in the last match, his first half running caused the Premier League champions a lot of concerns. Isak and Wirtz didn't quite start this quickly, so is Barcola starting to deliver on that hefty cheque?

Barcola is the marquee attacking signing in the wake of Mohamed Salah's departure this summer. Salah graced Anfield with his world-class ability and delivered titles. Barcola arrived as a back-to-back European champion with Paris Saint-Germain.
When signings like these are made, there is expectation, which leads to pressure. But Barcola insists he is not feeling anything of the sort - neither the huge price tag, nor Salah's shadow on the club.
"First of all, I wasn't the one who decided the transfer fee," he says. "So that's not been my problem.
"And regarding Mo Salah, he's a legend here. A huge one. He's done big things here and for that I have an enormous respect for him. But it's not pressure for me at all.
"I'm not Mohamed Salah, so I'm going to try to contribute whatever I can to the club and make my own mark on its history. I don't feel any pressure about that."
Those final words feel pertinent. Barcola has already achieved huge success in his career - delivering the piece de la resistance European trophy at PSG not once, but twice in successive years. But did he make his mark on that PSG success story compared to others?

"For me, it was the right time to leave PSG," he recalls. "I spent so many great years there and I won an enormous amount of trophies. But it was time.
"It was quite difficult because, over there, it was a real family. We'd built something very special together. On top of that, it was very difficult to leave and say goodbye to my team-mates. But ultimately, that's just how football is.
"When a club like Liverpool comes calling, it's a great thing. I didn't have any doubts and I just knew I had to come here. I'm happy to be here, and I hope things go well for PSG."
Barcola basically won it all at PSG last season - but at Liverpool there may need to be a bit more patience. Andoni Iraola has clearly improved the Reds off the back of Arne Slot's flawed final year, but defeats to Man City and Arsenal at Anfield have shown how far they are from the elite.
The weekend's 1-0 loss to Arsenal saw Liverpool fail to register a shot on target at home for the first time since Premier League data records began. They sit second-bottom in the Premier League this season for big chances created. If Arsenal are the level required, Liverpool have work to do.
So do expectations need to be tempered now? "No, I don't think it has changed the goals for the season," Barcola says. "I think we should have done better in a game like this. We had the chances to score, even to win the match.
"I think we need to work on being able to control the game more and play more football. Often, when we're in a game like this, we resort to long balls. But in my opinion, we should try to keep the ball on the ground more, because we have players with the quality to do that.
"We were really disappointed after the game but we know what we have to do better at. We're not going to give up. We know that other teams will drop points. So it's down to us to remain consistent until the end of the season."
In that case, Barcola and his team-mates need to get back on that training pitch. There's work to be done.

How Antonelli 'blew everyone away' to make Formula 1 history
- Published
Just after Kimi Antonelli clinched his first title to become the youngest world champion in Formula 1 history, Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen were united in their assessment of his achievement.
"Incredible," they both said. Coming from the two most successful champions on the current grid, the men who are first and third in the all-time list of F1 record-holders, it meant something.
That Antonelli shared the Mexico City Grand Prix podium with these two titans meant something, too.
To Antonelli, firstly, who said: "I will definitely frame the picture and put it in my house because it's just an incredible moment. And as well to see so much respect from two incredible drivers who have done the history of the sport is truly special and a moment that will live and will always be remembered."
So, too, though, for its symbolism. Antonelli seems destined to join them among the list of all-time greats of the sport, judging by the scale of his achievement this year.
"There are going to be others," said 1996 world champion Damon Hill, commentating for BBC Radio 5 live.
"I don't see anything else other than him getting better and better. He's going to have to go through hard times as well, but no one is going to doubt his incredible talent."
No one indeed. Not any more, anyway.

Antonelli's first title comes at the end of only his second season in F1. When he was drafted into Mercedes last year - to replace Hamilton, no less - there were those who said he was too inexperienced.
For some of last year, he looked it. There were flashes of promise, but by and large it was a shaky debut season, one that did not live up to Antonelli's billing as potentially the next generational talent.
So when it became clear that Mercedes would start this season with the best car, it was his team-mate George Russell, who had comfortably beaten him in 2025, who was favourite for the championship.
But that was without reckoning on the remarkable step forward Antonelli made in his development over last winter.
He finished the first race on Russell's tail. He took his maiden victory in the second, the first of five consecutive wins with which he took control of the championship. Since then, he has never looked like losing it.
Even when Mercedes' early season advantage was wiped out by their rivals, Antonelli was always there, always a factor. Which is more than can be said for Russell.
In that sense, it is important to see his achievement in context. Had the comparative performance between Russell and Antonelli carried on as it did last year, this championship may well have had a different complexion.
It could have been a season during which Russell and Hamilton were neck and neck in the title fight for most of the year - indeed, Russell has now slipped behind both Verstappen and Hamilton in the points table.
Instead, it has been a story of one driver's domination. His performances have been so strong that he has removed pretty much all jeopardy from the title fight.
That has not made it the most exciting season to watch, but it speaks volumes for the level at which Antonelli has performed. All because of the progress he has made - and his remarkable consistency.
"At his age," said Verstappen, "to be so solid, not make big mistakes, and of course also beat your experienced team-mate, he's just driven incredible, and I'm very proud of him, how he has handled himself this whole season."
Lando Norris, the outgoing world champion, was also effusive in his praise.
"It couldn't have gone to a better person," he said. "He's a genuine guy, very, very kind, and he has driven unbelievably well this year, better that what everyone was expecting of him.
"He's certainly not had an easy season in terms of his competition being incredibly high. He has gone up against the best drivers in the world, all in very good cars, and he's blown everyone away.
"I hope everyone gives him enough credit for what he's achieved this year. He's made everyone else look silly. He's driven that well and he's been able to click with his car, he's worked hard to understand how to drive this car and he's exploited it better than anyone else.
"So he should be very proud. He has achieved history and I am very, very happy for him."
For Antonelli, the difficulties of last year were formative, and critical in what he has been able to achieve this.
"The fact that some people said that I wasn't belonging to F1," he said, "or I wasn't ready for it - which at some point last year I probably looked like I wasn't - being able to experience those moments made me much more ready ahead of this year.
"Experiencing really low and difficult situations, high-pressure moments, really helped me to face certain situations this year and definitely they made me mature a lot as a driver, as a person.
"Still this year I've had moments where I could have done better, a lot better, so it's just a constant learning process.
"Last year being able to race straight into Mercedes, obviously straight under the spotlight, made me grow much faster than if I would have gone to a smaller team, for example."
One of those moments was this weekend.
He admitted after qualifying that he had been "tight", not driving as well as he could have, a result of the pressure of the moment.
"Austin, I was much more aggressive, much more present in the moment," said Antonelli, "while in Mexico, yesterday in qualifying, I was a bit more tense in a way because I also wasn't as intense in the way I was driving.
"So definitely, it hasn't been easy on that side. But now finally, we clinched it and now we can just enjoy the rest of the season."
The potency of the moment was clear to see after the race.
Antonelli admitted he was so emotional on the last lap as he followed Verstappen and Hamilton home that he was struggling to see.
"I lost probably two seconds because I was already crying basically and I couldn't see clearly ahead," he said. "I could see two Ferraris somehow with the tears.
"It was very special and a lot of memories went through my mind in that moment."
Then his father Marco and mother Veronica, who have been so important in his rise to F1, were there to greet him at the end.
Marco has been virtually ever-present this season, providing quiet support for his son whenever needed.
"To have my dad during the whole season was very important," said Antonelli, "because, first of all, he was the one keeping me grounded, especially after very high moments, but as well he was the one that was always there when I was facing a difficult situation or I wasn't feeling the best ahead of a session."
Then, in the champions' news conference, he became so emotional at one point as he remembered his late grandfather that he could not talk, and had to take a minute to compose himself.
"Oh my god," he said, after he had collected himself. "I cried way too much today. But it's good."

The revised Maximum Retail Price (MRP) list of anti-cancer medicines published by the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) raises serious concerns about excessive pricing and the exploitation of patients, noted medical health activists on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
Editorial | Bitter pills: on Court’s intervention, drug pricing
The NPPA, under the Department of Pharmaceuticals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, has released a list of 543 brands of anti-cancer medicines with their revised MRP that will be effective from November 9.
“The revised price list reflects the information submitted by companies up to October 27, 2026, and it will be updated as and when manufacturers submit their revised prices of non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs,” said a release issued by the Union government on Wednesday (October 28, 2026).
On October 17, the NPPA had announced Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) of 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs in public interest to address excessive trade margins, make cancer treatment more affordable, and improve access to anti-cancer medicines. Manufacturers were instructed to submit their revised list to NPPA.
The 137 non-scheduled anti-cancer drugs include immunotherapy medicines used in the treatment of over 20 types of cancer, Denosumab used by breast and prostate cancer patients, Pegfilgrastim used to prevent neutropenia in cancer patients, and Bevacizumab, which is approved for the treatment of colon, ovarian and cervical cancers.
Curbing profiteering
Stating that cost-based price control can further reduce medicine prices and curb excessive profiteering, Jan Swasthya Abhiyan India (JSA India), an organisation working for accessibility of medicines, said that controlling trade margins alone is insufficient. Life-saving cancer treatment must be affordable based on medical need, not a patient’s ability to pay.
In their statement, the group explained: “For example, the reported MRP of one brand of palbociclib fell from approximately ₹40,421 to ₹2,720 per pack, while thiotepa fell from approximately ₹80,072 to ₹7,150 per vial. Such drastic reductions raise serious questions about the pricing practices of pharmaceutical companies, including major Indian manufacturers of generic cancer medicines that have reportedly offered substantial trade margins while patients continued to face unaffordable prices.’’
It added that, several patented cancer medicines remain exorbitantly priced. The Trade Margin Rationalisation (TMR) policy has failed to ensure affordability, while excluding medicines supplied free under Patient Assistance Programmes from its calculations has further limited its potential impact on patients, said the group.
“The policy’s formula is also deeply flawed. Allowing a 42.8% markup over the Price to Stockist [PTS] legitimises excessive margins, particularly in a supply chain often involving only one or two intermediaries or direct sales to hospitals. A substantially lower markup, comparable to the 16% margin applicable to scheduled formulations under the DPCO framework, could have delivered greater benefits to patients. A one-time MRP reduction is not enough. Without permanent, enforceable margin caps, regular monitoring and verification by NPPA, excessive pricing can persist or re-emerge,” JSA stated in the release.
The NPPA must also strengthen its collection and maintenance of price data across supply chains and distribution channels, the group said, adding that companies should not be left to calculate and self-report revised MRPs without adequate independent verification.
Tanvi Singh, medical oncologist, MOC Cancer Care, said that cancer is an ailment whose treatment demands are extensive so when drug costs are high, patients may end up delaying treatment initiation, or skipping doses, or even discontinue therapy prematurely. All of these will in turn affect and compromise outcomes.
“Lowering drug costs is an imperative that can improve treatment continuity, reduce financial toxicity, and help patients complete the prescribed course of therapy. However, price caps are not enough on their own. Meaningful and sufficient improvement in affordability can be said to be achieved when price regulation is complemented by wider insurance coverage expansion of government reimbursement schemes, increased availability of quality generic and biosimilar medicines, robust Patient Assistance Programmes (PAPs), and greater access to comprehensive cancer care across the country,” said Dr. Singh.
Sandeep Nayak, chairman of oncology, MACS-Renova Oncology Institute, KIMS Hospital, Bengaluru, said: “The price control introduced by the government is a positive move. But low cost life-saving drugs should remain viable to manufacture and seller.”

22 అక్టోబర్ 2026న, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ సరిహద్దు వెంబడి పలు ప్రదేశాలలో భారత సైనికులకు చైనా బలగాలతో ఘర్షణలు జరిగాయని ఇండో-టిబెటన్ బోర్డర్ పోలీస్ (ITBP) డైరెక్టర్ జనరల్ శత్రుజీత్ కపూర్ అంగీకరించారు. చైనా సైనికులు నిర్ధారిత గస్తీ పద్ధతులను పాటించనప్పుడు వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LAC) వెంబడి పరిస్థితి “అస్తవ్యస్తంగా” మారుతుందని విదేశీ వ్యవహారాల మంత్రిత్వ శాఖ (MEA) ప్రతినిధి రణధీర్ జైస్వాల్ మరుసటిరోజు పేర్కొన్నారు.
ఈ నేపథ్యంలో భారత్, చైనా సైనికుల మధ్య ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలంటూ కొన్ని వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉన్నాయి. వీటిలో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: అక్టోబర్ 2026లో అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్ సరిహద్దు (LAC) వద్ద భారత, చైనా సైనికుల మధ్య జరిగిన ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వైరల్ వీడియోలన్నీ పాతవి లేదా అక్టోబర్ 2026 నాటి ఘర్షణలకు సంబంధం లేనివి. ఇవి 2021, 2024, 2025 సంవత్సరాలకు చెందిన పాత ఘటనలు, జూలై 2026 నాటి అమర్నాథ్ యాత్రకు సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు. కావున, ఈ వీడియోలు తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉన్నాయి.
వీడియో 1
ఈ వీడియో కనీసం డిసెంబర్ 2022 నుండే ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అంటే, ఈ వీడియో అక్టోబర్ 2026లో రిపోర్ట్ చేయబడిన భారత్-చైనా సరిహద్దు ఉద్రిక్తతల కంటే ముందే ఉందని, తాజా పరిణామాలతో దీనికి సంబంధం లేదని స్పష్టమవుతుంది. డిసెంబర్ 2022లో ప్రచురితమైన ఒక CNN కథనంలో, ఇదే దృశ్యాలను చూపిస్తూ, ఈ వీడియో సెప్టెంబర్ 2021లో చిత్రీకరించినట్లు పేర్కొన్నారు. ఈ వీడియో వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ సమీపంలో అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లో చిత్రీకరించినట్లుగా భారతీయ సైనకాధికారి ధృవీకరించారని ఈ కథనం పేర్కొంది.
వీడియో 2
వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలు రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇదే వీడియో కనీసం నవంబర్ 2024 (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లోకి చొరబడటానికి ప్రయత్నిస్తున్న చైనా సైనికులను భారత సైనికులు అడ్డుకుని దాడి చెయ్యడం ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుందని ఆ పోస్టులు పేర్కొన్నాయి. ఇండియన్ ఆర్మీ ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ విభాగం కూడా ఈ వీడియోను ఖండిస్తూ ‘X’లో చేసిన పోస్ట్ చేసింది.
వీడియో 3
ఈ వీడియోకి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు కనీసం జూలై 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, అమర్నాథ్ యాత్ర 2026 సందర్భంగా, జమ్మూ & కాశ్మీర్లోని బాల్తాల్ వద్ద ప్రవేశ ద్వారం దగ్గర యాత్రికులు నమోదు చేసుకోవడానికి, RFID కార్డులను పొందడానికి గుమిగూడిన దృశ్యాలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతుంది. ఇండియన్ ఆర్మీ ఫ్యాక్ట్-చెక్ విభాగం కూడా ఈ వీడియోను ఖండిస్తూ ‘X’లో చేసిన పోస్ట్ చేసింది.
వీడియో 4
మా దర్యాప్తులో డిసెంబర్ 2025 నాటి అవే దృశ్యాలతో కూడిన అనేక సోషల్ మీడియా పోస్టులను (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) గుర్తించాం. ఈ పోస్టుల ప్రకారం, ఆరోగ్య సమస్యలతో బాధపడుతున్న ఒక భారతీయ సైనికుడు వాస్తవ నియంత్రణ రేఖ (LAC) సమీపంలో విధి నిర్వహణలో ఉండగా స్పృహ కోల్పోయాడు. మీడియా కథనాల ప్రకారం, చైనా పీపుల్స్ లిబరేషన్ ఆర్మీ (PLA) సిబ్బంది అతనికి ప్రథమ చికిత్స, వైద్య సహాయం అందించిన తర్వాత, అతని సొంత యూనిట్కు అప్పగించారు.
చివరిగా, అరుణాచల్ ప్రదేశ్లో 2026 అక్టోబర్లో జరిగిన భారత-చైనా ఘర్షణల దృశ్యాలంటూ సంబంధంలేని పాత వీడియోలను షేర్ చేస్తున్నారు.

My Journey to the Center of America's Political Spam Text Hell
I've gotten nearly 2,000 campaign fundraising texts that were meant for someone else. I tried to find out why—and uncovered a labyrinth of politicians, data brokers, and shady tactics.
Just as my kid is nodding off for the night, it arrives: a ding. It’s Nancy Pelosi, texting to tell me that if I don’t donate $5 immediately, American democracy will basically collapse. A few minutes later, it’s Cory Booker, with an urgent request. Don’t even get me started on James Talarico.
Sometimes I’m driving, or making dinner, or trying to focus on my work, and another three messages arrive. Barack Obama NEEDS me. There’s a critical deadline approaching. A generous donor has offered an 800 percent match. Everything is at stake.
As I was writing that last paragraph, I got a message from Angus, a cat belonging to Sam Forstag, a Democratic congressional candidate in Montana. Angus needed me to know that Sam was out there working to flip Montana’s First Congressional District, taking on his Republican opponent and the wealthy special interests backing him.
I’m not sure what Angus expected me to do about it.
Political fundraising texts are a fact of American life. They’re intrusive, melodramatic, and relentless.
This year alone, I’ve received 725.
In the first 20 days of October, more than 190 arrived—nearly 10 a day.
On October 14, I got 21.
The strangest part is that most of these messages aren’t meant for me.
They’re meant for a family member who I’ll call John, for privacy reasons. John lives in California and has made small donations to Democrats. I live in New York and have made no political donations at all. We have different names, phone numbers, and bank accounts—a distinction that has apparently proven difficult for a substantial portion of the American political fundraising industry.
For years, I diligently opted out. I’ve replied “STOP” 49 times since 2021, by my phone’s count. Sometimes “Stop2End,” when that was the magic word. In November 2025, I told Jon Ossoff’s campaign some version of “stop.” It did not stop. Since then, I’ve received 13 more texts boosting his campaign, from nine different numbers.
When the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee texted to inform me that Bill Clinton, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden were calling me personally to action, I replied “eat shit.” That didn’t work either.
Exhausted, I decided this month to figure out what the hell was going on. Why did so many campaigns have my number? Why did they think it belonged to someone else? And why wouldn’t they fucking stop?
For starters, I downloaded my Messages history and pulled out the political texts I’ve received in recent years. Since March 2022, I’ve gotten 1,735, from 812 different phone numbers. By any measure, this is simply too many texts—nearly none of which were meant for me.
James Carville had written 27 times, soliciting money for at least a dozen political organizations. Ken Burns wanted help electing Jacky Rosen, then Roy Cooper, then Sherrod Brown. On April 2, 2025, the day after Cory Booker finished his 25-hour Senate floor speech, I received the same first-person appeal from “Cory” three times in less than two hours, sent by three different fundraising operations.
The thing is that John—the person these campaigns had me confused with—isn’t a particularly big donor. Federal Election Commission records show roughly 160 contributions since 2017, totaling about $1,700. The median gift was $6. This year, John donated six times, for a total of $51.
In the same period, my phone received 725 fundraising texts literally begging for his money.
The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee alone sent 60 of them—22 in the first 20 days of October—from 28 different numbers. My relative had given it $5, once, in 2020. The DCCC sent another 41 messages; it had received $8. House Majority PAC, which has never received a dime from John that I could find, kept offering to multiply contributions by as much as 900 percent.
I understand the logic of these messages on some level. They are cheap, and the strategy isn’t all that different from how a lot of scams work—spray out messages and pray someone will bite. You don’t need many people to respond for it to pay off. What I couldn’t understand, though, was how I’d gotten wrapped up in all of this. I didn’t have to look far for the answer.
Almost every text contained a link that, after a few redirects, led to ActBlue, the platform Democrats use to process donations. Helpfully, many of those links carried tracking codes—strings of letters and numbers identifying the fundraising appeal, the message being sent, and sometimes where the campaign got the recipient’s contact information.
An October DCCC link, for instance, contained acq_sms.p2p_fr_2026.10.13_b1_dccc_rent_4mtch_st. Squint a little and you can make out abbreviations for acquisition (“acq”), peer-to-peer fundraising (“p2p_fr”), and a rented list (“dccc_rent”). But one word kept appearing in these strings across messages from otherwise unrelated campaigns: Sterling.
Sterling Data Company is a relatively small firm that uses AI to help Democrats find people likely to give them money. In 2022, Forbes reported that Sterling had assembled a database of roughly 30 million political donors, with hundreds of details about some of them, including what cars they drove and what they watched on Netflix. Sterling says it uses that information to predict who might donate to a particular candidate.
Sterling appears to get much of its information from other data brokers, combining details about people’s age, location, politics, and donation histories into voter profiles that campaigns can buy or rent.
Of the 725 texts I’d received this year, nearly half contained tracking codes that appeared to reference Sterling. They came from dozens of PACs and campaigns, including the DCCC, DSCC, James Talarico, and Mark Kelly.
FEC records show that a Biden joint fundraising committee paid Sterling about $1.87 million for donor lists over four months beginning in November 2023. Around the same time, a text from the committee reached my phone with a code containing strl2b.
The DSCC’s first reported payment to Sterling came on November 22, 2023—the very day I received one of its texts tagged STL2. According to FEC data, the committee has continued paying Sterling, including roughly $250,000 this summer, which preceded another wave of Sterling-tagged texts.
Those recent texts all appeared to link back to a common platform. Dozens of campaigns had their own web addresses, but I could see that they used nearly identical software and tracking codes, often ending in tier1. Sterling’s own website advertises something it calls “Tier 1 contact data intelligence,” though I couldn’t establish whether the two were connected or who ran the system. Still, the breadcrumbs were leading me to suspect that, at some point, a Sterling database mixup had lumped John together with my phone number.
“High-frequency solicitation is a necessary evil,” Martin Kurucz, Sterling’s CEO, tells me when I ask about all of this. “Few people give, so every campaign chases the same donors, and texting at scale works too well to skip.”
Kurucz declined to discuss Sterling’s proprietary data but confirmed that the company handles the texting itself and can rent the same record to multiple campaigns. Sterling limits how often individuals can be contacted, he said, though he didn’t specify what those limits are.
“No contact database is perfect,” Kurucz says. Even matches made with moderate confidence are generally accurate enough to be worth using, he says. Wrong numbers tend to drop out of circulation because the recipients don’t engage.
Kurucz wouldn’t confirm that Sterling has caused the deluge of misdirected text messages my way, but he also didn’t deny it. Instead he offered some advice for making them stop: Don’t respond at all.
I found that there’s another way out: lawsuits. At least two people have successfully gotten a settlement out of Democratic organizations over apparently misdirected campaign texts, which presumably included never being contacted again.
That seems like a lot of work, though. Meanwhile neither of those lawsuits established how the wrong names got attached to their numbers. I still don’t know for sure how mine got mixed up with John’s. But the outcome is the same: The DSCC now texts me more often than my mother. Replying “eat shit” another hundred times won’t change that.

From Chelsea reject to Watkins 'upgrade' - Jackson makes fast Villa start
- Published
Nicolas Jackson's double to defeat Manchester City on Saturday capped an excellent start to the striker's spell at Aston Villa.
Signed from Chelsea as a direct replacement for Ollie Watkins - Villa's main source of goals for the previous six seasons - it was imperative the 25-year-old Senegal international hit the ground running in claret and blue.
Jackson has done just that, scoring seven goals in his first 11 appearances for Villa - six in the last six - and helping his new side to a 100% start in the Champions League and spearheading their recovery after a slow start to the Premier League campaign.
"The players, the manager, the team - everything is incredible," Jackson told BBC Match of the Day.
"I'm very happy that I'm here and hopefully we can do amazing things together."
Improved form at Villa Park
Jackson spent two full seasons at Chelsea after joining in 2023 and had a year on loan at German giants Bayern Munich before moving to Villa in the summer for a deal worth up to £65m.
There is a much smaller sample size from his time at Villa Park compared with his spell at Stamford Bridge, but on several metrics, he is showing signs of improvement.
Jackson scored 24 goals in 65 Premier League appearances for Chelsea, netting every 210 minutes on average, with a shot conversion rate of 15%.
That compares with four in seven games for Villa, averaging a goal every 138 minutes with a shot conversion rate of 21%.
One of the criticisms of Jackson at Chelsea was he had lots of chances and did not convert as many of them as he should.
In his early weeks at Villa, he is outperforming his expected goals tally by exactly two.
Both of their shots on target against City came from Jackson's right foot - and both ended up in the net.
'He looks like a really good piece of business' - Keown
England international Watkins scored 91 Premier League goals in 221 league appearances for Villa before moving to Saudi Arabia club Al-Hilal in August.
He was a consistent scorer, never failing to reach double figures for Premier League goals during each of his six seasons with the club.
The respective statistics of Jackson and Watkins from last season suggest Jackson is more involved in general play than the England forward, while also being involved in more chances.
If Jackson's current run of form continues, his fee may prove to be a bargain.
Former Villa and England defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport: "I've liked him all season. I think he's key to Villa's success.
"I think he's an upgrade on Ollie Watkins, I really do.
"Ollie was magnificent for them, but this guy is more of a predator [in and around the penalty area]. Pace will always trouble top defenders and he's got it in abundance.
"I think having worked with the manager before at Villarreal, he's sort of fast-tracking his quick development.
"He looks like a really good piece of business right now. The team suffered and you need a striker who can give you belief you can win games when suffering and this guy is a special talent.
"With a talent like that you can go a long way."
'So many players improve and thrive' under Emery
Saturday's win was achieved on the fourth anniversary of Emery's appointment as Villa boss.
Under the Spaniard, they have become fixtures in the upper echelons of the Premier League, regulars in European competition and ended a 30-year wait for a major trophy by winning the Europa League.
Results are one thing, but there are also numerous examples of players who have been rejuvenated or scaled new heights in their careers under Emery's management at Villa Park.
Former Scotland defender Rachel Corsie, who had a spell playing in the Women's Super League for Aston Villa late in her career, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Emery is quite unique. A lot of coaches will focus on the tactical detail, but he's so intense with it.
"I remember from when I was here that his car is always at the training ground. I know people will say that's a natural thing and the life of a manager, but I would say it's an incredible amount of time.
"He loves to get the detail right. He never gets tired of trying to better people individually and that takes an incredible amount of work. So many players come here, improve and thrive."
Jackson has prior experience of playing under Emery, having been coached by him at Villarreal, where he spent three years before Chelsea signed him for £35m.
Emery told BBC Match of the Day: "I knew him at Villarreal and he started playing the level he is now. I know his capacity to exploit his qualities and I know, as well, his humility.
"The mentality is coming through - how focused he is in life and professional career."
Speaking to TNT Sports, Jackson added: "It's not easy [to settle at a new club] but easier because of the coach and the players.
"It's an incredible dressing room with an incredible manager. I'm very happy to be here and hopefully I will score many goals."

The 57th episode of Health Wrap by The Hindu explores how researchers are using advanced imaging and reconstruction techniques to create detailed, three-dimensional maps of the human brain.
Zubeda Hamid, senior assistant editor, The Hindu, speaks to Mohanasankar Sivaprakasam, Head of the Sudha Gopalakrishnan Brain Centre at IIT Madras, about the technology, how the maps are created and what they could reveal about the human brain.
The episode looks at C-STROKE, a recently released three-dimensional atlas of a stroke-affected brain. Unlike conventional MRI scans, which provide images of the brain at a particular resolution, the new approach allows researchers to examine brain structures in greater detail and build comprehensive 3D maps.
The discussion explains how researchers prepare brain tissue, use imaging techniques and reconstruct the data to create these maps. It also looks at the different scientific and technological disciplines involved in the process and how detailed mapping could help researchers study the brain’s structure and changes associated with neurological conditions.
Another focus is the Centre’s plan to map more than 100 human brains across different stages of life. The project aims to build a larger collection of brain maps that could help researchers understand variations in brain structure, study neurological conditions and expand the available resources for brain research.
The episode also examines the potential applications of these atlases in clinical research and healthcare, including how they could contribute to a better understanding of stroke and other brain conditions. It discusses the possibilities as well as the work needed before such maps can be translated into clinical applications.
The episode can also be viewed on The Hindu health page along with the full playlist of The Health Wrap

After months of anticipation, the Food and Drug Administration gave tentative approval to Dr. Reddy’s Laboratories to make a generic version of a groundbreaking HIV prevention medicine, a key step in widening access for dozens of low- and middle-income countries.
The company, one of the world’s largest generic drugmakers, plans to start shipping the medicine next month as part of an effort propelled, in part, by several global health organizations to ensure the drug becomes available in lower-income countries as quickly as possible. The annual cost per person will be $40, comparable to daily tablets.
Known as lenacapavir, the injectable drug is widely seen as a game-changing tool for eradicating HIV because it offers virtually complete protection against contracting the virus with just one administration every six months. The brand-name version, which is known as Yetzugo in the U.S., is marketed by Gilead Sciences and was approved by the FDA last year.

Roli, the company behind expressive, touch-sensitive music devices like the Seaboard and Roli Blocks, has collapsed.
Although it hasn't been officially announced, Roli reportedly ousted its CEO and founder, Roland Lamb, earlier this year. Since then, Roli has all but dissolved. (In August, a new company called Instrumental Intelligence was registered with the UK government under Lamb's name, a potential move by the founder to acquire Roli's assets).
On Monday, Roli emailed users that two licensed insolvency practitioners were appointed joint administrators of Roli on October 20. The company went into administration, the UK process that manages corporate insolvency. This is the second time Roli has gone bankrupt.
That has left a small but bereft community of customers with no word on getting the products they paid for. The Roli community has expressed sadness, anger, or outright confusion. In Facebook groups, the r/Roli subreddit, and other forums, dismayed users have struggled to find recourse for Roli equipment purchases ranging from hundreds to thousands of dollars. The Roli subreddit has been awash with posts from customers who say they paid for orders months or years ago and have received no response or refund since then.
Existing owners also worry about the long-term impact. Roli instruments rely heavily on proprietary software launchers and companion apps to connect, map sounds, and configure settings. While the hardware still functions, users fear that lack of software support will eventually leave their gear bricked.
Roli has not publicly communicated about its future strategy with customers. The company did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment; Lamb did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Roli’s primary financial backers, investment firms TriplePoint Capital and Hoxton Ventures, also did not respond.
A Change of Seasons
Roli has faced financial struggles before.
The company started in 2009 but really took off after musician Pharrell Williams invested in 2017 and Sony’s Innovation Fund in 2018. Musicians like Dream Theater keyboardist Jordan Rudess supported and touted Roli’s gadgets. Ryan Gosling’s character played a Seaboard Grand in the 2016 movie La La Land. In the late 2010s, the tech and the company were hailed as a hit.
That tune changed in 2020. The British government’s Future Fund—a taxpayer-funded relief package issued to help businesses during the pandemic—partially bailed out Roli from a Covid-19-induced financial crisis. Even then, Roli went into administration for the first time in 2021. It survived by relaunching as Luminary Roli and focusing on music-learning devices like the light-up Lumi keyboard and the Airwave, a digital theremin that doubled as an AI piano teacher.
Through all of that, customers have had issues with how the company communicates. Users who ordered the Lumi keyboard found orders unexpectedly delayed, with no indication from the company on what was happening.
“One of the problems they have had ever since I started with the Kickstarter is communication and explaining things—telling people what's going on,” Lluís Gerard, a YouTuber who has reviewed Roli products for years under the handle WasabiNoise, tells WIRED. “There's always been too much secrecy about things, or then you'd realize, oh, there are these delays.”
Pull Me Under
Former Roli employees—who spoke with WIRED but asked not to be named to avoid jeopardizing future employment opportunities—alleged a company culture that revolved around Lamb’s whims. Every person we spoke with who worked with Lamb compared him to a Steve Jobs-esque character. One person described the experience of being at Roli as being in a movie, where Lamb saw himself as the main character and everyone else as extras or set pieces.
“I love the company, love the culture, love the people—I didn’t love working for him,” the employee said. “Everyone has their story with him. You're buckled into his car—and he’s not going in the right direction.”
In 2021, another former Roli employee, who also asked not to be identified, uploaded files on GitHub that include various notes chronicling Roli as a hostile workplace. One 16-page PDF is titled “Keeping Roland Happy” and includes multiple sections about how to handle interacting with a pathological narcissist. Several former employees independently described what they viewed as Lamb’s narcissistic behavior, describing him as an arrogant visionary.
“Roland is the archetype of a pathological narcissist,” one employee told WIRED. “Unfortunately, that's what he became. Incredibly brittle when challenged, absolutely shameless, quite reckless, incapable of learning or growth, would rather gamble than take any lessons from the previous experience. It was very disheartening to see.”
“The tragedy here is that it was always fundamentally a great company,” another former employee says. “A lot of what made it great was the sort of all-powerful vision of the founder. But that was so obviously the critical flaw.”
Begin Again
Along with other touch-sensitive devices like the Linnstrument and the Sensel Morph, Roli was a key company in the rise of MIDI polyphonic expression (MPE) devices. MPE technology lets players control a note’s pitch and timbre through touch-based movement. Pressing or sliding fingers over the device’s surface produces varying MIDI notes that capture more expressive playing.
While inventive, Roli’s instruments were altogether very niche—a hard product category to build an Apple-sized audience around. Roli certainly tried, partnering with Apple to sell its Roli Blocks in Apple Stores. Alas, the pandemic caused dire supply chain issues, and the company couldn’t keep up with orders. After the pandemic, bankruptcy, and the rebrand, little remained to push the company forward except the founder's will.
“This was one of the leading lights of music technology in the world,” one former employee said. “It was truly an inventing company—the stuff it made had never been made before. So it's a real shame.”
The response to Roli’s collapse hasn’t been pure dismay. After months of delays and frustration, Reddit users have gathered to mourn the company—and to make sure its devices keep working.
Sam Hocking, a UK audio engineer who runs an audio tools company called Demix.me, also owns multiple Roli Seaboard Blocks. Even before Roli went into administration, Hocking had been building software that could keep the equipment working as a capable MIDI device. He shared his vibe-coded configuration tools in the Roli subreddit and on GitHub, so Roli’s Grand, Rise, Airwave, and Block devices can work without the Roli launcher.
Hocking says his Seaboards are nearly 10 years old and still working. Despite the company’s rocky history and poor communication, he still wants to keep his devices. They’re high quality, cost a good chunk of money, and feel somewhat irreplaceable.
He’s not alone. Other users on the subreddit have joined in, adding their own tweaks and fixes to the software that may keep at least a few of these devices alive.
“They're quite a unique product; there's not another keyboard type out there,” Hocking says. “Nobody likes to spend money and then not be able to use it.”

A review of 578 patients who presented with breast-related concerns at the Head & Neck Cancer Institute of India (HNCII), Mumbai, over more than three years found that 82.5% had cancerous conditions and 17.5% had non-cancerous conditions. The diagnoses were confirmed through tissue examination.
The findings reveal patients assessed at the institute and cannot be generalised to the wider population or used to estimate the likelihood that a breast lump is cancerous.
Patients diagnosed with breast cancer ranged in age from 23 to 98 years, with an average age of 52.7 years. Tumour sizes varied, with 35.2% measuring up to 2 cm, 43.3% measuring between 2 and 4.9 cm, and 19.3% measuring more than 5 cm.
The institute also reported that 52% of patients had more than four lymph nodes positive for cancer. Lymph node involvement is one of the factors doctors consider when assessing the extent of breast cancer and planning treatment.
Mastectomy, which involves removing the breast, was the most common surgery recorded.
Recognising unusual breast changes and seeking medical advice can help establish a diagnosis and guide appropriate care. Not every lump requires cancer treatment, but changes should be assessed .

How one family gave a critical boost to gene therapy research
A family's fundraising for gene therapy research pays off
For stories on the science of healthy living, subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
When Eliza O'Neill was little, she was one of those kids who always needed to have an accessory, like a hat or a scarf.
"She would always go get my high heels from the closet and clop around in those — which she scared us to death," says her mom, Cara O'Neill, a pediatrician in Columbia, S.C.
But by the time Eliza turned 3, her parents noticed she was falling behind on developmental milestones. She was diagnosed with a pragmatic speech delay, meaning she had learned a lot of words, for example, but she wasn't using them in a typical way in social situations.
In 2013, one of Cara's colleagues suggested testing Eliza for a group of metabolic disorders — just to rule them out.
But the test came back positive for something called Sanfilippo syndrome.
Cara remembered learning about the rare inherited disease back in medical school.
"When they said the word, it all kind of came rushing back," she says. "And it was just this bale of dread, like, oh, my goodness, this is horrific."
Children with Sanfilippo have a faulty gene that leaves them unable to break down heparin sulfate, a molecule critical to normal cell function. As it builds up in the body, it causes severe complications.
Kids with Sanfilippo lose their ability to speak and walk. They have seizures, and they usually don't live past their teens, according to the Cure Sanfilippo Foundation, which the O'Neills started and continue to run.
For Eliza's dad, Glenn O'Neill, it took a little while after learning Eliza's test results for the diagnosis to sink in.
"It wasn't really until I got home that I realized how quickly the degeneration happened," he says. "And that was really the point where we said, 'Gosh. Whatever we need to do, we need to do it now.'"
Researching a treatment
At Nationwide Children's Hospital in Columbus, Ohio, researcher Haiyan Fu had been working on a gene therapy in mice for Sanfilippo since the late-1990s.
The therapy used a modified virus to deliver a working copy of the broken gene to patients' cells.
Fu realized the experimental therapy was promising. "And if we treat early, it could be potentially a cure," she says. "So I can't give up."
Keeping it going – and funded – was challenging, though. She thought she would have to quit in 2009. But the families of kids with Sanfilippo stopped her.
"They said, 'You can't leave. Can we give you some of the funds for you to, you know, carry on?'" Fu recalls, explaining that these families had helped her from the beginning and didn't want to see her work stop.
In all, eight patient foundations, including Ben's Dream and a Cure for Kirby, kept Fu's work going until the research was ready for the first human trial.
Raising the money
But a clinical trial would be expensive. Glenn O'Neill had an idea for how to raise the money.
"We reached out on a whim to some strangers that we found on the internet about making a viral video," he says, referring to filmmaker Benjamin Von Wong, who made them a video over a few days in 2014.
It worked.
In the spring of 2014, the Saving Eliza video helped the O'Neills break GoFundMe's record at the time, raising a million dollars in just a few weeks. Soon, it hit $2 million.
The money raised helped fund the first human trial, which started in May 2016.
The experiments were promising enough for the biotech industry to take notice.
Ultimately, a biotech company called Ultragenyx acquired the rights to the gene therapy in 2022 and kept studying it. A few years later, the company submitted data to the Food and Drug Administration for review.
The FDA approved the gene therapy in September. The one-time infusion is called Fayuvi.
"The treatment will work best the younger the child is because the more brain is remaining," says Ultragenyx CEO Emil Kakkis. "By the time they're 2 or 3 or 4 years old diagnosed, getting figured out, they've lost a lot of ground. And we have treated a few kids that were in the 6-month age that have done really well. And our view is that when you treat them really young, you actually get better gene therapy results."
Ultragenyx set the price for the treatment at nearly $4 million, tying it for the second most expensive gene therapy ever, according to 46brooklyn, a drug price research firm.
Kakkis says Ultragenyx is committed to making sure every patient is treated, regardless of the price. "There should be no logistical location, site or state or other kind of rule that stops us from getting the patient treated. We understand what [we've] got to do."
Moments after the FDA approval was announced, Fu got a call from Cara O'Neill — and messages from other families that funded her research. Some had lost a child along the way.
Fu says Fayuvi's approval is good news, but it brings mixed emotions for her: "It shouldn't take this long."
As for Eliza, she's almost 17 now. She was the very first patient to get the gene therapy as part of a clinical trial back in 2016.
Because she was 6 years old when she was treated with the gene therapy, she had already lost her ability to speak. It never returned, but she can communicate with picture cards and devices. Eliza goes to school. And this summer, she swam and learned to float on a pool noodle.
"I just feel proud of my girl. You know?" Glenn O'Neill says. "I feel proud of her. It's been a rough road for her, but we also know she's very lucky."

Cryptocurrency exchange Binance says it has replaced 90% of the amount stolen after a record $6.3bn hack of its platform by a group the FBI identified as being backed by North Korea.
The remaining 10% of tokens are less liquid, meaning they may take longer to buy, the company said in a post on X on Saturday. Co-CEO Richard Teng said separately that the company was “committed to covering the remaining 10%” and that “users will not bear the financial impact of this incident”.
Binance suspended user withdrawals after the hack, but said in its latest update that it was on track to resume them on Sunday.
The announcement came as the FBI on Saturday confirmed earlier suspicions from private investigators and analysts that a North Korea-affiliated group called TraderTraitor was behind the hack.
TraderTraitor is believed to be part of the Lazarus Group, which gained notoriety in 2014 when it was accused of hacking into Sony Pictures as revenge for The Interview, a film that mocked North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.
“The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026,” the law enforcement agency said in a statement.
The FBI added that it had observed “TraderTraitor actors” converting stolen assets into Ethereum, and expected those assets to be laundered further by converting them using decentralised finance and instant swap services.
It said it was urging private sector entities “to block transactions with or derived from addresses TraderTraitor actors are using to launder these stolen assets”.
Teng said on Friday that the breach was a “complex attack” involving a compromised laptop and malicious software designed to delete evidence of its activity, making it harder to trace and investigate.
Binance said it had set aside around $6.34bn of company funds to cover the losses.
“Our commitment remains the same: Binance will fully cover the financial impact of the funds stolen in this incident,” the company said.
The money spent re-buying tokens came from using part of its $1bn Secure Asset Fund for Users, a bitcoin reserve it holds to protect customers in the event of security breaches, as well as some of its Futures Insurance Fund, and the company’s own corporate treasury, it said on X.
The attack on Binance came as many observers express worries that the ever-expanding capabilities of artificial intelligence models could compromise cryptography and IT security protocols.
Bitcoin plunged nearly 5% after the news of the hack, while Ethereum dropped nearly 6% and BNB, native to Binance, tumbled nearly 10%.
The sheer scale of the hack has put a spotlight on the capacity of North Korea – which faces extensive international sanctions over its nuclear and missile programmes – to find illicit means to capture revenue.

Walt Disney Co. is moving toward thousands of job cuts, with the entertainment giant asking some managers to target 20% in annual cost savings, according to people familiar with the matter.
The savings could come from job eliminations as well as from expense reductions, said the people, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private.
Some of Disney’s operations, which range from theme parks, TV network and the movie studio, will be affected disproportionately. Chief Executive Officer Josh D’Amaro aims to reinvest a portion of the savings into film and TV programming, technology and the theme parks and cruise ship businesses, the people said.
The company has promised double-digit growth in adjusted earnings per share in the current fiscal year.
A representative for Disney declined to comment.
Disney has cut billions of dollars worth of costs and eliminated thousands of positions in recent years, with reductions impacting every division including ABC, Pixar, ESPN, the film studio and the experiences unit. The company had 231,000 people worldwide at the end of the last fiscal year.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 1 that Disney was planning a restructuring of its TV division as well as cuts at the company’s legal and global affairs unit.
Other entertainment companies including Netflix, Sony Pictures Entertainment and Skydance’s Paramount and Warner Bros. divisions have also cut jobs as revenue from traditional television declines and streaming subscriber growth slows. They also have to cope with more viewers turning to social media, online videos and streaming services backed by tech giants like Amazon.com and Apple.
At the Bloomberg Screentime conference in Los Angeles last month, Disney President Dana Walden said that “there is a need to constantly evaluate how you’re structured and how big is the organization. Technology set their sights on our business, and we must survive and thrive and grow, and that’s what we’re going to do.”
