Why it's important to never plug power strips into each other
Your power strip needs a wall outlet and not another power strip.
There are so many work-from-home devices nowadays that running a home office or a gaming area easily turns into a charging and power-consumption nightmare of tangled cords, ports and outlets. The idea of stringing power strips together by plugging one into the other (daisy-chaining) is a convenient, understandable solution. More outlets and ports mean more organization and power for each device. Unfortunately, it's not the greatest of ideas, especially if tripped breakers and house fires aren't on your to-do list.
The first problem is that adding sockets doesn't increase electrical capacity. Everything connected to the second strip draws electricity through the first strip's plug and internal components. The first strip is now carrying the combined load of the devices plugged into the second strip. The second problem is each strip's maximum rating, typically expressed in amps. If a second power strip is plugged into the first and the first is maxed out, the second strip could be the straw that breaks the proverbial camel's back, drawing too much and overheating the first strip.
Pushing too much current through the internal wiring and components of the first power strip generates "resistive heating." Given enough time, it can melt the casing and wire insulation, possibly igniting nearby materials. In the aforementioned home office scenario, flammable materials are abundantly present in most cases.
What to do when one power strip is no longer enough?
What to do when one power strip isn't enough depends on what you need. Do you need more sockets? Ports? More reach or more electrical capacity? Where low-power electronics are concerned, a single power strip that's more generous with its number of outlets is your best bet. Just make sure that the total load remains within the power strip's rating. A strip with 8 outlets doesn't necessarily supply more power than a strip with only 4 outlets. It's a separate consideration you have to be wary of.
If distance is the issue, find a strip with a longer cord. Don't reach for an extension cord as a matter of convenience. NFPA explicitly advises folks to avoid that arrangement, since extension cords have their own ratings and too many devices plugged in at once can exceed those ratings. Of course, you can do the math based on the cord's rating, the strip and everything plugged into it, but most people aren't aware of the limitations.
If a single strip is tripping the breaker, adding a new one and dispersing the devices won't solve the problem. In fact, treat it as a warning that requires your immediate attention. Never use a strip with damaged casings, scorch marks or loose connections. It's not something you can wrap in half a roll of electrical tape and call it a day.
What should you never plug into a power strip?
As it happens, plugging a power strip into a power strip isn't the only thing you should avoid. High-power appliances can easily overload a power strip if it's not rated to handle it. Space heaters are a common one in this regard. They draw a fairly substantial amount of current and should only be plugged into a proper wall outlet. Microwaves and refrigerators are other prime examples.
For the safest route, use ordinary power strips with ordinary devices like PCs and printers, or to charge your phone. Also, six outlets doesn't mean it needs six devices plugged into it at once. Check the devices and match them against the power strip's ratings. They may seem like it, but power strips are not all-purpose devices for whatever needs power at the moment.
Lastly, a surge protector doesn't change the dynamics here. Surge protection deals with sudden voltage spikes but, like power strips, it won't magically conjure more energy capacity. Basic safety guidance for surge protectors also advises against daisy-chaining. The potential consequences warrant a repeat: check the surge protector's or power strip's rating and what you're plugging into it. If it's not enough, simply use another outlet or purchase a separate power strip and use another wall socket to run it.

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.
“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.
Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.
The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.
“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”
According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.
Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.
Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.
“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.
That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.
“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.
The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.
I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.
The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.
R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.
After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.
Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)
“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”
But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.
“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”
With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.
During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.
Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.
“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.
R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.
Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)
R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.
“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.
Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.
It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.
“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”
Count it
A number worth knowing

Vibe check
Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.
“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.
The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.

Canada and Europe have announced a new alliance of like-minded nations to serve as both a “protective canopy under which our citizens can thrive” and a powerful hedge against the unpredictable nature of geopolitics, while welcoming other countries to join.
Speaking to reporters on Friday from Montreal, the prime minister, Mark Carney, and the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, called the new partnership the Alliance for the Future and said the “deepest possible partnership between Canada and the 27-member bloc had the potential to offer unprecedented stability and opportunity”.
“Our societies have been shaken by new storms,” Carney told reporters, referring to the damaging effects of the climate emergency but also the “erosion of democratic norms” and “the weaponization of trade”.
As they concluded their two-day summit, Canada agreed to contribute to a €90bn support loan for Ukraine. Leaders also said future discussions would lead to a more integrated market worth tens of billions of dollars, reduced trade and travel restrictions, and new educational opportunities for both sides.
While a trade war between Canada and the United States has seen Carney go hunting for new geopolitical partners, an over-reliance on American companies – especially for defence – has also given Canada pause.
Last week, Elon Musk throttled the speeds of Starlink and Starshield over Ukraine in mid-October, severely disrupting Ukrainian military and defense operations.
Carney has repeatedly raised the concern that Canada’s defense technologies could be at the whim of political actors or companies with opposing interests. Musk, a dual Canadian citizen, is a critic of Canada’s governing Liberal party and has advocated for provinces to separate.
Carney pointed to a planned merger between the Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere Inc and Germany’s Aleph Alpha GmbH as a step to lessening reliance on American AI giants. The tie-up will see the newly formed company have dual headquarters in Berlin and Toronto, and Canada’s federal government has announced a stake in Cohere worth up to C$1.6bn.
“We are not waiting for the future of AI to be decided somewhere else by those we don’t know, or by whom we don’t trust,” Carney said on Thursday.
Brussels and Ottawa also announced an agreement on Friday that would bringing Canada into Europe’s supercomputing network, giving Canadian access to European machines to train AI models.
In addition to lofty promises of helping to reshape the global order, or giving safe harbour to like-minded nations looking to weather uncertainty, Canadian and EU leaders also pitched their new, deeper relationship as one that addressed key sources of anxiety for residents, including the cost of living.
“When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, it’s the families that pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car,” Von der Leyen said, noting that previously trusted trusted suppliers of energy, critical minerals or semiconductors “are increasingly turned into instruments of pressure”.
“More competition, more choice,” Carney said earlier in the day, suggesting the alliance could find ways to build certainty around supply chains and “withstand shocks, together”.
The leaders once again brought up the prospect of Canada becoming an associate member. The designation is uncharted territory, said Von der Leyen, who added: “We have the ambition, trust, and creativity to shape it together.
“This [associate membership] is a partnership not against anyone else, but for our common strength.”
While the leaders committed to the idea of associate membership, they said a clearer scope of the role would come at a 2027 summit. Some EU members had bristled at the idea of Canada being given a legally meaningless designation that they fear confuses other nations looking for membership. Germany and other states had worked behind the scenes to remove the phrase from a draft of the summit statement. But Von der Leyen, who first floated the term, and Carney both again referred to “associate membership” at the summit.
European Council president Antonio Costa, meanwhile, said earlier that Canada was “by far the most European of the non-European countries”, a sentiment that reflected a belief that despite geography, there was a collective sense of shared values.
Costa said the two sides would pursue “the most closer, the most deepest, the most stronger association ever between European Union and a non-European country”.
Still, the mere fact of the summit has caused friction in the province of Quebec, where the separatist Parti Québécois was recently elected to a minority government. The premier, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, skipped the event after Ottawa’s refusal to let him speak publicly at it.
“The federal government would have us believe that the premier of Quebec being granted permission to serve shrimp cocktails at a reception constitutes an acceptable and sufficient form of influence for representing Quebec’s interests,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote in a social media post earlier in the week.
He said an invitation to sit at the head table was the federal government asking Quebec “to get back in line, with the vassalization and invisibilization of Quebec which that implies, in exchange for obtaining better seats to watch the party”.

Russian bombing kills 24 people at Ukraine aid centre, Kyiv says
- Published
At least 24 people were killed after Russian bombs hit an aid distribution centre, in an attack that Ukraine's leader has called "utterly horrific".
Five people were injured and 27 initially reported missing after at least nine 3,000kg aerial bombs hit the village of Komyshuvakha in the southern Zaporizhzhia region, regional head Mykhailo Semikin said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that after the first strike on the local school "used for humanitarian needs", there was a second attack on the place where people were sheltering.
He posted a video showing a huge crater left after Monday's attack, and rescuer teams searching through the rubble.
The Russian military has not publicly commented.
Zelensky initially put the death toll at 18, but Ukraine's state emergencies service DSNS later said 24 people, including two rescuers and four police officers, were confirmed to have been killed.
"The Russians could not have been unaware that the local residents who remained in Komyshuvakha received humanitarian aid there every week," the Ukrainian president wrote in a post on social media.
"This is yet another proof that Russia does not want any de-escalation."
He said that after a recent successful joint Russian-Ukrainian operation to evacuate civilians from the Russia-occupied southern city of Oleshky, "there was a moment when the next steps could show that peace is possible".
"With such killings, Russia is sending the exact opposite signal - Russia is counting on further killings," Zelensky said.
Meanwhile, Semikin described the Russian attack as a "terrible tragedy" for the village, confirming that "people are still under the rubble".
He said that rescue teams were working at the scene, but they were forced to halt their operation a number of times because of Russian drone attacks in the area.
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Deadly fire at CFB Wainwright renews compliance clash between oil operator and Alberta regulator
Sumerian Oil and Gas alleges wells in fire zone were not shut in following enforcement order
The deadly fire that swept across the Wainwright, Alta., military base has renewed a months-long regulatory battle between the provincial energy regulator and an oil and gas company.
Military officials have said there is no evidence that energy infrastructure was involved in the grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Oct. 17, which killed four soldiers and injured dozens more.
But in the weeks since the tragedy, Calgary-based Sumerian Oil and Gas has been speaking out against the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) about recent enforcement issues that led to hundreds of Sumerian wells on the military base being seized days before the fire.
In a series of public statements shared on its website and with CBC News, company officials allege that the AER failed to ensure the wells were secured before the fire.
They say Sumerian staff were the first to alert the regulator that night about the risk the wells could pose as the flames spread. As of Tuesday, the company website appeared to have been taken offline.
Officials with the AER have not responded to questions about the status of Sumerian's wells on or since the night of the training disaster. They also declined to comment on how the wells have been managed since Sumerian lost access and the assets were placed under the care of the Orphan Well Association (OWA) on Oct. 5.
'New compliance issues'
In a statement to CBC News Friday, Lars DePauw, president of OWA, said the agency has secured Sumerian’s wells at CFB Wainwright.
DePauw did not answer questions about when that work was completed or whether it happened before or after the fire.
“All Sumerian wells on CFB Wainwright have been inspected and shut in,” the statement said. “We continue to work on the new compliance issues we have identified. The OWA was not involved in any emergency response activities during the recent fire.”
OWA previously told CBC News that the AER’s Oct. 5 order against Sumerian was due to “significant non-compliance issues.”
While there are operational oil and gas wells scattered across CFB Wainwright, military investigators have said there is no indication that the fire was caused by oil or natural gas infrastructure, or that a gas line was struck. In response to questions about Sumerian’s assets on the base, military officials said there is no new information to share and the investigations remain active.
Call for ministerial review, legal challenge
Sumerian officials assert that the AER has unfairly targeted its operations for months. They have pledged to launch a regulatory appeal and seek a court injunction in an attempt to regain operational control of their assets.
The company has also asked Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean to launch a ministerial review into the regulator’s conduct. Jean’s office has not responded to repeated requests for comment.
In a series of statements issued after the Wainwright fire, Sumerian said it lost custody of its wells on the base two weeks earlier and hasn't had access since.
In the AER order on Oct. 5, all of Sumerian’s assets, including more than 300 well licences on CFB Wainwright, were placed under the care of the OWA.
The order followed a string of enforcement actions, unpaid regulatory fees and a pair of crude leaks that allegedly went unaddressed in Wainwright and Killam.
The order required the OWA to shut in the sites within 14 days, a timeline Sumerian officials had warned the regulator was impossible due to the complicated process required to access sites on an active military base.
“So far as Sumerian can determine, between Oct. 5 and Oct. 17 the OWA did not attend a Sumerian site on the range, shut in no well, and isolated no pipeline," the company told CBC News in a statement.
Sumerian officials said they called the OWA emergency line the night of the fire to report that the company's wells were “inside the fire area.”
“On the evening of Oct. 17, the OWA’s designated contact advised Sumerian that none of the Sumerian wells on the range had been shut in and that the OWA did not plan to attend the base until Oct. 27,” the company said in a statement posted to its website last week and emailed to CBC News.
Military officials have said the fire resulted from a training exercise, was initially reported on the base's grenade-launcher range — a "permanent danger area" that base firefighters couldn't enter — and quickly spread in strong winds.
Three separate investigations are underway, and, among other things, will look at the threat assessment of the fire.
In a statement to CBC News Wednesday, the AER declined to comment on Sumerian’s allegations and said it is unable to answer questions related to the Wainwright incident while it is under investigation.
Mandy Olsgard, a risk assessment specialist and former senior environmental toxicologist with the AER, was critical of Sumerian’s attempts to regain operational control.
The AER's order followed well-documented issues that raise legitimate concerns about the adequacy of environmental management under Sumerian, she said.
Rather than invoking a tragedy of unconfirmed cause to undermine the regulator's credibility, Sumerian should provide evidence that outstanding environmental protection obligations have been met, she said.
"They clearly were not managing their wells in a manner that was sufficient for the Alberta Energy Regulator and that's why they no longer have control of them."
Previous sanctions
Sumerian’s regulatory disputes date back to November 2025, when it acquired the assets of Cleo Energy Corp., which had been in receivership for more than a year while its operations racked up a series of enforcement orders.
The AER did not oppose the initial acquisition, but enforcement disputes continued to arise.
The regulator first ordered Sumerian to suspend operations in July, but the company challenged the order and was granted a temporary stay in the Court of King’s Bench.
When announcing the Oct. 5 order, the AER said it had authorized the OWA to suspend the wells and facilities out of concerns Sumerian “may not be able to provide reasonable care and measures” to protect public safety and the environment.
'Licence loss as a last resort'
The company, however, claims it was not given enough time to fix years-old operational issues before the AER clamped down and seized its assets.
Sumerian asserts that the AER violated its own principles of "education first and proportionate enforcement," punishing the operator for pre-existing conditions on unworkable timelines.
Sumerian claims the AER repeatedly miscalculated compliance and security obligations by attributing third-party or non-existent assets to Sumerian. Along with the company's call for a ministerial review, Sumerian is also demanding a regulatory audit of their assets.
“The deficiencies pre-date the restructuring, and the AER knew it,” the company said in a public statement about its dealings with the regulator.
“The company’s position is that the enforcement rests on conditions that pre-date its ownership, contradicts the AER’s own documents, and runs against the AER’s published policy of proportionate enforcement with licence loss as a last resort.”
Oil assets 'dotted' across Alberta
Olsgard said the adequacy of Sumerian's environmental management and its ability to meet regulatory obligations should be assessed on their own merits.
She said, however, the case is a reminder of the need for clear emergency management protocols for the thousands of abandoned and orphaned energy sites scattered across Alberta, and the dangers these operations, if left unsecured, could pose when seasonal wildfires spark.
"We are a petro state, and these are dotted all over our province," she said. "And given the increasing intensity and magnitude of forest fires, this should be something our provincial government is looking into.”

On October 24, All India Students’ Association (AISA) president Neha Bora arrived at Delhi’s Mandir Marg police station in a Toyota Camry. Bora had been summoned to appear before the Special Executive Magistrate (SEM) in connection with proceedings requiring her to furnish a peace bond following her participation in protests in the city, which Bora has denied signing.
Subsequently, several social media users began claiming that she owned the luxury car, questioning how a student could afford a vehicle reportedly worth Rs 60–70 lakh.
An X account, Tejash (@lord_geopolitic), shared an image showing the car’s registration number alongside a photograph of Neha. Calling the AISA president a “communist fraud”, the user questioned how Neha, a PhD student at JNU School of Arts and Aesthetics, could afford such an expensive vehicle and asked Grok about her source of income. The post garnered around 727,100 views and over 600 shares. (Archive)
Neha Bora is a communist fraud and a failed student who doesn’t have a job and only participates in protests, yet she is roaming around in a luxury car worth ₹60–70 lakh.
Hey @Grok, what’s her source of income? 🤔 https://t.co/5iCfUo6juP
— Tejash (@lord_geopolitic) October 24, 2026
Another X user, Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) posted a video showing the car entering the police station, claiming that “Only in India would unemployed students travel in luxury cars.” The post similarly implied that Neha owned the vehicle. This post amassed around 380,000 views and over 3,000 shares. (Archive)
“Student Leader” Neha Bora is coming to police station in a ₹65 lakhs Toyota Camry Car. Only in India would unemployed students travel in luxury cars 🤡 https://t.co/t3iKqjCK2K
— Monica Verma (@TrulyMonica) October 24, 2026
Several other users circulated similar claims, questioning how Neha could afford to travel in a “luxury” car while being a student and participating in protests. Some posts even insinuated that student protesters were receiving funding from undisclosed sources to “abuse Modi and India”.
A few of the claims are shown in the gallery below:
Fact Check
Alt News contacted Neha to ask about the details of the car. She clarified that the car did not belong to her but is her lawyer Abhik Chimni’s. She further stated that she does not own any vehicle. “I don’t have a car or any form of vehicle of my own. That car belongs to my lawyer Abhik Chimni. He not only has a successful career allowing him to afford a car but is also generous enough to offer to escort me inside the Mandir Marg police station in it,” she said.
“The escorting was necessary because a mob was chanting ‘Neha Bora Murdabad’, ‘Desh Ke gaddaron ko, joote maaron saalon ko’ amongst other slogans outside the police station…The Delhi Police took no steps to disperse the crowd until Abhik specifically mentioned it to the Magistrate and requested him to take measures to handle the hostile and possibly violent atmosphere outside the police station,” Neha told Alt News.
In the video, the number plate is visible and it is: DL12CY3747. Alt News obtained the vehicle’s registration certificate (RC), which identifies the white Toyota Camry hybrid EV with the same number plate as belonging to Neha’s lawyer, Abhik Chimni.
Speaking to Alt News, N Sai Balaji, former AISA president, who accompanied Neha to the Mandir Marg police station on October 24, corroborated her account of the situation outside the station.
According to Balaji, him and Neha initially reached the location in a cab. However, they encountered around 40 people whom he described as Right-wing supporters, allegedly raising slogans against Neha and threatening her safety. He said that Chimni then raised concerns with the police about Neha’s security and requested that the entrance be cleared. The police suggested that Neha enter the premises in a private vehicle, offering to allow a car inside the police station under police escort.
After the incident, Neha took to Instagram to describe the situation, stating that about “50-60” goons had gathered around 100 meters away from the station, allegedly raising threatening slogans against her.
View this post on Instagram
To sum up, the claim that Neha owns a Toyota Camry reportedly worth Rs 60–70 lakh is false and misleading. Neha denied owning any vehicle and the car’s RC identifies her lawyer, Abhik Chimni, as its registered owner.

How does this fluoride-free toothpaste compare when it comes to oral health?
How you brush your teeth — and what you use to do it — matters.
Recently, dentist Dr. Jin-Ho Phark says he's noticed patients asking about fluoride-free toothpaste options. Phark is an associate professor of clinical dentistry at the Herman Ostrow School of Dentistry of University of Southern California.
"There's a lot of interest from the patients," Phark says. "I hear that also regularly from students."
One product that patients are asking about in particular is a calcium phosphate mineral called hydroxyapatite. Many patients, Phark says, may have seen the products on social media, "being pushed by influencers and other people quite intensively."
The traditional fluoride toothpaste became common in the late 1950s, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, when Procter & Gamble Co. released Crest nationally. Over the next few decades, oral care products with fluoride as their active ingredient became widely available around the world. These products help protect the outer layer of teeth from cavity-causing bacteria.
And dental health is important because it's related to so many systems in your body, from your heart to digestion.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
"There are these connections made between your oral health, and the bugs that you have in your mouth, and systemic health and even the composition of your gut microbiome," says Dr. Livia Tenuta, a dentist who specializes in preventing tooth decay and associate professor at the University of Michigan School of Dentistry.
The claim
The promise of hydroxyapatite? Many of the things you care about when it comes to toothpaste: cavity protection, whitening, enamel-strengthening. But without fluoride.
Health experts widely agree that fluoride — a naturally occurring mineral — is beneficial to health. But curiosity is growing about fluoride-free options.
"There is an increasing number of people who are refusing fluoride totally, or hesitant to take it, especially for their children," says Bennett Amaechi, a professor of dentistry at the University of Texas at San Antonio.
That hesitancy stems from a history of skepticism about fluoride. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has blamed the fluoridation of water for a number of health problems, including arthritis, bone fractures, bone cancer, IQ loss, neurodevelopmental disorders and thyroid disease.
Low levels of fluoride are generally considered safe and key to preventing cavities. Amaechi says there's no concrete evidence about potential harms of fluoride when it comes to children's IQ. And research that has found associations between fluoride and IQ has looked at very high levels of fluoride — over twice what's recommended in the U.S. water supply. The CDC previously named the addition of fluoride to public drinking water one of the top 10 great public health achievements of the 20th century, alongside vaccinations and family planning. They also say fluoride in water reduces cavities by 25%.
Still, Kennedy's criticism of fluoride seems to have made its way to toothpaste — and opened up space for products that use hydroxyapatite instead.
So what is hydroxyapatite?
The hype around hydroxyapatite is, in part, due to its similarity to tooth enamel. There's also some research that suggests hydroxyapatite can help with tooth sensitivity.
Tooth enamel is mostly made of calcium and phosphate. Those minerals form the outer layer of your teeth, which protects the internal layers of tissues, nerves and blood vessels, from damage.
Your enamel is stronger than your bones, but still susceptible to damage over time from things like sugary foods and dental plaque. Bacteria in your mouth feed on sugars, and produce acids that eat away at the outer layer of your teeth. Tenuta says over time, that process sets the stage for tooth decay, often referred to as caries, or eventually cavities (a hole in a tooth that comes from this decay).
She says fluoride toothpaste helps protect teeth by "remineralizing" them with calcium and phosphate.
"When [fluoride is] available in our saliva, in the dental plaque that we were not very perfect in brushing, that fluoride that is left over after brushing with the fluoride toothpaste will actually bring minerals back to the tooth," Tenuta says.
Fluoride works with those minerals to form a new compound that protects teeth. It acts like a shield for your enamel. But you need to brush with fluoride toothpaste consistently. Dentists recommend twice daily to keep those minerals around in our mouths.
Hydroxyapatite is thought to work in a slightly different way. These products seem to get into tiny crevices in the tooth enamel.
Many hydroxyapatite products use a form called nano-hydroxyapatite, which has smaller particles that, in theory, can more easily penetrate pores in enamel, though research data is limited.
The evidence
Amaechi, who studies hydroxyapatite use, says fluoride is extensively researched, especially in long-term studies. But he says early research on hydroxyapatite is positive.
"When it comes to remineralization and preventing caries manifestation, it is as effective as fluoride," Amaechi says.
Amaechi was an author on a 2021 study in the journal Scientific Reports, that followed 177 children for almost one year, and compared hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste. The researchers tracked tooth decay in each group, and found that both groups had similar outcomes. That study included funding from Dr. Wolff Group, a German company that owns two brands that make hydroxyapatite toothpastes.
That company contributed funding to another study, published two years later in the journal Frontiers in Public Health. Researchers found similar results after tracking 171 adults, comparing tooth decay in participants using a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to those using a fluoride toothpaste for 18 months. Both groups showed similar outcomes, suggesting that hydroxyapatite worked as well as fluoride in the study. However, the participants in the study were mostly healthy young adults without any severe oral health problems.
Tenuta says she'd want to see more long-term studies, especially in people with high risk of tooth decay.
"There are very few studies and they recruited participants of low caries risk," she says.
One shorter-term study in 2019, published in the Journal of Investigative and Clinical Dentistry, did compare a hydroxyapatite toothpaste to fluoride toothpaste in 133 people who were at higher risk of caries. After a little over five months, the researchers found both toothpastes performed similarly.
The bottom line
Hydroxyapatite toothpastes tend to be more expensive than fluoride ones — some over a dollar more expensive per ounce.
For patients who are open to both options, "I will advise them to use fluoride because fluoride has more evidence supporting its efficacy," Amaechi says.
Tenuta agrees.
"I would recommend as a best option to stick to a fluoride toothpaste because that's what we have a lot of evidence behind," she says.
The American Dental Association, a professional group for dentists, said in an email to NPR they acknowledge more people are using products with forms of hydroxyapatite and that some evidence suggests those products can contribute to remineralization.
However, research on the ingredient is new, "and evidence regarding its clinical effectiveness remains limited and ambiguous, especially regarding clinical indications," wrote ADA Consumer Advisor spokesperson Dr. Ada Cooper.
Instead, the ADA recommends you brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes with a fluoride toothpaste, floss daily and regularly visit a dentist.

US Committee seeks outside investors for new commercial venture
LONDON/NEW YORK, Nov 3 : The US Olympic and Paralympic Committee (USOPC) is in the advanced stages of setting up a commercial entity to sell a stake in return for capital, two people with knowledge of the matter told Reuters.
Any deal would mark a significant shift for the USOPC, a non-profit organization that, unlike many national Olympic committees, relies heavily on sponsorships, licensing and other commercial revenue streams rather than government funding.
The plan has been in the works for months, according to minutes of USOPC board meetings which showed the proposed commercial entity would be named United States Olympic and Paralympic Ventures (USOPV).
"(USOPC CEO Sarah) Hirshland reported encouraging feedback from preliminary discussions with potential investment and strategic partners," the minutes said.
"Prospective partners generally validated the vision for the USOPV and strategic rationale underlying the initiative."
The USOPC is being advised by investment bank Raine Group, according to Sky News, which said the venture could be valued in the billions of dollars.
Raine did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The potential deal comes as the United States prepares to host the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles and seeks to capitalize on growing investor interest in sports assets and intellectual property.
USOPC CEO Sarah Hirshland told Reuters that her organization was preparing to transition away from its commercial partnership with LA28, known as United States Olympic and Paralympic Properties, which comes to an end after the Games.
USOPV COMMERCIAL MODEL IN PROGRESS
Hirshland said what the commercial model for the USOPV will be - and the details behind it - were "very much in progress" and declined to offer specific details on the commercial entity.
"This is a natural transition point and is one we've been talking about and preparing for for more than a couple of years," Hirshland said.
Following Los Angeles, the US will immediately turn attention to the 2034 Winter Games in Salt Lake City.
"We're obviously very focused on how do we create a sort of sustainable and consistent commercial strength that will both incorporate potential host cities, in this case obviously Utah 34, but also a structure that would allow for future host organizations," Hirshland said.
The move underscores how sports leagues and governing bodies are increasingly turning to private capital in a bid to unlock the value of their commercial rights and secure access to resources to fund future growth.
The USOPC said in a statement it was evaluating a range of commercial options to generate additional resources for athletes and national governing bodies while preserving its mission, governance and leadership.
It added that it had consulted athlete and federation representatives throughout the process.
The USOPC move comes after FIFA scrapped plans to create a $20 billion subsidiary to run the soccer World Cup and its other events, offering stakes of up to 20 per cent to external investors.
The proposal prompted a revolt across global soccer and the backlash threatened FIFA President Gianni Infantino's future with the sport's world governing body.

Last week, Anthropic introduced a new system prompt designed to stop its Claude models from re-creating specific, existing video games. While that move could help shield Anthropic from some liability, it’s unlikely to slow much of the massive wave of AI-assisted game porting and copying that has emerged in recent months.
A social media user and AI decompilation enthusiast going by the name “chasm” was among the first to note the prompt change late last week, saying a new rule seemed to be added to the Claude Code prompt on or around October 27. That rule—included in a json file under the name “tengu_heron_brook”—reads as follows:
Do build original games, games in a genre, and games from the user’s own designs and assets. Don’t build a recreation of a specific existing game, even if it is renamed or called original.
XDA later independently verified that the new rule appears in version 2.1.314 of the Claude Code binary, which was released on October 30. XDA also reported that the “tengu_heron_brook” rule had been used for other purposes in earlier versions and that the Claude Opus 5.5 model specifically seemed to have its own distinct and independent instructions restricting game recreations as part of its system prompt bundle.
Following chasm’s initial report, Anthropic software engineer Addy Osmani confirmed on social media that the company had “added two sentences to Claude Code’s prompt on Opus 5.5 to steer it away from recreating someone else’s specific game because using Claude to infringe IP is against our usage policy.”
He added that the new prompt was designed to still allow “original games, genre games, and games built from your own designs and assets,” even as a handful of issue reports on Anthropic’s GitHub suggest the new prompt is getting in the way of some game development use cases.

The world is set to miss its 2030 conservation goals as finance and action have fallen short, leaders recognized at a UN biodiversity summit in Armenia’s capital, where they agreed to step up efforts after a final overnight session.
Representatives from almost 200 countries gathered in Yerevan over the past two weeks to review progress on a landmark agreement set four years ago to protect about a third of the world’s land and seas by 2030.
The COP17 talks on biodiversity concluded on Saturday with a recognition that conservation efforts were so far too slow to realistically achieve the goals of the 2022 Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
A plan was agreed to accelerate progress ahead of the next summit in Ecuador in two years, dubbed the Yerevan Pathway. It would mean redoubling efforts to tackle subsidies and incentives that are harmful to nature, increasing financial, scientific, and technical support for developing countries, and strengthening monitoring and reporting mechanisms.
Steven Guilbeault, former Canadian minister of environment and climate change, said that finance remained one of the biggest obstacles to achieving global biodiversity goals.
The fact that a fund agreed at the last meeting—for companies profiting from genetic materials to voluntarily contribute to—stood largely empty was “especially disappointing.”
“We need to mobilize substantially more public and private finance, reform subsidies that harm nature, and ensure that funding reaches the countries and communities on the front lines of the nature crisis,” he said.

NEW DELHI: The National Land Monetization Corporation (NLMC) expects to generate an additional ₹4,000-5,000 crore from the sale of surplus land assets held by central public sector enterprises (CPSEs) by the end of the current fiscal year, over and above land parcels worth around ₹9,000 crore that it has already sold. Payments for several completed transactions are at different stages of processing, while the corporation is preparing to bring more land parcels to market, its chief executive officer Rohan Chand Thakur said on Tuesday. The next tranche of monetization is expected to come from surplus land held by CPSEs under the ministries of telecommunications, chemicals and fertilisers, petroleum and petrochemicals, and steel. Enterprises under these ministries have approached NLMC to monetize land assets at various locations, he said. Thakur was speaking on the sidelines of a pre-bid meeting for the proposed e-auction of a 5.119-acre land parcel owned by HIL (India) Ltd in New Delhi. The expected proceeds come as the government pursues an ₹80,000 crore target from disinvestment and public-sector asset monetization in fiscal year 2027 (FY27). It has so far realized ₹55,757.29 crore from stake sales in public-sector entities and ₹6,366.93 crore through other asset monetization initiatives, according to data on the Department of Investment and Public Asset Management (Dipam) website. Thakur clarified that NLMC's mandate is limited to monetising surplus land and building assets of CPSEs. This is separate from Dipam's disinvestment programme, which involves selling the government's stakes in public-sector enterprises. The latest proposed auction involves a 5.119-acre property in the Najafgarh Industrial Area along Rohtak Road, Shivaji Marg, with a reserve price of ₹829.69 crore. Several real estate developers, including Omaxe, M3M and Godrej, have expressed interest in the property, HIL (India) Ltd chairman and managing director Kuldeep Singh said today. The land has a road frontage of around 140 metres and offers development potential with a floor space index (FSI) of up to 400 under applicable transit-oriented development (TOD) provisions, subject to statutory conditions and approvals. It is currently designated for industrial use, though conversion is permissible under applicable norms and approvals. The proposed sale is NLMC's third publicly advertised e-auction in the past two months, as the corporation seeks to unlock value from surplus and underutilized land held by public-sector enterprises through competitive bidding. The latest exercise follows two earlier auctions involving assets of ITI Ltd and Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd (RINL). In August, NLMC invited bids for the outright sale of a 44.03-acre land parcel owned by ITI Ltd along Old Madras Road (NH-75) in Krishnarajapuram, Bengaluru. It also initiated the auction of 459 land parcels belonging to RINL, the corporate entity that operates Visakhapatnam Steel Plant. The plots, spread across 93,572.21 square yards, are located in Visakhapatnam. The RINL auction drew investor interest. In the first phase, held on 12 October, 150 plots were sold, fetching winning bids worth ₹366.33 crore against a combined reserve price of ₹312.48 crore — a premium of 17.23%. The highest bid exceeded ₹1.80 lakh per square yard. The second phase, covering the remaining plots, was subsequently rescheduled. NLMC, a wholly-owned government company under the administrative control of the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) in the finance ministry, was established to undertake and facilitate the monetisation of surplus land and building assets of CPSEs and other government agencies. It works with CPSEs to identify surplus properties, structure transactions and facilitate their sale through transparent and competitive processes. West Ham approach Parker after sacking boss Nuno
- Published
West Ham United are expected to appoint Scott Parker as head coach after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo.
The 52-year-old Portuguese head coach has paid the price for West Ham's disappointing start to the Championship season, having overseen their relegation from the Premier League last season.
BBC Sport understands that the club are in advanced talks with former Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham boss Parker and he could be confirmed before Wednesday's Championship trip to Cardiff City.
The former England midfielder had four seasons as a player with the Hammers and led Bournemouth and Burnley to promotion from the Championship as a manager.
- Green backs 'proven' Parker for Hammers job 
  - Published2 hours ago
- Nuno is out - who next for West Ham? 
  - Published5 hours ago
- What happens now at relegated West Ham? 
  - Published24 May
Widely seen as favourites for automatic promotion, the London side are currently eighth in the table, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough.
They have won two of their past six games and have lost back-to-back home matches - going down 3-2 to Southampton and then 3-1 to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday - losses that have seen them drop down from second place.
Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left the club.
Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of the side for their Championship trip to Cardiff City on Wednesday night.
"Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club's objectives and expectations remain on track," a West Ham United statement read.
"West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.
"The process of recruiting a new head coach is already under way."
The decision means West Ham are looking for their fourth permanent manager since David Moyes left London Stadium in May 2024.
His successor Julen Lopetegui was sacked after just six months in charge with the Hammers mid-table having won six of their 20 Premier League matches.
He was replaced by former Chelsea and Brighton boss Graham Potter, who oversaw a 14th-placed finish, but was sacked after only eight months in charge with the club 19th in the table.
The club opted to stick with former Wolves and Tottenham Hotspur boss Nuno despite him being unable to turn around the club's fortunes. They were relegated at the end of last season after finishing two points behind Spurs.
Despite that, this season had a troubled start for the Hammers - they failed to win any of their first three league matches and were 19th in the table.
A run of four successive wins in the first half of September, where they scored 16 goals and went top of the table, appeared to show they had adapted to the second tier, with a 6-0 win over Wrexham the highlight of the run.
Just two league victories have come since - a 6-0 win at nine-man Lincoln City and a 1-0 victory at Swansea City followed draws with London rivals Millwall and QPR.
A squad that Parker can work with?
Having posted losses of more than £104m, relegation meant West Ham had to sell players over the summer.
The departures of the likes of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville, El Hadji Malick Diouf, James Ward-Prowse and Freddie Potts secured the club about £150m in transfer revenue.
They used some of that cash to pay Celtic a Championship record £22m for midfielder Arne Engels and spent a reported £12m on Norwegian winger Edvin Austbo.
Experienced campaigners Joel Veltman and Manor Solomon also joined on free transfers from Brighton and Tottenham respectively while they kept key players such as England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech midfielder Tomas Soucek and Greek defender Konstantinos Mavropanos.
Soucek missed the first two months of the season with an ankle injury while some of their other signings have yet to deliver. Engels has three assists and no goals in 12 games while Austbo has scored twice and had two assists having started just two league matches.
It is a squad that is capable of turning things around, especially under a manager with Championship promotion experience such as Parker.
'West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club'
Analysis - Simon Stone, BBC Sport chief football news reporter
Given the estimated £200m loss in revenue it is imperative the club goes straight back up to the Premier League.
Two wins in six, a run which has dropped West Ham to eighth in the table, four points off second-placed Swansea in the final automatic promotion place, is not good enough.
Scott Parker is the obvious choice as replacement and West Ham are wasting no time in getting the deal done.
Parker made 129 appearances in a four-year stint with the Hammers. He won the club's player of the year award three times and was at West Ham when he was named Football Writers' Association player of the year in 2011.
West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club and the culture and is someone the fans can get behind.
Equally as important, he has already been promoted from the Championship three times, at Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.
West Ham will hope he makes it number four next May.
'The expectation is for an immediate return to the Premier League'
Analysis - Phil Parry, BBC Radio London sport editor
There were some who thought that Nuno would leave the club in the summer after they failed to survive their relegation battle, but the stability that he offered and his experience of guiding Wolves out of the Championship were seen as positive reasons to welcome his continuation at the helm.
The 6-0 thumpings handed out to Wrexham and Lincoln are contrasted with some disappointing home defeats, including the past two outings at London Stadium.
One of the major concerns has been the slow starts to games. They have conceded the opening goal in four of their past six in the Championship and have picked up just two points from those matches.
It has been suggested that the team just don't appear to appreciate the intensity and urgency of games at this level and are still a little too ponderous in the first half.
The Hammers have just been through a run of matches against teams who are in good form and are sitting high in the table, but losses in two of those games, both at home, have proven costly for Nuno.
With the squad at their disposal and the fanbase that backs them, it will be an attractive job for the next head coach, but whoever it is will be aware that the expectation at London Stadium is for an immediate return to the Premier League and falling short of that objective is risky for long-term prospects.

The U.S. health regulator has accepted Merck’s experimental targeted drug for a priority review based on data from a late-stage trial where it extended survival in women with an advanced form of endometrial cancer.
The drug, sacituzumab tirumotecan, also known as sac-TMT, delivers a cancer-killing payload to cells that carry a protein called TROP2, which is common in endometrial tumors.
The trial enrolled 776 patients whose cancer had returned or progressed after earlier treatment. Patients were randomly assigned to sac-TMT or to a chemotherapy their doctor chose, either doxorubicin or paclitaxel.
Results showed sac-TMT reduced the risk of death by 32%, with patients living a median of 19 months compared with 12.1 months on standard chemotherapy.
The treatment also reduced the risk of cancer progression or death by 41%, with patients remaining progression-free for a median of 7.2 months compared with 3.9 months on chemotherapy.
In addition, about 35% of sac-TMT patients saw their tumors shrink, compared with 17% on chemotherapy.
A regulatory decision is expected by June 2027, Merck said. The trial data was presented at the ESMO medical congress.
“Based on discussions with the FDA, the company is hopeful for an approval before the PDUFA date to bring sac-TMT to patients as quickly as possible,” said Dean Y. Li, president, Merck Research Laboratories.
Severe treatment-related side effects were more frequent with sac-TMT, affecting about 54% of patients compared with 41% on chemotherapy. About 3% of patients stopped treatment due to side effects.
About 68,000 cases of endometrial cancer are expected to be diagnosed in the United States in 2026, with over 14,000 deaths, according to the American Cancer Society.
Jefferies analysts project peak sales of roughly $900 million in endometrial cancer for the drug and $9 billion across all potential indications.
Merck is developing the drug with Chinese biotech firm Kelun-Biotech, which discovered the therapy.

The Trump administration truly cut down not one but four large, old cottonwood trees on the border in Lochiel, among the many efforts to clear land for border wall construction. Crews cut down three trees on July 27, followed by the fourth on Oct. 5. A widely shared video highlighted the moment crews felled the fourth tree. However …
… Reported estimates placed the collection of trees anywhere between 100 and 250 years old. A scientist examining a sample of the fourth tree estimated its age at a maximum of 146 years — still a very old tree, though at least a century short of some claims.
In October, people shared a story alleging U.S. President Donald Trump's administration cut down a 250-year-old "grandmother" tree located directly on the southern border in Lochiel, Arizona, to make way for border wall construction.
For example, on Oct. 7, a YouTube account posted a video (archived) captioned, "A giant cottonwood 'Grandmother Tree' was torn down in Lochiel, Arizona, to expand Trump's border wall. Despite activists trying to protect the 250-year-old tree for more than two months, DHS removed the tree as protesters screamed."
Other users shared the story about the purported 250-year-old "grandmother" tree on Facebook (archived), Instagram (archived) and Reddit (archived). One popular political commentator, Brian Tyler Cohen, claimed (archived) the tree was not just 250 but rather 300 years old — dating back to the early 18th century.
Research of all available data concluded that the Trump administration truly cut down a large, old cottonwood tree — which some people referred to as a "grandmother" tree — directly on the border line. The Department of Homeland Security oversaw crews that reportedly cut down not one, but four old Fremont cottonwood trees on the border in Lochiel, among the many efforts to clear lands for the president's double border wall construction. The fourth tree appears in the above video.
However, a thorough reading of all the data found the collection of trees, while older than 100, to perhaps be well below 250 years old. A scientist examining a sample of the fourth tree estimated its age at a maximum of 146 years — still a very old tree.
Due to the apparent embellishment of the tree's age, we've rated this claim mostly true.
The Washington Post reported that the trees were located in a 60-foot-wide strip of federal land known as the Roosevelt Reservation. Former President Theodore Roosevelt established the swath of land in 1907 along the southern borders of California, Arizona and New Mexico to combat opium smuggling and enforce immigration policies.
Snopes contacted locals connected with this story to receive more insight. We also emailed Customs and Border Protection to ask questions. The White House declined comment and referred us to CBP.
Building the wall
During Trump's 2016 presidential campaign, he repeatedly touted strict immigration policies, perhaps most notably promising time and time again that Mexico would pay for a wall to help bring down the number of people crossing into the U.S. over the southern border.
Fast forwarding to Trump's second term, on July 27, crews reportedly associated with the Arizona-based Fisher Sand & Gravel Co. — receiving billions of dollars in U.S. government funds for border wall construction, including in Lochiel's Santa Cruz County — cut down three cottonwood trees, as shown in several different videos.
DHS official monitored the situation and reportedly handcuffed at least one person.
A group of activists with concerns about the trees and the local ecosystem then formed a "tree sit" together at the fourth and final tree.
After more than two months of banding together, on Oct. 5, Fisher crews reportedly cut down the fourth tree, once again with DHS officials, some wearing face masks, on guard and making at least a dozen arrests — if not more.
We contacted Fisher to confirm its crews were directly involved with chopping down the four trees, as well as to ask if the company wished to share a statement, and will add that information if it responds.
Estimating the trees' ages
Our research to find estimates of the trees' ages located news media outlets citing various figures. For example, a High Country News article identified the collection as "the 100-plus-year-old trees." An NPR headline, citing Phoenix's KJZZ, mentioned "250-year-old trees," while the story itself identified the trees as residing in "a 150- to 200-year-old grove."
Aside from those reported estimates, at least one scientist visited the site to collect tree samples for further study. Ceci Martinez, a graduate student at the University of Arizona's Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, obtained at least two tree samples, the Arizona Republic reported — including one sample from the fourth tree before crews cut it down. For that tree, she estimated the age as "a maximum of 146 years old."
Asked by the Republic about how important the actual age is when it comes to the threat of being cut down, Martinez applauded the activists who attempted to save the trees. She mentioned that while "tree people are obsessed with how old trees are," cottonwoods serve "a very different function":
They're intended to grow tall, big, provide shade and habitat. They get a lot of attention because, like the jaguar, they are these big important things.
But being old is not what I think of when I think of how important they are. The value for me in these trees isn't them being ancient or 200 years old. The value is the role they play in the ecosystem. And these cottonwoods do a lot.
Kate Scott, who who cofounded the local Madrean Archipelago Wildlife Center and was one of the activists present during the tree sit, reportedly referenced "the eastern-most cottonwood" — possibly the tree crews felled on Oct. 5 — as "grandmother." The "grandmother" term for the trees possibly originated from her or was at least popularized by her own conservationist efforts, if not also possibly by locals and indigenous people.
Russ McSpadden, working with the Center for Biological Diversity, credited Scott with "largely" establishing the "grandmother" term as one of "endearment and respect used for the trees." McSpadden sent a statement to us about the loss of the trees, saying in part, "Where those trees brought life together, the border wall now cuts it apart."
We also reached out to Scott to request comment and will update this article accordingly.
Agency response
In an email, a Customs and Border Protection spokesperson told us the agency recognized the importance of protecting the environment, wildlife and cultural resources during border wall construction. The statement also highlighted the purported harms of unauthorized border crossings resulting in "substantial amounts of trash, pollution, and damage to natural resources, including sensitive habitats and agriculture."
That statement read, in part:
U.S. Customs and Border Protection identified four cottonwood trees on federal land in Lochiel, Arizona, that needed removal for planned border wall construction. Preconstruction surveys found no active migratory bird nests, and environmental monitors were present at the start of clearing activities to ensure work was limited to the identified trees. As of Oct. 5, 2026, all four trees have been removed.
In a news release, the Grand Canyon Chapter of the environmental conservation organization the Sierra Club featured alleged video proof from July 26 showing a kingbird actively nesting in one of the three trees that crews cut down the following day. The organization claimed that evidence showed CBP "lied" about being careful to not destroy trees with active nests.
Erick Meza, who works as a border program coordinator for the Sierra Club, told us he recorded the video. He said in the group's release, in part, "Without any justification, double walls are going up everywhere and they are being built without environmental impact studies, without community consultation, and without regard for the species that depend on these habitats." He also mentioned arrests of people protesting the border construction work.
For further reading, we previously reported about other claims of the Trump administration chopping down trees for projects happening in Washington, D.C.

A previous NPR analysis found both parties spending deep and wide in a competitive landscape that spans 70 districts, ranging from longtime tossups to newly-competitive seats in deeply conservative areas.
Republicans came into Election Day with a narrow 218-214 seat advantage in the House and facing severe headwinds as the party in power. This midterm cycle has also seen a record number of departures from Congress, and polls show voters aren't happy about things like the economy and the ongoing war in Iran.
So what separates a good night for Democrats from a blue wave that sees dozens of House seats change hands? Here's NPR's cheat sheet to four types of House races to watch as results come in:
Early polls closing
The first results of the night with national implications will likely be from Kentucky's 6th Congressional District (KY-06) and Indiana's 5th (IN-05), two districts where polls close first (in the 6 p.m. ET hour) and whose 2024 margins for President Trump (15 and 17 points, respectively) could act as a preview for how much voters have soured on Republicans.
Democrats and Republicans alike have spent heavily in the Kentucky race, where Democrat Zach Dembo faces Republican Ralph Alvarado, so the increased investment is worth noting as a factor on the outcome. If Democrats flip one or both of these races, then it will likely be a long night for the GOP.
Florida also counts and reports its votes quickly, and is home to more than a half dozen races that are viewed as toss-ups or slightly favor one party or the other, so as these districts have projected winners there will be more insight into other races across the country.
Like the Kentucky contest, both parties have spent significant sums in races like the open seat in FL-22 with Democrat Pia Dandiya facing off against Republican Casey Askar and incumbent Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz versus Republican Scott Singer in the newly-redrawn FL-25 race.
Other races to watch: FL-27, NC-11, SC-01, VA-01
Last-minute big spending
In the final seven days of the midterms, a handful of House races have seen more than $10 million in ad spending, according to data from AdImpact. It's a sign of where both parties think the saying "It all comes down to turnout!" is more than a cliche. That includes districts in Michigan, such as MI-07, where progressive Democrat William Lawrence is challenging incumbent Republican Tom Barrett in a seat that Trump carried by just over one percent in 2024 and the open MI-10, where Democrat Christina Hines faces Republican Mike Bouchard.
New York Republican Rep. Mike Lawler in NY-17 could be one of the rare Republicans who holds on to his seat thanks in part to his party's ad spending advantage in the closing stretch against Democrat Cait Conley.
Three of Iowa's four House races, IA-01, IA-02 and IA-03 are on the list of most expensive, in part because of the competitive governor and U.S. Senate races that are also on the ballot and driving up turnout.
Other races to watch: CO-08, PA-01, WA-03, WI-03
Redistricting
This year's Supreme Court decision rolling back part of the Voting Rights Act led to many Republican-led states redrawing their House maps to eliminate districts that favor Democrats in a typical election year – but this year is not typical.
Now, the political environment has deteriorated so much that seats like AL-02, held by Democrat Shomari Figures, OH-09 held by Democrat Marcy Kaptur and NC-01 held by Democrat Don Davis are all considered toss-ups at best and favoring the Democrats at worst for Republicans.
In Texas, Latino voters seem poised to swing back to Democratic candidates and could prevent Republican Eric Flores from flipping the seat held by Rep. Vicente Gonzalez in TX-34 or Tano Tijerina from unseating Democratic incumbent Henry Cuellar in TX-28.
Other races to watch: CA-22, FL-09, FL-14, TX-35
The outer edges of the map
As results continue to be reported, one thing to watch is how far into conservative communities the increased support for Democrats can go.
One race that has received a surprising amount of ad attention is in Arkansas's 2nd district (AR-02), where incumbent Republican Rep. French Hill faces a well-known challenger in Democrat Chris Jones. By the time polls close, closer to $10 million will have been spent in the final months on the Little Rock-based seat that Trump carried by 15 points in 2024.
There are also many districts in states that redrew their maps where the Republican gerrymander could backfire, like Ohio. In both OH-10 held by Republican Mike Turner and OH-15 held by Republican Mike Carey, Trump won by closer to 10 points in 2024. They're also in a state with competitive governor and Senate races and stretch between the suburbs and exurbs of Dayton and Columbus with an electorate that could swing away from the GOP.
The margin in North Carolina's Senate race, where former Gov. Roy Cooper is expected to win against former Republican National Committee Chair Michael Whatley, could determine if races like NC-03 are in play as well too. Rep. Greg Murphy's district absorbed more Democratic-leaning voters after the latest map redraw.
Other races to watch: NC-09, NY-21, TN-09, WA-05

Women recruited from economically weaker sections were being offered ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 for an egg donation cycle, while those operating the alleged racket made an average of about ₹3 lakh from each cycle.
Malkajgiri police widened their investigation into the exploitation of women, falsification of records and the role of IVF and fertility establishments.
The 43 women rescued during simultaneous raids in Hyderabad have undergone medical examinations, including blood-group and fitness tests. Police are now verifying their medical histories with IVF centres to establish their treatment records.
The investigation has raised concerns over how the women were recruited and whether they gave informed consent for the procedures. Police said women from economically weaker sections were targeted and that, in some cases, intermediaries allegedly even completed their signatures on documents. Investigators are examining possible falsification of records and whether the women fully understood the procedures they were being recruited for.
Police are tracing the payments and commissions involving organisers, recruiters and intermediaries who connected the women with fertility-related establishments.
The investigation is now expanding to medical establishments. Police are preparing to serve notices to the District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) and conduct searches at ART and fertility centres. Some hospitals have also approached police and informed them that employees found to have been involved had been removed.
Investigators are examining how women from West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and other states were recruited, transported and accommodated in Hyderabad before being referred for egg retrieval procedures. Their medical records, consent documents and the procedures they underwent are also being scrutinised.
All eight accused arrested in connection with the Hyderabad cases have been remanded to judicial custody. Further investigation is underway.
