The “unprecedented” spread of the Ebola outbreak means it could reach the UK and other countries, according to one of Africa’s top health officials.
As the current outbreak reached 10,000 cases, with almost 5,000 deaths, Dr Jean Kaseya, director general of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), compared the outbreak to the Covid pandemic, which first took hold in China before spreading to countries across the world, claiming millions of lives, and ravaging health systems and economies.
“We want all countries to know that they are not safe if they don’t take appropriate measures,” he said.
“Each country, not only in the African region, but all continents, must now increase the preparedness level and the possibility for treatment.
“It is the first time three African regions have been affected [by Ebola]. The geographic extension of this outbreak is unprecedented,” he said.
Kaseya said leaders around the world should realise that although the brunt of the health crisis is affecting Africa at the moment, the situation could change. “We shouldn’t forget that at the beginning of Covid, many countries said there was zero risk of being affected, but a few months later, they became the hotspot,” he said. “We don’t want to see the UK and other countries become the hotspot.”
This outbreak, the 17th in the Democratic Republic of the Congo since Ebola was identified, was caused by the Bundibugyo virus and has become the largest and deadliest in the country’s history.
Ebola is a highly contagious, severe, and often fatal illness. It is spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies, such as during funeral preparations.
On 15 May, DR Congo’s health ministry declared an outbreak in Ituri province, though sequencing shows it had begun in February. It has now spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, while last week, in west Africa, Nigeria confirmed a case in the capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus.
France is the only non-African country to have confirmed a case of Ebola so far – a doctor who had returned from DR Congo – in June.
The Bundibugyo virus has no approved treatment, though vaccine trials are under way. The results should be available in three to six months, said Kaseya.
Of the total 10,091 cases, 10,060 have occurred in DR Congo, with 4,887 deaths. Two people have died in Uganda, and two in Kenya.
The response to the crisis has been hampered by inadequate protective equipment and unpaid health worker wages, leading to strikes. Conflict in DR Congo as well as mistrust towards officials in affected areas, misinformation and global aid cuts have further complicated the situation.
Kaseya will convene a meeting of African health ministers on Wednesday to urge greater cross-border cooperation. He wants governments to introduce screening and testing for people coming from affected regions at points of entry and exit.
“The main message to ministers is that they have to understand they could be affected, and we don’t want them to be surprised by what could happen,” he said.
At a meeting in November with African heads of state, Kaseya will call for a “corridor of peace” in conflict areas. “Currently, we have colleagues in Ituri who want to go and support the population, but they cannot because of insecurity,” he said. “I have to say to leaders, this outbreak is not for rebels, it’s not for the official army, it’s for everyone. Ebola can affect everyone … We need to come together to have a kind of agreement on how to protect each other.”
Kaseya called for a global effort to fund the response. He said governments had pledged $3bn (£2.3bn), but that more than $2bn was still outstanding. African countries had committed $120m, he said, while the rest is meant to come from international donors including the US, the UK and the EU.
“We need this money now,” he said. “We must understand that failure to provide funding now to African countries [will result in more being spent] because the outbreak will continue to move. If we have other countries affected we’ll be talking about trillions of dollars because it will require a lot of support to stop this outbreak.”

Health tech startup Clinics On Cloud has raised ₹120 Cr (around $12.5 Mn) in its Series A funding round from Model42, the medtech-focused investment arm of UAE-based backer Enlightened Minds Investments. The Pune-based startup raised the fresh funds at a valuation of ₹600 Cr ($63.3 Mn) In a statement, the startup said that it plans to utilise the fresh capital to bolster its AI-led healthcare capabilities, expand research and development (R&D), and accelerate the growth of its micro-clinic ecosystem. A chunk of the funding will also be used to strengthen its manufacturing capacity, scale strategic partnerships with healthcare providers and expand global footprint. “For eight years, we have built Clinics On Cloud with a simple belief that quality healthcare should never depend on someone’s pincode. This investment gives us the opportunity to take that vision global…,” said Clinics On Cloud cofounder and CEO Abhay Agarwal. Founded in 2018 by Abhay and Manashrri Agarwal, Clinics On Cloud manufactures and deploys AI-powered “health ATMs”, portable box clinics and mobile medical units that deliver point-of-care preventive health checkups and telemedicine consultations. These solutions enable hospitals and government agencies to set up temporary micro-clinics. It claims to have so far seen more than 3,500 deployments across 200 cities in India and seven other countries. Having screened more than 1.2 Cr patients so far, the startup claims to cater to the Indian Army, Navy and the Border Security Force (BSF). The Pune-based startup now plans to position UAE as its global expansion hub, with an eye on exploring new markets across Africa, the US and Southeast Asia. The fundraise comes amid growing investor interest in the healthtech sector, which is seeing renewed funding activity on the back of AI adoption. In September this year, smart ring maker Ultrahuman raised $70 Mn to fuel its integrated healthtech playbook. In July, another AI-powered healthtech startup CARPL.ai also bagged $10 Mn in its Series A funding round led by International Finance Corporation (IFC). In the same month, actor Kunal Kapoor banded together with crowdfunding platform Ketto’s cofounders Varun Sheth and Zaheer Adenwala to launch healthtech startup MetaGO. At the heart of all this is the homegrown healthtech market, which is projected to become a $37 Bn opportunity by 2030.

From 'model minority' to target, anti-Indian hate on the rise
A 19-year-old man's alleged plot to carry out a mass shooting at a Hindu temple in suburban Chicago last month is drawing attention to a recent and steep rise in anti-South Asian and anti-Hindu hate. Police in Palatine, Ill., announced that on Oct. 11, a college student and Taco Bell cashier named Alexandros Paporakis tried to carry out the attack at the Sri Venkateswara Swami Temple in Aurora, Ill., roughly 40 miles west of Chicago. They said the plot was averted by a jammed gun.
"Something of this scale … has not been directed at South Asians before," said Rohit Chopra, professor of communications at Santa Clara University and visiting fellow at the Center for South Asia at Stanford University.
Two decades ago, the predominant narrative about Indian immigrants to the U.S. was glowing, describing the relatively small population as a "model minority." But Chopra says that over the last four years, a combination of growing anti-immigrant populism, economic anxiety and rising political visibility have dramatically changed the script. Today, he said, online and political discourse more often depict Indian Americans and a broader community of people of South Asian descent in conspiracist, degrading and dehumanizing ways.
"It's become a question of who is American, and deliberately trying to keep the Hindu- and Indian-American community out of those conversations entirely with these sort of preconceived notions and bias against the community," said Prasiddha Sudhakar, a board member of the Network Contagion Research Institute. Sudhakar was formerly a researcher at the NCRI who coauthored some of that organization's reports on the topic.
Most concerning, said Sudhakar and Chopra, is that the toxic online rhetoric they have documented has moved from fringe social media platforms to mainstream ones in a short period of time. And, they said, they see strong connections between online hate and offline violence.
"It didn't start off as mainstream, maybe even like a year or a few years ago. You still saw it on the internet," Sudhakar said. "But what has actually become more important now is that this is reaching many different parts of society in a scale that we've never seen before."
A massacre averted
Paporakis has been charged in Illinois with making a terrorist threat and unlawful possession of a rifle, both felonies. Police said his coworkers called to report the attempted massacre. One of them, according to an affidavit filed by a Cook County assistant state attorney, had spoken by phone with the defendant shortly after the attempted attack. The affidavit further states that Paporakis had also sent that coworker messages, including an eight-page document he had written outlining his motivation for the alleged plot.
Later that day, police said that a search of Paporakis' apartment turned up a bag containing an AR-style rifle, 300 rounds of ammunition, eight loaded magazines, one loaded extended magazine and body armor. They also found a gas can and items bearing Nazi symbols and anti-Indian slurs.
"The seriousness of this alleged threat cannot be overstated," said Palatine Police Chief William Nord at a press conference.
Court filings state that the written document was filled with "derogatory and racially charged slurs" directed at "people of Indian ancestry, Jews and African Americans," and that it described those groups as "subhumans." It also indicated that the defendant had settled on the temple location two months prior, but had been planning an attack for two years. In the writings, the defendant allegedly described himself as "a sociopathic white supremacist Neo Nazi filled with hatred, fantasizing about mass murder nearly every day."
The day that the defendant allegedly went to the temple coincided with the beginning of a major Hindu nine-day festival. Among the many in attendance were U.S. Congressman Raja Krishnamoorthi , D-Ill., and his family. Krishnamoorthi has since called for the FBI to investigate the incident as a federal hate crime.
Grafting antisemitic conspiracy theories onto a new group
Sudhakar, whose research was published through the NCRI, said that fringe social media spaces such as 4chan and Gab were the original loci of denigrating and dehumanizing rhetoric about Indians and South Asians. But around 2022, Sudhakar said, her research started to see some of the negative attitudes morph into full-blown conspiracy theories. One of them was a baseless theory about a "Brahmin Organized Government."
"This is the idea of, oh, there's like this elitist group of people that are of high class, high privilege that are sort of occupying the entire government, that this is all like some sort of secret ploy," Sudhakar said.
The term echoes the conspiracy theory of the "Zionist Organized Government," or "ZOG," widely espoused by neo-Nazis. This baseless narrative posits that a cabal of powerful Jews runs global affairs, and closely ties with the Great Replacement Theory. It claims that Jewish puppetmasters are deliberately diluting the power of white Christians by promoting immigration, interracial relations and diversity.
Sudhakar said the main distinction is that the anti-Indian conspiracy theories center more heavily on fears over immigration and jobs, rather than changing demographics. Just as the narratives position people of Indian origin as all-powerful, they also invoke dehumanizing tropes about Indians as "dirty" immigrant "invaders" being brought to the U.S. to displace technology sector workers.
"What we saw was that what began as sort of this anti-Hindu meme that began on 4chan started moving into these mainstream platforms [like X]," she said. "And every time that you'd see Indians or anyone of Hindu origin kind of gain prominence, that these same code words would also be increasing."
Sudhakar said those spikes coincided with events such as Parag Agarwal's appointment as CEO of Twitter, Sriram Krishnan's selection as former White House policy adviser on Artificial Intelligence and the installation of Usha Vance as second lady.
But 2025, said Sudhakar, was when online anti-Hindu and anti-Indian hate truly mushroomed. Chopra, the professor at Santa Clara University, found the same, in research co-authored for the Center for the Study of Organized Hate. It found that between January 2025 and June 2026, anti-South Asian hate speech on the social media platform X was 240% higher than it was in January 2024.
"I think the right has very effectively succeeded in making the H-1B visa issue a political hot button," Chopra said, noting that Indian nationals account for more than 70% of H-1B visas. "Every time there was some development to do with the H-1B visas or a remark that might be made by a figure in authority, you'd find a spike in hate online on X."
A community new to fighting back
Since the alleged temple massacre was disclosed to the public, calls are growing within the Hindu and Indian communities in the U.S. to speak more vocally about racism. Congressman Krishnamoorthy released a video urging the community to become more engaged. Chopra said that in some ways, the rapid uptick in anti-South Asian hate online has been possible because there has been little organized opposition.
"The South Asian community is particularly vulnerable for, I think, a number of reasons. One is this combination of high median income of certain groups of visible success … combined with the fact that it does not have significant political power," Chopra said.
The rise of Indian Americans on the political stage in recent years has been significant, given that estimates put the community's population only around 5 million. These figures include Usha Vance, FBI Director Kash Patel, former Director of National Security Tulsi Gabbard, Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and former GOP presidential candidate Nikki Hayley. But Chopra said that these milestones do not equate to the political power of an organized constituency.
"It doesn't have the kind of political power that can … significantly shift elections, Chopra said.
Additionally, explicit racism directed at South Asians has become disturbingly evident within the political arena, Chopra said. In September, a Republican candidate for statewide office posted a screenshot to X of cheering University of Texas football fans after a team victory. It featured a crowd of revelers that included many of South Asian and Asian origin, with the candidate's comment that "social media is exposing how many Americans have been displaced by foreigners. It's everywhere and far worse than any of us could imagine."
The Department of Homeland Security also set off controversy when it shared an image of a poster captioned "Transformers," with an image of a Sikh man and the words "Get off our roads, you don't know how to drive Mr. Singh." The message was understood to refer to an August 25 tragedy, in which a commercial truck driver of Indian nationality illegally made a U-turn on a Florida highway, and killed three people. After a backlash, DHS took the post down.
But while calls are mounting for the community to organize, there are unique challenges. For one, said Pushpita Prasad of the Coalition of Hindus of North America, Hindu temples do not serve quite the same function as houses of worship do in many other religions.
"We don't belong to temples and we are not part of congregations," Prasad said. "So for us, organizing and finding our voice and sharing information is that much harder."
Additionally, Prasad noted that the economic and professional success of many people of Indian origin in the U.S. masks the uncertainty many may feel about their long-term status in the country. According to the Pew Research Center, two-thirds of the Indian population in the U.S. are immigrants, and of those, nearly half are not naturalized citizens.
"If you happen to come from India, you will find that a lot of Hindus who may be very well off have a great job, seem very well established, they're not really able to speak because they're in that weird sort of immigration limbo," Prasad said. "So that's another reason why a community that seems well off, at least in media chatter, is not as vocal or as organized as it probably should have been."

Bengaluru-based spacetech soonicorn Pixxel’s founder and CEO Awais Ahmed has dismissed questions over the startup’s Indian ownership and control following online criticism over the launch of its US subsidiary, Pixxel Federal. In a post on X, Ahmed said Pixxel remains headquartered, owned, managed, and controlled in India, rejecting allegations questioning its corporate structure and national credentials. “First, Pixxel is Indian-HQed, Indian owned, Indian-managed and Indian-controlled,” he said, adding that its primary Indian entity was incorporated in 2018, before any of its international entities. Ahmed said the Indian entity is not a subsidiary of a US company and remains the primary vehicle for executing Pixxel’s Indian government, space, and defence programmes. Pixxel Federal’s board and CEO would have authority only over the US subsidiary and its operations, with no control over the startup’s Indian government programmes or domestic business, he added. The clarification follows Pixxel’s announcement that it had established Pixxel Federal to pursue US government contracts across civilian, defence, and intelligence agencies. Pixxel’s Ownership Structure Ahmed said Pixxel has faced targeted social media attacks, anonymous emails to government customers, and attempts to cast doubt on its ownership, technology, and credentials. Addressing its shareholding, he said Indian investors, including the founders, collectively hold the largest share by percentage, followed by investors from Singapore, the UK, and the US. No international investor has unilateral control over Pixxel beyond customary investor protections, he added. Ahmed also said intellectual property developed for Indian government projects remains under Indian ownership and control, with these programmes executed through Indian entities and governed by Indian laws. He said Pixxel’s overseas presence predates Pixxel Federal, with its existing US entity incorporated a few months after the Indian company in 2018 to serve American and international customers. Pixxel plans to set up entities in more countries as it expands globally. “We intend to build a global space company rooted in Indian engineering. That means selling Indian technology worldwide, hiring internationally, establishing local entities where required, and complying with each country's laws,” he said. The CEO said separate entities are necessary in regulated sectors such as space and defence to meet national security, export control, licensing, and customer confidentiality requirements. “Having one entity isn't some extraordinary achievement in governance, and having several isn't evidence of questionable patriotism,” he said. He added that Pixxel plans to go public in India in a few years, when its complete corporate structure would be disclosed for public scrutiny. Ahmed’s response follows comments by fellow Bengaluru-based spacetech startup GalaxEye, which said it consciously chose to remain headquartered in India despite considering other locations. In a post on X, GalaxEye said its founders and investors had decided to build the business from India. It also highlighted its single-entity corporate structure, saying all its contracts and bids had been pursued through GalaxEye. “Every contract and every bid we have applied for has come from a single entity: GalaxEye. We have kept our corporate structure simple and our governance clean,” it said. Without naming any company, GalaxEye referred to the practice of setting up multiple entities across jurisdictions to qualify for and secure projects, saying it had chosen not to follow that approach. “That discipline has a cost in the short term. We believe it pays back in trust, and trust is what a space company is ultimately built on,” it added. Pixxel Expands Its Government Business Founded by Ahmed and Kshitij Khandelwal, Pixxel develops hyperspectral imaging satellites that capture data across multiple narrow wavelength bands, revealing details on the Earth’s surface that conventional satellite imagery may miss. Its new subsidiary, Pixxel Federal, will offer Earth observation technologies, satellite mission systems, and geospatial intelligence services to US government agencies. It also plans to establish an office near Washington, DC, to work more closely with government customers and partners. The expansion builds on Pixxel’s existing engagements with NASA and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), including a contract under NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme and an NRO Strategic Commercial Enhancements contract. In September, Pixxel raised $100 Mn in a Series C funding round co-led by Temasek and Seraphim, taking its total funding to around $195 Mn. In India, a Pixxel-led consortium is developing a 12-satellite Earth observation constellation under a public-private initiative with IN-SPACe.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle
- Published
If Matthias Jaissle was unsure what Newcastle fans thought of his team's latest error-strewn performance, he certainly knew at full-time after a second defeat by Everton inside a week.
Despite another miserable showing by Jaissle's side, the Toon Army had stuck by the team from start to finish before a chorus of boos echoed around St James' Park at the final whistle.
The frustration and anger from the stands came after a 1-0 defeat which included a goalkeeping howler by Lukas Hornicek, a red card for substitute Jacob Ramsey and another blunt attacking performance.
"Big frustration, big disappointment," said Jaissle after a fourth defeat in six Premier League games.
"After a performance like that I can understand the reaction from the fans. That's the reality and I am responsible for that.
"We need to work on the things we need to improve and after today that is a lot."
Newcastle's final game before the November international break is away to Fulham on Saturday, before facing Arsenal (home) and Brighton (away) when the Premier League resumes later in the month.
"It's not my first time as a manager in this situation," added Jaissle, whose side were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Everton on Thursday.
"The only way is togetherness and showing unity."
Will the German - who became the Premier League's second youngest coach in the summer - find the solutions to get Newcastle's season back on track, with fans starting to run out of patience?

'I fear a little for Newcastle'
No Premier League side has lost more home games in 2026 than Newcastle (7), while they have now lost 16 of their past 18 league games when conceding first.
The Magpies have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their past 14 home league games - the longest run in their league history.
It all points to worrying times, with Jaissle just three months into a four-year contract.
"I fear a little for Newcastle," former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher said on Sky Sports.
"They have a young manager and young players. You are always going to question the manager when the team is not winning.
"I think it is going to be a tough season. At home, especially, it feels flat and boring, and I never expected to say about Jaissle's Newcastle. You expected it to be front-footed and exciting, coming from the Red Bull model."
Newcastle are in the bottom half of the table, with 11 points from nine games.
It was always going to be a period of transition following Eddie Howe's exit, after five years in charge, and the arrival of 38-year-old Jaissle, after successful spells in Saudi Arabia and Austria.
In addition, Newcastle lost a number of key players in the summer including Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes.
At the start of the year, Newcastle United's chief executive David Hopkinson said he could put them "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.
That now seems a long way off amid suggestions the ambitions of the club's Saudi Arabian owners, the Public Investment Fund, are running out of steam.
Jaissle was not helped on Monday by his goalkeeper, with Hornicek allowing a routine shot to squirm under his body for Thierno Barry to tap home the winner.
The Newcastle boss claimed Barry's winner should have been disallowed for a foul on Fabian Schar in the build-up, but he conceded his players had struggled to show the bravery required to get back in the game.
"It's almost like a negative spiral," he said. "I'm not happy with the referee decision.
"Unfortunately we couldn't deliver actually over the whole 90 minutes. It was not our game and our style of playing.
"That is something we are very frustrated and disappointed about. If you cannot deliver when it counts then you don't deserve to win.
"We were not brave enough in possession, too many long balls."
Jaissle admitted Newcastle are lacking belief in the midst of their miserable run.
"There are certain moments with not too much confidence, not only with the young lads but also with the more experienced ones," he said.
"It's a difficult period. We also know you can only overcome that as a unit. We worked hard and it looked good but unfortunately we couldn't deliver.
"We will analyse in detail and try and make things better against Fulham."
'You can sense nerves in the ground'
Newcastle have problems at both ends of the pitch.
While they have managed just 12 goals in nine league games, they continue to struggle to keep clean sheets.
They registered 17 attempts against Everton but only two of those were on target, and they have scored just once from their past 47 shots in all competitions.
Newcastle have faced the most shots of any Premier League team this season, including 15 or more in seven of the nine top-flight matches they have played.
While only Sunderland (6) and Hull City (5) have committed more errors leading to goals in the Premier League this season.
Meanwhile, this was Everton's first top-flight away win since February - when they won at St James' Park.
"I've been a fan so I understand the frustrations when they're not getting what they're expecting," said captain Dan Burn after the game.
"You can sense that nervousness in the ground.
"When you're not winning games there's always a lack of confidence. The fans weren't happy. That doesn't make it easy to build confidence when you're in that atmosphere.
"Between the boxes we do OK, but we're not ruthless enough going forward or defending our own box."
Jaissle added: "When the goals are not coming easily then you lack confidence. You have to stick together."

The star attraction of the new iPad Mini is its 8.5-inch display. That’s a slightly larger screen than the previous generation, yet the overall dimensions are barely bigger. But the change from IPS to OLED is what matters. It’s a Tandem OLED Super Retina XDR display, based on the same technology as the iPad Pro—though it doesn’t have the 120-Hz refresh rate. Nor is it quite as bright: It can reach 600 nits in SDR and 1,200 nits in HDR, which is 400 nits less than the iPad Pro. It’s more or less similar to the M6 MacBook Pro, though. Not the OLED MacBook Pro, but the Mini-LED model.
The iPad Mini OLED’s brightness is sufficient for most uses, even in bright lighting conditions. But you can take it to the next level by opting for a nano-texture display, which is totally worth the extra $100 it costs. (It’s the model I tested.) It’s not an antireflective coating or a matte layer; it’s actually etched into the glass. The result is a surface that almost entirely diffuses outside light without reducing the screen’s perceived brightness. Reading outside with the iPad Mini is particularly enjoyable, as the nano-texture display not only resists reflections but even gives it a paperlike crispness. This option is also available on the MacBook Pro and iPad Pro, and there’s really nothing else like it.
The iPad Mini one-ups its siblings in sharpness. Its smaller size gives it 19 percent higher pixel density than every other iPad. And yes, it really does look incredibly clear and sharp.
There’s more to it than the display. Part of the magic is how lightweight it is—barely over half a pound, and it doesn’t feel much heavier than my phone in my hand. One-handed use feels completely natural. That’s always been true of the iPad Mini, but this latest version emphasizes that even more.
Lastly, the color options have been pared down from four to just two. The lighter goldish Starlight is still available, but now there’s the introduction of the blackish, navy-blue Midnight. This is a finish carried over from the MacBook Air. The more playful Blue and Purple color options are both gone, as is Space Gray. More options are always better, but for a device that costs $700, I can see why these more professional colors make sense.
Meant for the Road
Apple has also completely redesigned the iPad Mini’s four-speaker sound system, and a couple of interesting changes are happening. As part of its process of making the device IP67 water-resistant, Apple removed the speaker grille from the sides to create a completely sealed enclosure. Instead, the tweeters sit behind two small slits on the edges of the display glass. And then bass drivers are built directly into the display. Apple calls it an Acoustic Display.
The stereo image sounds fullest when you hold the device in portrait, as long as you keep your fingers away from the display. The vibration caused by the location of the speakers isn’t terribly noticeable unless you have the volume on full blast. Overall, the audio sounds decent for a device this size, but it won’t compare well to larger devices like an iPad Air or MacBook Air. But for watching videos or the occasional movie, it suffices.

Polls are looking pretty bleak for Republicans—and the Trump administration’s various attempts to interfere with the elections haven’t been too successful either.
In recent weeks, the Department of Justice, helmed by Attorney General Todd Blanche, a proponent of conspiracy theories about widespread noncitizen voting in the 2020 election, has pulled out all the stops to sow doubt in voters’ minds about the security and validity of the electoral process.
To do this, the DOJ has spent the last year demanding unredacted voter rolls, issuing executive orders to wrest control of elections from states, raiding election offices, proposing new laws to disenfranchise millions of citizens, and claiming that noncitizens were voting en masse across the country. (Incidents of verified noncitizen voting are vanishingly rare, as multiple bipartisan investigations have shown.)
There have also been escalating threats by the DOJ against election officials. On Thursday, the DOJ sent letters to election officials in all 50 states warning them that they would pursue criminal action if they failed to preserve election records for 22 days. Earlier that week, a federal judge had admonished the Trump administration for making similar threats around criminal prosecution against election officials in a different case.
“They're trying to create chaos and distrust in the system,” says Shelby Wayment, staff attorney at UCLA Law’s Safeguarding Democracy Project. “They're trying to file these now knowing they have virtually no chance of winning and then after they can claim the election was fraudulent.”
“This Department is following the facts and the law, not anyone’s political timetable,” a spokesperson for the DOJ tells WIRED, pointing out that the previous administration’s Justice department sued Alabama and Virginia ahead of the 2024 election, claiming the DOJ was at the time trying “to stop them from removing suspected noncitizens from their voter rolls.”
Experts say that while the DOJ’s current legal efforts, including escalating fights in Alaska and California over candidates and voter rolls, are faltering, they’re also designed to lay the groundwork to question the results of this week’s vote.
“We have to expect absolutely, if the election doesn't go the way the president wants, that we will see the administration’s attempt to sow doubts in the election and maybe even challenge those results, but I'm also not worried about it,” David Becker, a former DOJ lawyer and the head of the Center for Election Innovation and Research, tells WIRED.
“They have failed at everything they've tried to do. Our systems have held firm. Our institutions have held firm.”
34 federal district courts have ruled against Trump since he took office in 2025 blocking access to voter rolls and preventing executive orders being implemented, according to analysis from the Brennan Center.
Former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division Justin Levitt thinks that a lot of the actions taken by the Trump administration are about a show of force and optics more than anything else. “What you’re seeing now is a ton of marketing. They are trying to communicate that they're in charge, and I think it's not working,” says Levitt, now a law professor at Loyola Marymount University. “But it is really important to remember that the federal government isn't in charge of the election process. State and local officials are.”
WIRED has laid out the details of the DOJ’s legal efforts in California, Nevada, Washington, and Alaska below, which have all been met with disdain from local and state officials.
California
California is officially a hotbed of election controversy. In October, the DOJ filed a federal lawsuit seeking a court order against California to compel them to sequester mail-in ballots associated with approximately 20,000 voters, claiming that these voters were noncitizens. On Wednesday, a federal judge in a strong-worded order rejected the request.
“Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch,” US District Judge David Carter wrote in his order filed late on Wednesday.
Almost immediately, the DOJ filed an appeal and a federal court quickly denied it.
The judge pointed out that similar claims from the administration about noncitizens on voter rolls hadn’t held up to scrutiny, and he had “further questions of credibility” about how they arrived at that number in the first place.
Last week, a federal judge also ruled that the DOJ had to turn over its list of around 20,000 names to the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, so that the group could analyze the dataset. On Saturday, the group submitted a legal filing stating that an analysis of the list found that over 40 percent of the names weren’t even in the state’s current voter files. In response, the DOJ has suggested that the publication of their analysis violated the terms of the lists released to them, and is urging a federal judge to consider whether contempt charges might be applicable here.
“The DOJ has clearly written rules that prevent it from engaging in any investigative activity close to an election—rules that private attorney Todd Blanche cited when representing his client, Donald Trump, in September 2024,” Becker says. “But the DOJ continues to violate its own policies.”
To cap it all off, the DOJ issued grand jury subpoenas to California’s local election officials last week, indicating that despite repeated court losses it has no intention of backing down.
Alaska
In October, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit designed to block certification of the election result in Alaska’s Senate race if Democrat candidate Mary Peltola wins.
The reason for the lawsuit is the presence of a spoiler candidate on the ballot with a similar name as the incumbent Republican candidate Daniel Sullivan. The DOJ’s lawsuit was filed despite the Alaska Supreme Court ruling in the summer that Daniel J. Sullivan Jr could remain on the ballot as no laws had been broken.
A New York Times investigation last week alleged that Democrat-aligned operatives were involved in getting a spoiler candidate on the ballot, though Peltola’s campaign denied any involvement in the effort to get Daniel J. Sullivan Jr on the ballot. Asked about whether the common practice of putting spoiler candidates on the ballot was illegal, Todd Blanche said “it certainly should be.” On Truth Social, Trump said Peltola “should be removed from the Ballot and prosecuted.”
“I just want to clear the air: I knew nothing about any other candidates on the ballot except for me and the incumbent,” Peltola told supporters in Juneau last week. “I am not interested in tricking voters.”
On Thursday, Alaska Governor Michael Dunleavy ordered an investigation to determine whether state criminal or civil charges could be pursued against Peltola. In an interview with NewsNation, Dunleavy said that he could not commit to certifying victory for Peltola if that investigation was still ongoing.
“Dunleavy’s threat to overrule the will of Alaskan voters exemplifies what Alaskans hate about partisan politics and shows why he’s the least popular governor in the country,” a Peltola campaign spokeswoman tells WIRED. “Mary won’t be intimidated by Dunleavy, Sullivan, or any of their DC allies who are trying to steal this election from Alaskans before votes are counted—and she’s going to win this race by focusing on solutions to Sullivan’s price hiking policies and putting Alaska first.”
On Friday, the DOJ held a press conference in Anchorage and said that, in addition to their lawsuit seeking to block the certification of the election result if Peltola wins, they were also launching their own investigation to determine if federal civil or criminal charges could be applicable in this case. "We are aware of … the sprawling conspiracy to prop up Daniel J. Sullivan as a sham candidate,” said US Attorney for the District of Alaska Michael Heyman.
On Sunday, a federal judge threw out the DOJ’s lawsuit, ruling that their request likely violated Alaskans' right to a secret ballot. Hours later, the DOJ asked a federal appeals court to overturn the ruling.
Nevada
In July, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) claimed that they had identified over 270,000 noncitizen voters in just four states: California, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and New Jersey. But that bold assertion soon started to unravel.
DHS officials had also claimed that there were 15,903 noncitizens on Nevada’s voter rolls, but then later conceded in a meeting with Nevada officials that they didn’t have evidence. The number of suspected noncitizens on voter rolls then dropped down to 185, but there was no evidence to support that claim either.
“As for the 185 individuals, our records indicate that they were citizens,” Nevada’s Deputy Attorney General Greg Ott wrote in a letter to DHS. “You have provided nothing of substance to suggest otherwise.”
“The Department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross referenced them with known illegal aliens in our systems,” a DHS spokesperson tells WIRED about the situation. “It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections.”
Ott added in the letter that while Nevada takes allegations of noncitizen voting seriously, “it also has a strong interest in preventing the wrongful disenfranchisement of voters” and is “committed to preventing the chilling effect on the right to vote from taking actions based on unfounded and unverifiable allegations of noncitizen voting.”
Washington
Last week, the DOJ claimed that federal data appeared to show that 400 noncitizens were registered to vote in the state of Washington and demanded that officials isolate those ballots, describing them as “the tip of the iceberg.”
They received another withering letter in return: “The timing of your letter is profoundly disappointing,” wrote Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs. “If you had valid concerns about voter registrations, the time to raise them was a month ago.” Hobbs added that their decision to publicly raise their concerns so close to the election was “not a sign of good faith to ensure a free, fair, and accurate election.”
Hobbs added that the DOJ had failed to provide individualized proof that any of the people on the list were ineligible to vote, and didn’t offer any information about how they arrived at the lists of names or what sources were used. “Given the Department of Justice’s recent acts of election interference in California, Alaska, and now in Washington, it would be particularly inappropriate for Washington to simply assume the Department’s unsupported allegations here are credible.”
Texas
While not a filing by the Justice department, the Potter County Republican party has filed a lawsuit seeking to prevent the state from certifying the vote unless all Texas ballots are counted by hand.
The GOP’s basis for demanding a manual audit include purported threats from artificial intelligence’s ability to supposedly hack into virtually any voting machine undetected, a claim presented without evidence, and the presence of voting machine parts manufactured in China. Levitt, the former deputy assistant attorney general at the DOJ’s Civil Rights Division, described the lawsuit as “nuts.”
“That would be the technical term,” Levitt said. “I wish that they had filed the thing in Comic Sans on the back of a Burger King placemat, because I think that would help people evaluate how serious it is.”

Four men have been held for allegedly assaulting three Assamese workers at a fast-food outlet in Bengaluru after they complained that the noodles served to them were too spicy, police said on Monday.
The incident occurred late on October 29 at an eatery in Doddathoguru, under the Electronic City police station limits, they said.
CCTV footage of the alleged assault also surfaced online, showing the men attacking the workers.
According to police, a group of men allegedly in an inebriated state confronted the staff over the spice level of the noodles, following which an argument broke out.

The police subsequently traced and apprehended four men -- Ravi Kumar (31), Puttaswamy (35), Manohar (31) and Siddaraj, all residents of Doddathoguru.

It's true that on Oct. 27, Couric published an article under her own byline criticizing Trump. The veteran journalist didn't label it an "open letter" but it appeared to serve that purpose. She made the piece available as a paid, members-only story on her Substack blog. However …
… Some social media users shared the article with dozens of changes, including apparent omissions, that weren't reflected in Couric's published piece as of this writing. For example, Couric's article didn't call Trump's rhetoric "disgusting." The full article on her blog featured more paragraphs, sourcing with links and other details that were missing from the social media versions.
In late October, people shared a claim alleging journalist Katie Couric wrote an open letter to U.S. President Donald Trump in which she called his rhetoric "disgusting."
According to social media posts, Couric penned the piece to criticize Trump on a range of issues including immigration policy, "weaponization of the Justice Department," corruption and tariffs. She also purportedly wrote that Trump started the war in Iran contrary to his own campaign promise of no new wars and chided him over his "love affair" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
While it's true that Couric wrote and published a members-only piece excoriating Trump on her Substack blog ("How Do I Oppose Thee? Let Me Count the Ways"), it's false that a version of the letter rapidly spreading on the internet is identical to what Couric actually wrote. Therefore, we've rated this claim a mixture of true and false elements.
As the prime example, on Oct. 28, a Facebook user posted (archived) some text allegedly sourced from Couric's piece. The user wrote an introduction reading, "Most people outside of MAGA consider Katie Couric a thoughtful and fair journalist. Here's her letter to President Trump that lists the reasons she opposes him. Please share."
Snopes readers searched our website using various queries, for example "Katie Couric letter," "Katie Couric letter to Trump" and "Did Katie Couric write a letter to Trump." A search also located a similar X post (archived).
Couric truly published a paid, members-only article that appeared to double as an open letter to Trump, titled "How Do I Oppose Thee? Let Me Count the Ways," on her Substack blog. She labeled the article as "A few things to note before you vote (OK, maybe more than a few)."
However, the version of Couric's article circulating on social media contained dozens of changes, including apparent omissions, that distinguish it from the original. As one of many examples, Couric's piece did not call Trump's rhetoric "disgusting." The social media version also stripped out all evidential links sourcing Couric's many claims and omitted some of the paragraphs featured in her original text. Therefore, we rated the claim that Couric wrote the piece a mixture of true and false information.
The above-mentioned Facebook user published his post on Wednesday and only later updated it to add a link to Couric's Substack article.
About eight hours before that user shared the post, someone captured an archived version of the beginning of Couric's article. At that point in time, the word "disgusting" did not appear, indicating the Facebook user may have taken some liberties editing Couric's piece for social media.
The general drift of Couric's criticism remained mostly the same in the Facebook post. Even so, we make note of the fact the latter was worded differently and was inauthentic.
We contacted a representative for Couric to request comment and to ask if Couric changed her article after its initial publication. We haven't yet located evidence suggesting Couric updated her article without making note of the changes. We also sent a message to the Facebook user to ask if he changed words and omitted parts of Couric's text for his post, and will update this article if we receive any further information.
Regarding open letters to Trump, we previously investigated whether musician Tommy Lee wrote an open letter to Trump calling him a "f***ing lunatic."

Supreme Court rejects Trump's request to stop California counting disputed votes
- Published
The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.

The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.
About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.
In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".
On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.
California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.
They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible.
The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.
President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.
Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.
The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch".

How Kenyans got caught in $130m US ghost student scam
- Published
In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.
Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.
On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.
Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.
Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.
The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.
Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.
Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.
His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid.
US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.
The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.
At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.
"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.
The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.
"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.
But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.
People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.
"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.
He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.
The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.
Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.
The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.
"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.
The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.
In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.
With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.
The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.
In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.
Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.
Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.
If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.
Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

This woman defied lethal cancer. Can mRNA vaccines make that possible for others?
Donna Gustafson is living a cancer patient's fantasy.
At 72, the retired accountant hikes, travels, lifts weights, and exchanges adoring glances with Ed, the husband she married 50 years ago. All these moments are happening while she shows zero evidence of the Stage II pancreatic cancer that was supposed to kill her years ago.
"I have had 100% quality of life; I am back to where I was prior," Gustafson says.
"She's better than that," her husband interjects. "She's sassier, and she's in the best shape of her life — there's no question about that."
Seven years ago, Gustafson became the world's first recipient of an mRNA vaccine designed to treat pancreatic cancer, a highly lethal disease diagnosed in about 70,000 Americans every year. There are few effective treatments for the disease, but Gustafson's was a personalized version, created using samples of her tumor, aiming to reprogram her immune cells — training them, essentially, to recognize distinctive mutant proteins on cancerous cells and kill them.
mRNA vaccines having a moment
It's been a big year for cancer vaccines using mRNA, especially after drugmakers Merck and Moderna released results last month from the first major successful trial of mRNA vaccines for skin cancer, showing a 42% reduction in recurrence and death over two years.
A combination of technologies using mRNA, genomics and AI, helped create these vaccines, which are also being tested on lung, kidney, bladder and brain cancers. But researchers don't yet understand why some trials have failed, while others show eye-popping results in the form of people like Gustafson.
Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.
Gustafson, who splits her time between New Jersey and Florida, says she wasn't scared to be first to test this concept against pancreatic cancer. She credits her three grown daughters for finding and getting her into the trial. "It was a no brainer," she says. "I knew that statistically, the odds of my survival were low, and I was very happy to be offered some type of hope."
Gustafson received nine doses of the vaccine, along with surgery and chemotherapy. She was part of a small clinical trial involving 16 pancreatic cancer patients. The vaccine worked on half of the patients, and seven of those eight are still alive today.
For patients on these vaccines, treatment is also an easier option. It does not compare to chemotherapy, which requires hours of infusion and comes with after-effects that were "barbaric" for his wife, Ed Gustafson says with a shudder.
By contrast: The shots felt like nothing, Donna Gustafson says. "I had no symptoms, no side effects — to the point where I was actually worried that maybe it was not helping."
But it was. Very swiftly.
Surgeon and scientist Vinod Balachandran ran the trial at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York City. The vaccine used in his research is made in an expansive lab made up of hallways of freezers, desks, centrifuges and cytometers. Patients' responses to the treatment are measured in the lab. The oncologists and mathematicians who work there are dedicated to decoding pancreatic cancer, then reverse engineering the mRNA necessary to fight it.
A research analyst pulls up a graph on her computer, showing dozens of superimposed green lines — each representing the number of times an immune cell reproduces, Balachandran explains.
Looking at the graph representing Donna Gustafson's immune cell count, Balachandran notes how the lines shoot up, then remain high and flat — "a 10,000-fold increase" — reflecting how her immune system mass produced cancer-attacking cells and sustained it, for years beyond her last shot. "It just tells us that this response lasts," Balachandran says.
Balachandran says it was the strength and durability of such responses in half of the patients that, for him, blew open the possibility of mRNA vaccines. "Well, if you could generate such a strong immune response in the toughest of cancers, could this similarly develop cancer vaccines for a broad array of human cancers?," he says.
Promising future
This technology is now at an inflection point — with patients, doctors, researchers and investors. The National Cancer Institute, for example, is working on a partnership with private companies to fast-track research and development of more mRNA cancer vaccines. Balachandran and Sloan Kettering are part of that, with plans to expand production of personalized vaccines for patients on site.
Donna Gustafson says she and her husband have felt overwhelmingly lucky over the past seven years.
"I saw two more grandchildren be born and grow, many birthdays, holidays and Christmases with my family," she says.
With her husband, she's created and ticked off many items off her bucket list: skydiving, summiting, celebrating their 50th anniversary with the expectation of many more to come.
"We've done so many things — we probably have done so much more," Ed Gustafson says, before his wife picks up his sentence, "...if we had not had this experience."
"We live so much more for the day now," Ed Gustafson says, looking at his wife.

Working at the White House might be one of the most exclusive and prestigious jobs in the US, but you'd be surprised by how much some of the people around the president make each year.
For starters, having the top job — that is, being the president of the US — brings in a salary of $400,000, which some independently wealthy presidents, such as John F. Kennedy, Herbert Hoover, and Donald Trump, have chosen to donate instead.
While the figure is significantly higher than what the average American makes — $72,800 in 2025, according to the Social Security Administration — it's also less than you would need to be in the top 1% of earners across all US states.
In 2025, the top 1% of earners in Maryland and Virginia, which border the District of Columbia, earn $677,543 and $701,792 annually, respectively.
Government salaries often lag behind what professionals earn in the private sector, since serving the public isn't as lucrative as maximizing shareholder value. Still, to say that those working at the White House are underpaid would be an overstatement.
On July 1, the White House shared with Congress the salaries of all employees inside the president's executive office, including aides, advisors, and staff leaders, as it is legally required to.
Some of the highest-compensated workers around the president include policy advisors and legal counsel, while others are responsible for the president's communications and personnel management. Lower-paid roles include research assistants and press assistants.
Other notable names, like Marco Rubio and David Sacks, declared a $0 salary from the office of the president, either forgoing their salary or receiving compensation from other branches of government.
The White House did not respond to a request for comment.

భారత్లో పార్లమెంటు సభ్యులు కొనుగోలు చేసే కార్లు, ఏసీలు, విమాన టిక్కెట్లపై వస్తు సేవల పన్ను (GST) మినహాయింపు ఉంటుందని, అలాగే టోల్ టాక్స్ మినహాయింపు, ఉచిత రైలు ప్రయాణం వంటి సదుపాయాలు ఉంటాయంటూ సోషల్ మీడియాలో ఒక పోస్టు ప్రచారమవుతోంది. ఇందులో ఎంతవరకు నిజముందో చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: భారత ఎంపీలు కొనుగోలు చేసే కార్లు, ఏసీలు, విమాన టిక్కెట్లపై జీఎస్టీ మినహాయింపుతో పాటు టోల్ టాక్స్ మినహాయింపు, ఉచిత రైలు ప్రయాణ సదుపాయాలు పొందుతారు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఎంపీలకు ఉచిత రైలు, విమాన ప్రయాణాలతో పాటు టోల్ టాక్స్ మినహాయింపు ఉన్న మాట నిజమే. కానీ, వారు కొనుగోలు చేసే కార్లు, ఏసీలుపై వారికి ఎలాంటి జీఎస్టీ మినహాయింపు లేదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా ఎంపీలకు అందే ప్రయోజనాల గురించి పార్లమెంట్ అధికారిక వెబ్సైట్లో ఉన్న వివరాలను (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) పరిశీలించగా, ఒక ఎంపీ తన జీవిత భాగస్వామి, బంధువులు లేదా స్నేహితులతో కలిసి దేశంలో ఎక్కడికైనా ప్రయాణించేందుకు ఏడాదికి 34 సింగిల్ విమాన టికెట్లను ఉచితంగా పొందుతారు.
అలాగే, రైలులో దేశవ్యాప్తంగా ఎక్కడి నుంచి ఎక్కడికైనా ప్రయాణించడానికి ఎంపీతో పాటు వారి జీవిత భాగస్వామి లేదా మరో వ్యక్తికి ఫస్ట్ క్లాస్ ఏసీ లేదా ఎగ్జిక్యూటివ్ క్లాస్ రైలు టికెట్లు ఉచితంగా లభిస్తాయి. వారితో పాటు వచ్చే సహాయకుడికి కూడా ఉచితంగా ఏసీ టూ-టైర్ (2-Tier) పాస్ అందుతుంది.
ఇక భారత జాతీయ రహదారుల ప్రాధికార సంస్థ (NHAI) నిబంధనల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, ఎంపీలు ప్రయాణం చేసే వాహనానికి జాతీయ రహదారులపై టోల్ టాక్స్ నుంచి మినహాయింపు ఉంటుంది. ఎంపీలు తమ పదవీ కాలంలో రెండు వాహనాలకు టోల్ ఫ్రీ ఫాస్టాగ్ (FASTag) లను ఉపయోగించుకోవచ్చు.
అయితే, ఎంపీలు కొనుగోలు చేసే కార్లు, ఏసీలు లేదా ఇతర వస్తువులపై జీఎస్టీ మినహాయింపు ఉంటుందనడానికి ఎలాంటి ఆధారాల్లేవు. ఎంపీల ప్రయోజనాలను వివరించే ‘The Salary, Allowances and Pension of Members of Parliament Act, 1954’ లో గానీ, ప్రభుత్వ అధికారిక ప్రకటనల్లో గానీ ఇలాంటి వెసులుబాటు ఉన్నట్లు ఎక్కడా పేర్కొనలేదు.
చివరిగా, ఎంపీలకు ఉచిత విమాన, రైలు ప్రయాణాలు, టోల్ టాక్స్ మినహాయింపు ఉన్న మాట వాస్తవమే అయినా, వారు కొనుగోలు చేసే కార్లు, ఏసీలపై జీఎస్టీ మినహాయింపు వర్తించదు.

In late October and early November, a rumor spread that the gold covering of recently regilded equestrian bronze statues in Washington, D.C., was melting off.
U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Arts of Peace and Arts of War statues to be regilded to mark the 250th anniversary of the foundation of the U.S. on July 4. However, the statues' renovation did not end until more than a month after that date.
The claim spread across social media, including on Facebook and Reddit. On X, a post said, "$5 million gold refurbishing is now melting off the horse statues in Washington, D.C." (archived):
The post included an image showing drip streaks at the foot of the statue, suggesting the coating was dissolving off of the statue. There was no indication the image had been fabricated or misleadingly edited. We ran the image through the artificial intelligence detector Pangram, which found no evidence of AI generation. (It is worth noting these detectors are not infallible, however.)
The Mirror US, a tabloid, republished the image showing golden drip streaks from the top of the statue's pedestal, suggesting the new coating was melting off. The Irish Star, a digital outlet, also amplified the claim.
While the National Park Service confirmed there were streaks at the foot of the statue, Snopes could not directly confirm whether the streaking really meant the gilding of the statues was melting off. For this reason, we have left the claim unrated.
"The visible streaking is associated with moisture draining through an intentionally designed system to prevent condensation from accumulating within the statues," a spokesperson for the National Park Service, which oversees the statues' conservation, told Snopes in an email. "The streaks do not indicate damage to the gilding or the recent restoration work."
We have reached out to The Gilder's Studio, which received the contract to regild the statues. We are waiting for a response.
A search on the U.S. government spending database confirmed the U.S. Department of the Interior awarded $5.1 million to The Gilder's Studio, a company in Maryland, for "THE FULL CONSERVATION AND REGILDING OF FOUR (4) MONUMENTAL EQUESTRIAN BRONZE SCULPTURES." The contract was awarded on April 21, 2026, and it ended on Sept. 30.
The goal was to cover the statues in 23.75-karat gold, according to The Washington Sun (previously known as Notus.com). One X user pointed out that the melting point of gold was "2000 degrees" (the exact melting point of gold is 1,947 degrees Farenheit, which corresponds to 1,064 degrees Celsius). The fact that it was supposedly "melting off," the person said, suggested the statues had not, in fact, been covered in gold.
Meanwhile, an X user posted a video saying the streaks were from the golden coating dissolving from the rain (archived), rather than melting.
"Like all National Park Service lands, monuments, and historic sites, the Arts of War and Arts of Peace statuary require ongoing stewardship and care to ensure they are preserved for future generations," the NPS spokesperson added in the email. "The NPS will continue to monitor the condition of the statues as part of its regular preservation and maintenance program."
Some of Trump's efforts to refurbish monuments across the U.S. capital for the 250th anniversary of the country's foundation have been thwarted. For example, Snopes covered multiple claims about the renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, including the claim that it started to peel immediately after it was repainted.

Danish minister visits India to advance green energy, trade partnership, maritime ties
Lidegaard, who visited Mumbai and New Delhi during November 2-3, described India as an increasingly important partner for Denmark
Moves by India and Denmark to take their unique Green Strategic Partnership into its next phase got a boost during Danish business minister Martin Lidegaard’s visit to the country that focused on strengthening cooperation in trade, innovation, green technologies and maritime affairs.
Lidegaard, who visited Mumbai and New Delhi during November 2-3, described India as an increasingly important partner for Denmark, economically, technologically and geopolitically. Denmark has strong skills that can support India’s ambitions in areas such as renewable energy and AI, he said.
The next phase of the bilateral Green Strategic Partnership, established in 2020, envisages enhanced cooperation in areas of shared economic and strategic interest. A new joint action plan and more high-level visits in support of the partnership are currently being prepared.
“I am in India to learn about the speed and scale of your country’s transition, strengthen our partnership and open doors for Danish companies,” said Lidegaard, who began his visit on Monday in Mumbai, where he visited APM Terminals, operated by the Danish shipping company Maersk, and discussed new economic opportunities with Maharashtra Governor Jishnu Dev Varma.
In New Delhi, Lidegaard met commerce minister Piyush Goyal to discuss growing trade and economic opportunities against the backdrop of the expanding bilateral partnership and the upcoming India-European Union (EU) free trade agreement. More than 200 Danish companies operating in India employ more than 100,000 people.
He also met Union ports and shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal to discuss cooperation in green shipping, sustainable port development and green corridors. He also advanced the India-Denmark energy partnership while meeting Union renewable energy minister Pralhad Joshi and participating in the Bharat Renewable Energy Summit & Expo 2026.
Discussions focused on expanding commercial opportunities and Denmark’s support for India’s transition to a more efficient, reliable and sustainable energy system. Denmark is the second-largest government contributor to the International Solar Alliance outside India.
