LOWVILLE, N.Y. — A child in rural northern New York has died after contracting measles, marking the state’s first death from the disease in 30 years, state officials announced Monday.
The child died in Lewis County, about 93 miles (150 kilometers) north of Syracuse, Gov. Kathy Hochul said.
The U.S. stopped the domestic spread of measles in 2000 by maintaining high vaccination rates, but they have fallen in recent years to below the 95% coverage needed to prevent outbreaks of the viral disease.
Hochul, a Democrat, said the child’s death is “a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses.”
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed three measles-associated deaths in the U.S. this year, but state health departments have reported higher numbers. Pennsylvania health officials have reported five deaths this year and are investigating a possible sixth.
Hochul declared a disaster emergency in early October because of measles cases in neighboring states and in rural areas of New York. The executive order extended the pool of people who can administer measles vaccines to include paramedics, midwives and others, and it allowed nurses to join doctors in ordering testing.

NEW YORK — A person in Washington state has died from complications of the bird flu, the first such U.S. death in a year.
The Yakima County resident, who had previous health conditions, was exposed to avian influenza at a dairy with infected cattle and had been hospitalized. The person died Sunday, county health officials said.
Two other U.S. deaths have been tied to bird flu since it became a national public health concern in 2024. The first, announced in January 2025, was an elderly person in Louisiana who had a version of bird flu known as H5N1. The other, in Washington state, died in November 2025 from a rarer version called H5N5.
Yakima County officials did not release any additional details about the person who recently died. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said the person was infected with H5N1.
County officials have reported that 33 dairy herds recently have tested positive for H5N1.
They say three human infections have been linked to exposure at a dairy, and that the Yakima Health District is working with the state health department to find people who were in close contact with those people and monitor them for symptoms.
The H5N1 bird flu has been spreading widely among wild birds, poultry, cows and other animals for several years. Health concerns escalated in early 2024 when infections spread among U.S. livestock. Its presence in the environment increases the chances that people will be exposed, and potentially catch it, officials have said.
More than 70 human infections have been reported in the U.S. since the beginning of 2024, according to the CDC. But there is no known person-to-person spread and the risk to the general public is low, the agency says.
The agency analyzed the genetic sequence of the virus from the person who died in Washington and found no changes that would make the virus spread more easily or cause more severe illness, a CDC spokesperson said Monday.
Officials continue to urge people who have contact with sick or dead birds to take precautions, including wearing respiratory and eye protection and gloves when handling poultry. People who work on farms are considered to be at higher risk.
— Mike Stobbe

Popular Australian children's author jailed over child exploitation offences
- Published
Australian children's author Craig Silvey has been sentenced to seven months in jail for possessing and distributing child exploitation material.
In handing down her sentence, Judge Hayley Cormann called Silvey's actions "repulsive" and "degrading".
In January, Silvey was arrested after police raided his home in Western Australia and seized several electronic devices. In May, the 44-year-old pleaded guilty to possessing and distributing child exploitation material and in October he was jailed pending his sentencing.
The father-of-three is best known for his award-winning young adult novel Jasper Jones and children's book Runt, both of which were later made into movies.
"You have devastated and betrayed the trust of thousands of people, and you've let entire communities down," Cormann said on Monday, according to WA Today.
Police said Silvey had online chats, in which he discussed child exploitation, open at the moment they turned up to raid his house.
In them, the court heard, Silvey had described himself as "extremely open minded" and "obsessed with taboos".
He'd discussed his sexual interest in children as young as five with another user of a pornography site, and detectives found images and videos of other adults abusing children on his devices.
He was initially charged with four offences, but prosecutors later dropped two.
Prosecutors said Silvey contributed to the "cycle of abuse" victimising the children in the images, and argued a harsh sentence was required.
However, the author's defence lawyer said he did not have a "sexual interest in children" and was seeking out "the most depraved material" as a form of "emotional" self harm.
"His behaviour provided temporary relief from psychological agitation," Eloise Barker said.
She said Silvey had displayed genuine remorse for his offending, and that his high profile and the resulting media scrutiny - which lead to his former partner and children relocating interstate - was already a form of punishment.
Judge Cormann did not accept many of her arguments, and said Silvey's offending was extremely serious.
"These children, the victims of this type of offending, are real and are traumatised… the consequences for them from these abuses are long lasting and very, very traumatic," she said, according to The Australian.
Silvey was sentenced to seven months in jail, backdated to 22 October. He is eligible for parole.
Silvey's coming-of-age novel Jasper Jones sold more than half a million copies and was awarded the Book of the Year Award by the nation's peak publishing body in 2010.
The novel, set in Western Australia with two teenage boys as the main characters, was also shortlisted for the International Dublin Literary Awards and the Miles Franklin Literary Award.
It was later turned into a film starring Toni Collette and Hugo Weaving in 2017 as well as a stage play.
Another of his acclaimed works is 2022's Runt, about the adventures of an 11-year-old girl and her stray dog and set in the Australia outback. It was also adapted for film in 2024, featuring Celeste Barber.
Since his arrest, publishers and book shops have pulled his works from shelves while schools in some states have removed Jasper's books from teaching lists.

Two attacks in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have killed 4 workers responding to the Ebola outbreak and injured 5 others.
The attacks occurred overnight on a shared living camp in Biakato Mines and an Ebola response coordination office in Mangina.
“We are heartbroken that people have died in the line of duty as they worked to save others,” said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, World Health Organization Director-General. “The world has lost brave professionals.”
The dead include a member of a vaccination team, two drivers and a police officer. No WHO staff are among those killed, one staff member was injured.
“My heart goes out to the family and friends of the first responders killed in these attacks,” said Dr Matshidiso Moeti, WHO Regional Director for Africa. “We are doing everything possible to bring the injured and front-line workers in the impacted areas to safety. These constant attacks must stop. We will continue to work with the DRC Government, partners and MONUSCO to ensure the security of our staff and other health workers.”
In the last week, there were 7 cases of Ebola, down from a peak of over 120 per week in April 2019.
“Ebola was retreating. These attacks will give it force again, and more people will die as a consequence,” said Dr Tedros. “It will be tragic to see more unnecessary suffering in communities that have already suffered so much. We call on everyone who has a role to play to end this cycle of violence.”
The situation is still evolving. WHO will provide updates as new information comes in.

An Indian court has ordered the release of two leaders of India’s Cockroach movement, who were jailed last week amid a mounting state crackdown on youth-led protests.
The two leaders of the Cockroach Janta party (CJP) movement, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, had spent a week in Delhi’s Tihar jail after being arrested by Delhi police last week.
On Wednesday, a special magistrate ordered that Das and Ranka be released, despite efforts by police to keep them in prison. They were made to sign a bond pledging no further breach of peace.
Their arrest came after a draconian police crackdown on a CJP march held in the capital two weeks ago, to protest alleged manipulation of the country’s electoral roll, led to the barricading of central Delhi and thousands of young people being detained.
Das and Ranka were taken into custody for a second time days later after they jumped police barricades and held up an Indian flag at a site in central Delhi that police had cordoned off.
The pair were charged with trespass and violating the peace and sent to jail for five days, which was then extended by two further days. Their detention had provoked outrage among leaders and supporters of the youth movement, who accused the government of “cowardice” for jailing CJP leaders for holding a peaceful protest.
After the magistrate’s ruling on Wednesday evening, Das said that “truth has triumphed”.
The release of the two leaders is likely to come as a blow to the ruling Narendra Modi government, which has implemented an unforgiving crackdown on recent protests that have erupted across India.
The CJP, alongside the opposition alliance, student groups and civil society, have been calling for the resignation of the chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing a revision of the electoral roll that benefits Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) and has led to more than 130 million names being deleted from the voter register. The BJP has denied any interference.
The CJP began as an online satire earlier this year, but has since grown into a fully fledged political movement, challenging the powerful Modi government. Over the summer, it was Cockroach-led protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister after sustained demonstrations.
Abhijeet Dipke, the founder of the CJP movement, vowed over the weekend that the Modi regime and threat of jail would not intimidate the Cockroaches. Dipke was also detained on Friday after he called for a peaceful demonstration in central Delhi where CJP supporters would gather and wave the Indian flag in solidarity with Das and Ranka.
He had said that, once his fellow Cockroach leaders were released, they would “gather, re-strategise, and determine how to move forward”.
“The illegal arrests and detentions we have witnessed over the past few days indicate an attempt to intimidate us,” said Dipke. “But we will not be cowed down or retreat. This is a long battle and we are prepared for it.”

For Ukraine's Kherson region, a short ceasefire meant a momentary return to normal life
A brief ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region has ended
KHERSON, Ukraine — In this city where Russian drones usually fill the skies, Olena Soboleva could not easily walk down the street to meet her best friend, Anna Herasimenko.
Then came last week's truce, negotiated by First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, in a corner of southern Ukraine that included Kherson.
This weekend, the two friends, both 21, took the opportunity to venture outside to autumnal skies clear of drones and guided bombs.
"No drones, no explosions," Soboleva says. "No one wants to kill you."
They passed families strolling with their kids, shoppers stocking up on supplies and couples holding hands. They lined up at a cafe filled with paintings of cats.
"The city seems alive," says Herasimenko, "just like it used to be."
Over the weekend, she had also ventured to a salon.
"I did my nails," she says, showing off fresh burgundy polish. "The streets are full of people, just as they were in the past."
Loading...
The truce ended Sunday night. Russia and Ukraine agreed to it in order to help Oleshky, a town across the Dnipro River from Kherson. Russian troops occupied Oleshky in 2022 and mined the land around it. Food and medicine rarely got through. NPR spoke to the families of residents there, who said their loved ones survived on pickles and boiled weeds.
Over the weekend, hundreds of Oleshky residents were evacuated, eventually escorted into northern Ukraine on buses. Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman — the country's independent watchdog for human rights — thanked Melania Trump for ensuring that the ceasefire, which lasted from Oct. 27 to Nov. 1, happened.
"I believe they can be upheld and honored," Lubinets said about truces between Ukraine and Russia.
Even a short pause in hostilities was a respite for Kherson. Russian troops occupied the city for several months in 2022, until local partisans spied for Ukrainian soldiers, who then forced the Russians out of the city.
Since 2024, Russian troops based across the river have hunted Kherson residents with FPV (first-person-view) drones strapped with explosives. The highway into Kherson is shrouded in tunnels of heavy mesh nets to protect locals from these drones. These anti-drone nets also cover Kherson's streets and many of its buildings.
This weekend, cars pulled up next to the Greek-style monument marking the city's gateway.
Svitlana Vorobiova, a retired police officer, drove here from a safer city where she now lives. She took photos with her children at the monument.
"I have a place in Kherson, and my parents are also here," she says, and her voice breaks. Tears fill her eyes.
"I brought my son with me," Vorobiova says. "He hasn't been here in four years. He said, 'I cannot believe I'm in my hometown!'"
Inside the city, Volodymyr Mykolaienko, a former mayor of Kherson, strolls past the crushed remains of a once-grand administrative building. Locals stop him and shake his hand. He says he's happy to see so many people outside.
"I walk around the city a lot these days," he says. "I cannot sit still at home."
Mykolaienko, 66, spent years as a prisoner of war in Russia, confined to tiny rooms, starved and tortured. Russian troops arrested him in Kherson in early 2022, when the city was under Russian occupation. Mykolaienko was freed last year in a prisoner exchange and returned to Kherson, where his family still lives.
This truce allowed him to visit his father's grave. The cemetery is in a part of the city that's usually filled with drones.
"I could not hold myself back," he says. "I was able to do exactly what I have long wanted to do — to talk to my father, pray, thank him for my life and to tell him what was happening to our city."
At a busy bus stop, oncology nurse Olena Yehorova smiles at a gray-haired man playing folk music on his accordion.
"This truce has been such a relief," she says. "The people in our city have been able to breathe. Of course, we still walk around with caution, because you cannot trust the Russians."
She couldn't help looking up at the sky. A few hours later, the truce was over. She said she expects new attacks to resume at any time.
NPR's Polina Lytvynova contributed to this report from Kyiv.

A video claiming to show a woman police officer mistreating a Muslim man is being shared on social media (here, here, here). Let’s verify the claim made in the post.
Claim: The video shows a woman police officer mistreating a Muslim man.
Fact: The video is scripted content on the channel named‘Amit Dixit Social Message’. The video carries a disclaimer that the video is fictitious. The channel features several videos with the same characters seen in the viral video. Hence, the claim made in the post is FALSE.
A reverse image search using keyframes from the viral video led us to an extended version of the footage uploaded to a Facebook page named ‘Amit Dixit Social Message ‘. The video carries a disclaimer that the video is fictitious.
The same video from a different angle is uploaded to a YouTube channel with the same name on 19 September 2025, with the title in Hindi: ‘Salim misbehaved at the police station; The police put him inside.’

TRAI mandates AI-led complaint centres, 16-hour human support
TRAI mandates 24/7 AI-enabled complaint centres, human support for 16 hours daily, faster appeals and penalties up to ₹20 lakh for mishandled cases.
The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) has directed telecom operators and internet service providers (ISPs) to run round-the-clock complaint centres that can be handled by AI agents, while mandating human assistance for at least 16 hours a day. It has also introduced penalties of up to ₹20 lakh per quarter per service area for improper disposal or handling of consumer disputes, under amended telecom consumer complaint redressal rules released on Monday.
TRAI said the rules would be published in the gazette.
For the first time, the telecom regulator has included AI-based customer care services in a binding rule under the Telecom Consumer Complaint Redressal (Fourth Amendment) Regulations, 2026. The rules, amended after more than a decade, were last revised on July 1, 2014.
The amended regulation 3(3) requires AI systems to “operate with appropriate human oversight” and consumers to receive “a notification” that they are speaking to an AI agent.
Under the amended rules, service providers will be charged ₹1,000 for every complaint and ₹5,000 for every appeal found to have been wrongly disposed of, with penalties capped at ₹20 lakh per quarter per service area.
TRAI also directed operators to submit quarterly performance reports, including number of complaints and appeals received, disposed of and pending, time taken for disposal and feedback survey results, in a format specified by the regulator.
Late submission of quarterly reports will attract penalties of up to ₹5,000 a day for 15 days and ₹20,000 a day thereafter, capped at ₹10 lakh per licensed service area.
The draft regulations were released on May 7, with stakeholder comments invited until June 12 and countercomments until June 19. TRAI received 32 comments and 24 countercomments, which it uploaded to its website. An open house discussion was held on July 17.
Operators opposed the 24x7 complaint-centre requirement on cost grounds. In its explanatory memorandum, TRAI said some stakeholders objected to round-the-clock operations, “citing disproportionate costs and limited benefit”.
The regulator responded that the requirement “does not necessarily imply deployment of the same level of resources 24x7”.
TRAI received 73,081 complaints in 2025-26, up from 44,733 in 2023-24, pointing to dissatisfaction with operators’ grievance redressal systems.
Some stakeholders have also questioned whether TRAI can impose penalties through regulations. The penalties under the current rule are new, however the regulator has been imposing financial disincentives under the Standards of Quality of Service of Access (Wireline and Wireless) and Broadband (Wireline and Wireless) Service Regulations, 2024. This was also a concern for some stakeholders who said this may result in double penalties on telecom service providers. But TRAI said the two serve “distinct regulatory objectives”.
The telecom regulator has also scrapped the advisory committees and replaced them with oversight committees in every service provider to oversee and periodically review the functioning of its grievance redressal mechanism. Consumer groups, who sent 22 of the 32 comments on the draft, opposed the move, with one saying it makes the system “operator reviewing operator”.
TRAI said the committees caused delays, making the appellate process inadequate. Appeal timelines have also been halved, with consumers getting 15 days instead of 30 to appeal and the appellate authority is required to decide within 15 days.
Other key changes
Helplines must use a standard IVRS menu with separate options for complaints, appeals and queries, along with a human option and a call-back facility. Complaints can be registered through apps and websites, with status updates by SMS and email, and service must be offered in a state official language besides Hindi and English.
After every closed complaint, consumers will be asked to rate the resolution from 1 to 5, and the results will be published quarterly. Disputes must be resolved through a non-chargeable numbers instead of a dedicated toll-free system, providers must set up dedicated desks and accessible apps for persons with disabilities, and records must be kept for six months, up from three.
ISPs with 10,000 or fewer subscribers are exempt from the rules, which consumer groups said leaves small-town and rural users without a remedy. Satellite service providers are also covered under the rules, while OTT services are outside TRAI’s jurisdiction.
The rules take effect 30 days after Gazette publication. The oversight committee, survey and reporting rules apply after 60 days, and the 24x7 centres, IVRS and app rules after 90 days.

Gajju Khan is smiling as he sits in an unfinished building in the northern Indian state of Punjab in the late afternoon. The 87-year-old is hopeful that before he dies he will hear the azaan, the Muslim call to prayer, echo across his village once again when the mosque is completed.
The last time he heard it here was when he was eight years old, living with his parents in Tira Maloya, a village in Chandigarh, not far from where he lives now.
He is also excited because the mosque has been funded almost entirely by the Sikhs and Hindus living in his village of Jakhiwal, in Fatehgarh Sahib district. Even though he fondly remembers how Sikh neighbours sheltered him and his brothers when brutal sectarian violence erupted during partition in 1947, he never expected a house of worship to be rebuilt for the 18 Muslim families who remain in the village.
“This was my maternal home. My parents sent my two brothers and me here to save us from the bloodshed – they were killed back in our village,” says Khan. “Sikhs hid us from the patrols of men with sticks and burning torches.”
Khan reserves his deepest gratitude for Bibi Rajinder Kaur, 77, a Sikh villager who persuaded her grandson to donate a parcel of their farmland to build a mosque. She did so, she says, because every other faith had a place to gather, while local Muslims had none.
“There is no deed better than giving someone a place to worship,” Kaur says. “Also, it felt like we needed to appease God for the blood this land had seen. The Muslims in our village had to travel 4km [2.5 miles] to another village just to pray.”
During the partition of British India, the border severed Punjab in two, unleashing catastrophic communal blood-letting and forced migrations that virtually emptied the eastern, Indian side of the region of its Muslim population. Hundreds of village mosques were abandoned, desecrated or turned into cattle sheds and storage units.
But over the past decade, several rural Sikh and Hindu communities have quietly stepped forward to restore these places of worship. Even in villages without a Muslim population, people have invited Muslim farmhands and clerics from nearby districts to pray in these newly revived mosques.
About 50 miles fromJakhiwal, in Sangrur district’s Punawal village, Jaspal Sharma, who comes from a family of Hindu priests, donated his land for the construction of a new mosque and hosted a feast for the entire village at its inauguration in February.
Sharma, 48, says the donation was about neighbourly duty. The village has 550 households, of which just a very small proportion are Muslim.
“It’s right opposite our house, so the sound of prayers five times a day creates a lively atmosphere. We like it,” says Sharma. “And it wasn’t just us; everyone in the village, Hindus and Sikhs together, contributed what they could. Some gave money; others donated bricks and cement.”
For Sukhjinder Singh Pandher and his brother, restoring a local shrine in Malerkotla’s Umarpura village was an act of filial reverence. Their grandfather fled west Punjab during partition to settle in India.
“Nobody is treated as different here,” says Pandher, sharing a cup of tea with his Muslim neighbours on the bare floor of the restored mosque. “Eid and Gurpurab [Sikhs’ most holy festival] are celebrated by both communities with the same fervour.
“We live as one and no matter what happens in the rest of the country, the mood here is that of love and unity. Punjab’s conscience cannot tolerate cruelty against a being, irrespective of caste and religion,” he says.
Pandher points to the syncretic traditions and blending of cultures that are deeply rooted in Punjabi history, noting the popular belief that the 16th-century Sufi saint Hazrat Mian Mir was invited to lay the foundation stone of Sikhism’s holiest site, the Harmandir Sahib, or Golden Temple, in Amritsar.
Inspired by the former shahi, or chief, imam of Punjab, Maulana Habib-ur-Rehman Sani Ludhianvi, non-Muslim villagers have contributed to more than 165 such mosques in the past nine years.
“Partition tore at the natural fabric of Punjab,” says the current shahi imam, Maulana Muhammad Usman Rehmani Ludhianvi, who succeeded his father in 2021. “This state itself is an inquilab [revolution]. Online, there is immense polarisation, but on the ground in our villages, ordinary people are still choosing to protect each other.”

How sporting events are being impacted by Middle East conflict
- Published
The 2027 Asian Cup is just the latest event to be postponed in the Middle East amid concerns about missile attacks by Yemen's Houthi movement.
The 24-team tournament - Asia's version of the Euros - was scheduled to take place in Saudi Arabia from 7 January to 5 February next year.
The Asian Cup has now been delayed by almost a year, and will be held between 23 December, 2027 and 21 January, 2028.
Sport in the region had already been heavily affected by the US-Iran conflict, which led to the cancellation of the Bahrain and Saudi Arabian Formula 1 Grand Prix weekends in April this year.
Now the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi at the end of the year are also in doubt due to that ongoing situation and the current conflict involving the Houthis. If they are cancelled, F1 would have lost four of its 24 events this year.
It is not just football and F1 that have been forced to cancel, reschedule or move high-profile events, and many more remain under threat.
BBC Sport takes a look at the situation across the sports.
Football
The Saudi Pro League has, for the most part, managed to carry on as usual.
Several domestic league games had to be postponed, including three fixtures last month as the situation escalated.
The games were moved in the immediate aftermath of the attack on a major airport in Riyadh - though the SPL said they were switched "as a result of mandatory minimum rest periods between matches and to accommodate logistical requirements".
Following the postponement of the Asian Cup, this weekend's full round of Saudi Pro League has been called off.
The league once again has not attributed this to conflict in the region, instead saying the calendar would be recalibrated after the cancellation of the Asian Cup to achieve "a more balanced distribution of fixtures".
The AFC Champions League has been affected as well.
Cristiano Ronaldo and Kingsley Coman were among Al-Nassr's star players who did not to fly to Uzbekistan this week "given the pressure of matches and the amount of travel involved".
Al-Wasl of the United Arab Emirates also opted not to fly to Saudi Arabia to play Al-Nassr, and the match will be rearranged.
Meanwhile, the wife of Ollie Watkins, who plays for Riyadh-based Al-Hilal, posted on TikTok that she would be staying in the UK with their two children "until it calms down".
"We've had a bit of a plot twist," said Ellie Watkins. "I have come back to the UK for a little bit.
"There's just a little bit of conflict and things going on over in Saudi and we basically decided just to stay here.
"I felt like I needed to do that for the kids so there is some form of normality until we can get back out there and all be together."
Other well-known stars playing in the country include Gabriel Martinelli, Tijjani Reijnders, Darwin Nunez, Ivan Toney, Alexandre Lacazette, Ruben Neves, Sadio Mane and Joao Felix.
Formula 1
Andrew Benson, F1 Correspondent
Formula 1 has a major dilemma about racing in the Middle East both at the end of this season and the beginning of next.
Most pressingly, the 2026 season is due to end with races in Qatar on 27-29 November and Abu Dhabi on 4-6 December.
As things stand, the sport is pressing ahead with plans to go to those races after being given security reassurances from various governmental sources that it should be safe.
There are, though, many people within the sport with misgivings about going.
Should the situation in the Middle East deteriorate in the next week or so, they could be called off and replaced with a single event in Imola in Italy on the Abu Dhabi weekend.
The 2027 season is scheduled to start in Bahrain on 12-14 March, with Saudi Arabia hosting on the following weekend.
But as things stand between Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni Houthi separatists, that race could not go ahead, and is likely to be cancelled if nothing changes by December.
Bahrain and Saudi Arabia are linked by a causeway, at the Saudi end of which is a facility belonging to state oil company Aramco, which has been targeted by the Houthis, while it joins Bahrain close to the F1 track.
So Bahrain is also be in jeopardy.
One option being discussed is to hold that race in Malaysia, as was done in October this year.
Other motorsport
The Dakar Rally was due to take place in Saudi Arabia in January but has been moved "following recent developments in the region".
Now the 2027 edition will begin in Loule-Faro in Portugal and end in Marrakech in Morocco.
Saudi Arabia had hosted the previous seven editions of Dakar, and the intention is to return in 2028.
Rally Saudi Arabia, part of the 2026 FIA World Rally Championship, which was scheduled for 12–15 November, has been cancelled.
But MotoGP will still take place this weekend at the Lusail International Circuit in Doha, Qatar, with three races left in the season.
It will go ahead without the Yamaha team, which has been advised against travelling from Japan.
Tennis
The Six Kings Slam, which should have begun on Saturday in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, has been postponed by two months.
It is now scheduled to run from 27 December to 30 December at the ANB Arena, located about 31km away from the King Khalid International Airport, which was the target of an attack on 10 October that killed 13 people and injured 308 others.
Novak Djokovic, Alexander Zverev, Carlos Alcaraz, Alex de Minaur, Taylor Fritz and Learner Tien are due to compete.
But the 2026 WTA Finals, this weekend's season-ending championship of the women's tour, will not take place in Saudi Arabia.
A mutual agreement was reached to terminate a hosting agreement early, and it will instead take place at Indian Wells in the United States.
Boxing
Saudi Arabia regularly hosts title fights and high-profile bouts.
Only last week, Mexican legend Canelo Alvarez reclaimed the WBC super middleweight championship against Christian Mbilli.
But the whole of the card did not survive as Lindolfo Delgado withdrew from his IBF lightweight title fight against Arthur Biyarslanov over safety concerns.
Next on the schedule is the Zuffa Boxing event, which will feature Carlos Adames against Welshman Gerome Warburton in Riyadh Season 13, on 14 November.
WWE
The WWE Crown Jewel 2026 event will still take place this weekend, but at a new venue.
It was originally scheduled for the Kingdom Arena, before being switched to the ANB arena.
The reigning men's and women's world champions of WWE's Raw and SmackDown face each other.
Roman Reigns, Sami Zayn, Liv Morgan, Chelsea Green, Bron Breakker, Austin Theory, Penta, Je'Von Evans, Cody Rhodes and Randy Orton are on the bill.
Other sports impacted
The FIFAe Finals, an esports tournament series organised by Fifa, should have taken place in Jeddah last month but was cancelled.
This week's UCI Urban Cycling World Championships, for the world's leading riders in trials and BMX Freestyle, in Riyadh was called off too, with a decision due "on the sporting consequences of this announcement".
The PIF Saudi International event, the season finale of the Asian Tour, will not be held between 18-21 November at Riyadh Golf Club.
After "an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament" the decision was taken to call it off.
And on Tuesday, the Professional Triathletes Organisation said it was moving the Saudi Arabia T100 and World Triathlon Cup, in Jeddah, from the end of this month to 16-17 April.

Washington, Nov 03: The US has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a US official says.
Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke Monday on condition of anonymity, said “Iranians using surface to air missiles against US assets” had been targeted.
The strikes, which appeared to be limited as opposed to a full return to hostilities, came on the eve of crucial American midterm elections. Trump has previously said the US wouldn't launch strikes on Iran before the midterms.
The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on US gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.
Vice President JD Vance told reporters earlier Monday that he just spoke to Trump about talks with Iran and said that “the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.”
US Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism on Monday that a deal can still be struck to prevent President Donald Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the crucial midterm elections in the United States.
Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details about the contents of that correspondence. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with “medical supplies and various things.”
But Vance on Monday suggested there's reason to believe that the US and Iran could still come to an agreement.
“We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians,” Vance told reporters on Monday when asked about the letter. “I actually just spoke with the president of the United States about an hour ago about this. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We're going to keep on working at it.”
Vance's comments came as the region remains on edge about the prospects of the US resuming full-scale operations against Iran. The backchannel efforts are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the 8-month-old war that's rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.
Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for another wave of strikes on Iran after Tuesday's elections in the United States, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.
A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu to form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.
The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the US lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.
They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.
One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the US administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision.
Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.
Other US allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.
The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump's discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.
Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone on Monday with US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about “the latest regional and international developments" and the Houthis' continued attacks on Saudi Arabia.
Trump downplays scale of Iran conflict on Election Day eve
Netanyahu had pushed for renewed strikes even before the Israeli election as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
But the war has also loomed large for American voters ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.
Oil prices dropped sharply on Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war between the US and Iran appeared to show signs of headway. Rising prices at the pump, a byproduct of the war, have been a weight on Trump's Republican Party as it tries to maintain control of both chambers of Congress.
Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost US taxpayers at least $47 billion.
“I don't know if you even call it a war, because we haven't been doing any fighting for months,” Trump said.
Netanyahu has not commented on Iran since the Israeli election, and there was no word from his office on the latest call with Trump.
Iran says it is prepared for war while pursuing diplomacy
Iran wants guarantees that the US will implement its side of any agreement. The US and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was engaged in negotiations over its disputed nuclear program.
Iranian officials say publicly they are prepared for war or diplomacy.
The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, met with Iran's military chiefs and said the response to “any kind and level of threat” from the US or Israel should be immediate and without “geographic limits,” and urged an expansion of the list of potential targets.
A recent analysis by The Associated Press found that Iranian strikes on more than two dozen US bases since the start of the war have caused billions of dollars in equipment damage.
Khamenei has not been seen publicly since the opening strikes by Israel and the US on Feb. 28, which killed his father, the previous supreme leader.
Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, told state television that “the tone has completely changed” from the US and called it a “very good sign.” He also gave no details about the letter he received from Vance, which Iran acknowledged last week, and said he had not responded.
Meanwhile, Vance told reporters on Monday that the Republican administration's foremost concern is Iran agreeing to take substantive action on its nuclear program.
“We do think that there is a pathway there, but it really does require a firm commitment and a verifiable commitment that they don't rebuild that nuclear program,” Vance added.

What a new global study on pain reveals about women’s experiences
The study’s findings about women having a higher prevalence of pain across anatomical sites, resonate with observations from India, say experts, noting that even so, women’s pain has historically been under-recognised, misunderstood, or inadequately treated
pain killers and a woman in pain, expression of suffering.
| Photo Credit: blueclue
Women are more likely than men to report pain across every one of the 11 anatomical sites examined in a global study involving more than 6.1 million people across 118 countries. The study found that differences were particularly pronounced for facial pain, headaches and abdominal pain.
Published in Nature Medicine, the study found that women had 83% higher relative prevalence of facial pain, 74% higher prevalence of headaches and 60% higher prevalence of stomach or abdominal pain than men. Women were also more likely to report high-intensity and widespread pain, highlighting a disparity that extends beyond the occurrence of pain to its severity and distribution.

Kolkata witnessed an unusual procession on Saturday, October 31, as thousands of book lovers took to the streets carrying books instead of political flags. Called “Let’s Walk for Books”, the march was organised in protest against the alleged vandalism of Left-affiliated bookstalls by BJP workers and police during Durga Puja festivities across West Bengal.
The procession began at College Square, the hub of Kolkata’s literary and academic life as well as the publishing industry, following an appeal circulated on social media over several days. Among those who urged people to join were prominent academics, writers and public figures, including Pabitra Sarkar, Shamik Bandyopadhyay, Jawhar Sircar, Kumar Rana, Malini Bhattacharya, Ziad Ali, Paranjoy Guha Thakurta and Shobhanlal Dasgupta.
The appeal, which urged participants to carry a book each, said books were facing a ‘barbaric’ attack across the state.
Bookstalls have long been part of Durga Puja festivities in Bengal, along side fairs, music, theatre and poetry events.
This year, however, several bookstalls were allegedly vandalised, their organisers assaulted, and books thrown onto the streets and trampled underfoot, the appeal noted. In Jadavpur, an attempt was allegedly made to demolish bookstalls with the help of central forces. A Kolkata Municipal Corporation garbage truck was also brought in to remove newly printed books.
The appeal described the incidents as an assault on Bengal’s cultural traditions and warned that continued attacks on books could damage the state’s reputation and values. It called on writers, artists, students, teachers, publishers, booksellers and others to assemble in front of the Vidyasagar statue at College Square, carrying a book of their choice as a symbol of resistance.
The Rally
Responding to the appeal, people began gathering around College Street from 3 pm. Students from colleges and universities joined participants across generations, from middle-aged people to the elderly. Almost everyone carried a book.
The collection reflected a wide range of political, literary and religious traditions. Participants carried works by Rabindranath Tagore, Karl Marx, Bhagat Singh, Sukanta Bhattacharya and Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, alongside books by contemporary writers such as Arundhati Roy. Some carried works by Syama Prasad Mookerjee, while others held copies of the Bhagavad Gita, the Ramayana, the Mahabharata and books on Swami Vivekananda.
Scheduled to begin at 3.30 pm, the march started around 3.45 pm, with several thousand people taking part. In a city accustomed to processions marked by political flags, banners and party slogans, this one stood out. Participants carried books and sang songs.
They sang the Bengali translation of Turkish poet Nazim Hikmet’s song “They Don’t Let Us Sing”, as well as Rabindranath Tagore’s “Bnadh Bhenga Dao”. International protest songs, including “We Shall Overcome” and its Bengali version, “Amra Korbo Joy”, also featured in the procession.
Large banners, or tifos, carried messages such as “Don’t Burn Books, Read Them” and “Books versus Bulldozer”.
The procession also offered glimpses of solidarity among participants. An elderly newspaper vendor distributed candies to those taking part. In a video shared on social media, he said he had joined the march because of his love for books. Although financial difficulties had prevented him from completing his education, he said, he had always loved reading and ensured that his daughter completed her education.
Starting in front of College Square and Calcutta University, the march passed the National Book Agency and the iconic sweet shops, Putiram and Mouchaak, on Surya Sen Street, before entering Bankim Chatterjee Street. It then proceeded past the College Street Coffee House and Presidency University before returning to College Square.
Several videos shared on social media showed people standing on balconies and outside shops, recording the procession on their smartphones. Marchers waved at onlookers along the route.
Left leaders Mohammed Salim, Sujan Chakraborty and Biman Basu also joined the procession, walking at the back.
After the march, the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA) organised a brief cultural programme in front of the College Square gate. Activists performed songs including “Tu Zinda Hai”, Paul Robeson’s “Ol’ Man River” and Bhupen Hazarika’s Bengali adaptation, “O Ganga Boichho Keno”.
Addressing the gathering, senior Left leader Biman Basu said people who believed in reading books had come together for the march. He added that efforts to promote reading must continue whenever books come under attack.
Participants said the protest was not about defending any particular political ideology. A book, they said, was neither Left-wing nor Right-wing; it was simply a book. Some described the attacks during Durga Puja as an assault on education, free thought and rationalism, and said they had joined the march to collectively resist such incidents in the future.
SFI central executive committee member Shuvajit Sarkar (in blue shirt in photo below), who participated in the march, said, “Fascists and communal forces oppose books because books promote rationality and reject blind subordination. We will defend books and continue the struggle against the divisive politics of the RSS and BJP until we defeat it.”

Prices on gaming laptops are out of control. The ongoing memory shortage has made laptops more expensive across the board, but it's hit gaming laptops especially hard. Some manufacturers have even resorted to launching “new" gaming laptops in 2026 with the RTX 4050 as the starting configuration—and that graphics card is more than three years old.
Given this landscape, there's really only one gaming laptop under $1,500 that I feel comfortable recommending. That's the Lenovo LOQ 15. It's not the thinnest or most powerful gaming laptop in the world, but for this price, there's nothing else like it.
It's not that the price of the LOQ 15 hasn't gone up over the past year alongside its gaming-laptop brethren. (It certainly has.) For the first few months of 2026—the good old days—it was selling for less than $1,000. But even then, it was technologically ahead of its rivals in a number of ways, offering strong performance paired with a high-quality IPS display. So many cheap gaming laptops come with pitifully desaturated screens that put a damper on the gaming experience. That's really what sets the LOQ 15 apart from the competition.
Also significant is the fact that, right now, you can buy the LOQ 15 with an RTX 5060 for just $1,300. That's not any cheaper than it normally has been (at least not for the past few months). However, the RTX 5060 is a big upgrade over the RTX 5050, especially with the 100 watts of power that the system can throw at it. Every game I tested could play at well over 60 frames per second at the medium preset, including heavier games like Black Myth: Wukong and Monster Hunter Wilds. You can always push frame rates higher by adjusting settings further or by adding a dash of upscaling.
Amazon has the RTX 5060 configuration, which also comes with 16 GB of RAM and 512 GB of storage, for $1,300, but Lenovo also has a killer deal on the RTX 5050 configuration that's about as cheap as it gets: $999 for an RTX 5050 (and otherwise identical specs). I've tested a number of other gaming laptops that sell for around this price, such as the MSI Cyborg A16 and the Acer Nitro V 16, and none can compete with the LOQ 15. I've also tested the Alienware 15 and Lenovo LOQ Essential 15 recently, and both suffer from the same problem.
As much as I wish I could recommend a budget gaming laptop that's newer, none I've tried have successfully dethroned the Lenovo LOQ 15. While you could wait until Black Friday to see if prices dip further, note that I haven't seen much fluctuation over the past few months. For example, it wasn't on a deeper sale during the October Amazon Prime Day—and yet, it was still the best gaming laptop deal you could get.

Counterattacking centuries from Yashasvi Jaiswal and Yash Rathod were the highlight of the final day of play as India A and New Zealand A settled for a draw in the 2nd unofficial Test at the Hagley Oval in Christchurch on Tuesday.
The pair put on an unbeaten 247-run partnership off just 245 balls to take India A to 282/2 in the second innings, after which the two captains shook hands to seal the result.
The start of play on the final day was delayed for over one-and-a-half hours following a wet outfield after light showers in the morning, prompting the sides to take an early Lunch.
New Zealand A was on the ascendancy immediately after the contest began, picking up two early wickets with India A still trailing its first-innings total. Sai Sudharsan endured a soft dismissal, chipping a ball into the hands of leg-gully in the first over of the day.
Devdutt Padikkal was then bowled first ball by a peach from Brett Randell in the very next over. With the 11-over new ball moving in the air, Jaiswal and Rathod had to tread the waters carefully.
Once the ball lost its shine, the batters looked to be more aggressive in their shot making. It did not help skipper Rhys Mariu’s case that two of his bowlers — Fraser Sheat and Jayden Lennox — were not available to bowl after picking up injuries.
The captain had to turn to the part-time spin of Dean Foxcroft and Matt Boyle to be able to rotate his pacers at the other end.

Two Democratic women running for Congress were in car accidents during the last week of October: Mary Peltola, a U.S. Senate candidate in Alaska, and Heidi Kuhn, a U.S. House candidate in Tennessee. Both experienced injuries that weren't life-threatening and are back on the campaign trail.
U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur, an Ohio Democrat running for reelection, was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries after a hit-and-run car crash in August, not October.
There is no evidence the women were deliberately targeted, contrary to suggestions of foul play from social media users.
Social media users are spreading a rumor that three Democratic congressional candidates, all women, have been involved in car crashes in the days leading up to the 2026 midterm elections.
The claims spread on Facebook and X. Different posts shared different timelines for the supposed incidents; while some posts claimed that the crashes happened in the span of just a few days, others said they happened over the course of several weeks. Most posts implied or said that the car crashes happened within the month of October.
Snopes readers asked us to verify these claims; one reader asked on Oct. 29 whether Democratic women "running for office in deep red states" have been "involved in suspicious car accidents this week."
These posts are referring to actual car crashes involving three Democratic women running for Congress. However, one of the three women — U.S. Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, who is running for reelection — was injured in a hit-and-run in early August, not October.
Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate for a U.S. Senate seat in Alaska, sustained minor injuries in a car crash on Oct. 24. Heidi Kuhn, who is running for a U.S. House seat in Tennessee, was in a multicar collision in Memphis on Oct. 23, sustaining whiplash, as well as a broken nose and upper jawbone, she said.
As of this writing, all three women have returned to the campaign trail.
We have rated this claim as mostly true because posts online largely got the details correct, aside from the timeline regarding one candidate.
Despite speculation on social media that foul play was somehow involved, there is no evidence as of this writing that any of the three women was deliberately targeted. The three campaigns did not return requests for comment on the car crash conspiracy theories.
Here's what we know about each inciden:
Marcy Kaptur
On Aug. 2, Kaptur's Washington office announced in a statement that the congresswoman "was a passenger in a vehicle on her way to a church service when the car she was traveling in was struck."
"She is active, alert, and being treated for non-life threatening injuries," the statement said. "She expressed her deep gratitude to the hundreds of constituents who have reached out and looks forward to returning to a full schedule soon."
A week after the incident, Kaptur posted a video on YouTube stating that people's good wishes had made a "huge difference in my very rapid recovery," and that her campaign manager, who also was in the car, was in "good shape." She said in the video she would not return to Washington until September. Her social media indicates that by Sept. 6, she was back in public, actively campaigning for reelection.
In October, prosecutors in Toledo, where the crash occurred, charged Jahiem Wright, 24, with four counts of vehicular assault and two counts of failure to stop after an accident in connection with the crash.
Nothing in public court documents indicates that the car crash was purposeful or meant to deliberately target Kaptur (see Case No. CR2026-01446 using the Lucas County Clerk of Courts case search tool.)
Samantha Crist, the prosecutor on the case, said she would forward our email requesting more information to her office's spokesperson, who did not immediately respond. The Toledo Police Department also did not immediately return a request for more information.
Here's how the Toledo Blade, a reputable newspaper in the area, described the incident:
Wright is accused of being the driver of a speeding silver Nissan Altima that lost control after striking a puddle in the 3200 block of North Detroit Avenue during heavy rain and colliding with a black Ford Bronco carrying Ms. Kaptur and her campaign manager, Kegan Zimmermann, as they headed to a church service. The Altima's driver then fled the scene on foot.
Despite Kaptur, 80, being the longest-serving woman in Congress, polling suggests she is in a very close race with her opponent after Republicans redrew her district for the fourth time.
Mary Peltola
On Oct. 25, Peltola's campaign team released a statement announcing that she was postponing several events after she sustained "minor injuries" in an Oct. 24 car collision (emphasis theirs):
Unfortunately, last night while en route to the Alaska Federation of Natives Annual Banquet, the vehicle transporting Mary and her family was struck by another driver, causing minor injuries that required medical attention. Following the accident, Alaskans for Mary Campaign Manager Cheryl Bruce issued the following statement regarding upcoming "Alaska Always Tour" events:
"Mary and her family sustained minor injuries but are in good spirits. Unfortunately, per the advice of medical professionals, Mary's upcoming events in Fairbanks and Bethel will be rescheduled for later in the week as she takes time to recover. Mary is disappointed that the accident is delaying the start of her Alaska Always Tour, and she is eager to get back on the campaign trail to speak directly with Alaskans about her plan to take on the rigged system and lower costs for working families."
Events scheduled in Fairbanks and Bethel for Sunday, October 25th and Monday, October 26th will be promptly rescheduled in the coming days. Events scheduled in Homer, Kenai, Seward, Juneau, Anchorage, and Palmer will continue as scheduled. The campaign will release an updated schedule.
By Oct. 27, Peltola was back at rallies, per photos from her campaign website.
A bulletin from the Anchorage Police Department said that its preliminary investigation found the car carrying Peltola was rear-ended by another car. That collision caused the car with Peltola in it to careen into a third car.
A police spokesperson said in an email that there was "no indication at the time that the collision was targeted or intentional."
"The investigation remains active and ongoing," the spokesperson said on Oct. 30.
Peltola is in one of the most closely watched races this year as she seeks to replace Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan. Polling suggests she has a slight edge over her opponent.
Heidi Kuhn
Kuhn's campaign team said on Oct. 24 that she and her husband, Matt, "were involved in a serious car accident" on Oct. 23.
The Democratic candidate later shared a video on her Facebook page, in which she said she and two others were injured in the crash.
"We were pretty shaken up," Kuhn said. "This was quite a traumatic accident and we certainly have given thought to what could have happened and feel incredibly grateful."
Memphis police spokesperson James Clements did not respond to a question as to whether any evidence suggested Kuhn was deliberately targeted, and whether there was an active investigation ongoing into the cause of the collision.
Instead, Clements sent via email what appears to be a police report of the incident, without identifying which car contained Kuhn:
On 10/23/2026 at 19:26 hours, Officers responded to a crash at I-240/Poplar Ave.
Driver 1, driving vehicle #1, was merging onto I-240E from Poplar Ave. Driver 1 advised that as she was merging, vehicle #2 jerked to the right and slammed on its brakes. Driver 1 was unable to stop before striking the rear of vehicle #2.
Driver 2 driving vehicle #2 was northbound on I-240E in lane 4. Driver 2 advised they were slowing due to traffic when his vehicle #2 was struck hard from behind by vehicle #1. Due to the contact, vehicle #2 was shot to the left, across traffic, where it was then struck by vehicle #3. Vehicle #2 then spun, and the front end made contact with the center median wall.
Driver 3, driving vehicle #3, was northbound I-240E in lane 2. Driver 3 advised that she was driving straight when vehicle #2 came across lanes in front of her. Vehicle #3 was unable to stop before striking vehicle #2, causing it to spin and strike the center median wall.
MFD transported driver 2 and passenger 2 to the hospital in non-critical condition. MFD transported driver 1 to the hospital in non-critical condition. Driver 3 and passenger 3 advised they were uninjured.
Based on the fact that Kuhn said the car in her video that she was hit multiple times and "spun," it seems likely she was in the second vehicle.
Per her Facebook page, Kuhn visited an early voting site on Oct. 28, indicating she's back on the campaign trail. She's facing the Republican incumbent, Rep. David Kustoff, and appears to be a longshot candidate in a safely Republican district.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.
- This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe
