On Sunday night, millions of Ukrainians were sent an alert to their phones that would usually spark panic and fear.
Citizens were told that there was an imminent threat of radiation, chemical attacks and fighting on the streets of Kyiv through an app used by the government to issue nationwide notifications in emergencies.
It was quickly followed up with a clarification that the system had likely been hacked by Russia and that no such threat existed.
“The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference,” read a follow-up message on Telegram. “There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel.”
Shortly after, Russia told its citizens that Ukraine had hacked its systems to warn its people of imminent nuclear strikes.
Neither country has claimed responsibility and it is unclear where or how the incidents were sparked. But they have been widely interpreted by officials and analysts as tit-for-tat attacks, started by Russia.
A hacker within the Ukrainian “hacktivist” community told the BBC that the breach of the Russian alert system was likely to be a “retaliatory attack” by Ukraine.
The ensuing chaos has laid bare the increasingly devastating impact of cyberattacks.
According to the Ukrainian security service (SBU), citing its cybersecurity department, more than 16,000 Russian cyberattacks and “critical cyber incidents” had been neutralised between the start of the war in February 2022 and July this year.
Brigadier general Volodymyr Karasteliov referred to one large-scale DDoS attack that lasted three hours against a nationwide Ukrainian television channel.
“The botnet generated up to 200,000 requests per minute from nodes in Asia, Europe, and the United States,” he said.
“The attack targeted the website's application layer, with hackers imitating the behaviour of real users in an attempt to overload the server with complex requests and make the site unavailable.”
According to research published in PLOS in April 2024, Russia ranked as the number one hotspot for cybercriminals worldwide, followed by Ukraine.
Cybersecurity firm CybelAngel noted that the attacks between Russia and Ukraine are largely asymmetric. The company’s REACT team recorded 1,651 cyber incidents targeting Ukrainian entities with 575 targeting Russian entities, between January 2025 and January 2026.
“The asymmetry isn’t new, since the prior twelve months looked nearly identical in shape and scale,” it said.
Experts told The Independent that the attacks serve a more sinister purpose than simply the disruption of communication systems.
“A message from your air raid alert system generates emotion straight away, almost like a phishing email, with that sense of panic and urgency, and you respond and react,” says Adam Pilton, cyber security adviser at Heimdal.
“That’s exactly why the air raid systems were hit. The attack strikes at the point where people trust their government.”
He compares the incident to the cyberattack on ASOS a few weeks ago, explaining that when communication is disrupted from official platforms, it leads to uncertainty and confusion for civilians.
“If you can’t trust communications that purportedly come from official platforms, whether a business or your government, then what can you trust? That’s exactly the purpose of this attack, to erode trust,” he says.
Pilton reiterates that the purpose of the strikes is to sow panic and uncertainty despite claims that the systems are legitimate targets as communication platforms.
“Russia has claimed that this is not an actual air raid system but just a communication platform. Whether that’s true or not is irrelevant. What matters is that people look to their leaders to understand what’s happening,” he explains.
“There’s a degree of trust in those communications. If they receive an official communication, they will follow it. That’s different from the media, which they’ll take with a pinch of salt and probably look a bit further.”
Speaking to the BBC, Oleksandr Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee and a member of Volodymyr Zelensky’s Servant of the People party, said that the country and its people are prepared for all scenarios.
“It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities,” he said.

India’s second-richest man, Mukesh Ambani, is launching what could be the country’s biggest-ever initial public offering (IPO), despite a stock market downturn.
Mumbai-based Jio Platforms, a telecoms company backed by Meta Platforms and Google, is hoping to raise up to 302bn rupees (£2.4bn) and is targeting a 10.3tn rupees valuation when it floats on the stock market from Wednesday.
Set up a decade ago as a subsidiary of Ambani’s conglomerate Reliance Industries, and led by Akash Ambani, the oldest son of patriarch Mukesh, Jio offers low-cost broadband to millions of Indians.
Jio secured 212 anchor investors on Monday before its blockbuster IPO. They include some of the world’s largest fund managers, such as: BlackRock; Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund; the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority; Fidelity Investments; Schroders; JP Morgan Asset Management; Franklin Templeton; Invesco; and Prudential.
On Wednesday, shares will be offered to retail investors, and the IPO is set to close on Friday.
Reliance Industries said in a stock exchange filing last week that Jio had set a price range of 1,065 rupees to 1,119 rupees a share for its maiden share sale, offering up to 270m new shares.
The family-owned conglomerate has been encouraging its 400,000-plus employees to buy shares, offering them a discount of 54 rupees a share.
At the top end of the price range, Jio would be worth 10.3tn rupees, which would make it India’s fourth-largest company, behind its parent Reliance Industries, Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. It would be more than twice as much as the 4.9tn-rupee valuation in 2020, when Meta and Google invested in the company.
However, the top valuation is far below initial expectations of more than £110bn when the telecoms group posted a draft prospectus in the summer.
It comes amid a broader stock market slowdown in India, with the blue chip Nifty 5o index down more than 12% this year.
Jio launched its telecoms services in September 2016. It gained 16 million subscribers in the first month, and topped 100 million subscribers within 170 days, according to Reliance Industries. It is credited with making mobile internet more affordable, by triggering a price war. The company intends to expand further into artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital infrastructure.
Isha Ambani, who sits on Jio’s board as a director, told investors last week that the business idea was spawned by the poor connectivity she and her brother Akash faced when they returned to India on a break from studying in the US in about 2009-10. She struggled to submit a college assignment online because the internet was not working.
“What followed was a conversation about why should India be left behind,” she said. “Akash firmly believed that the answer and solution to this was creating a digital technology platform company.”

King's former horse wins prestigious Melbourne Cup
- Published
Australian jockey Ethan Brown has ridden Point of Law, a horse previously owned by King Charles, to victory in this year's Melbourne Cup, the country's most prestigious race.
Point of Law, which was bought from the King earlier this year for an undisclosed sum, was considered an early favourite.
Brown pushed Point of Law from the middle of the pack to take the lead with just a few hundred metres to go.
The Melbourne Cup has run in Australia since 1861 and is often referred to as the "race that stops a nation". With a prize of A$10.2m ($7.04m; £5.3m), it is the country's third richest race, but is considered the most prestigious.
"Don't wake me up, this is every jockey's dream," Brown said in a post-race interview.
Brown said he was telling himself "just stay cool, stay patient" as Royal Supremacy raced more than a dozen lengths ahead, before pushing Point of Law from the middle of the pack to overtake on the home stretch.
The King sold Point of Law to a group of investors including former AFL player Chris Judd and his wife Bec.
Trained by Ciaron Maher, the three-year-old thoroughbred won the Geelong Cup last month.
"He's going to be a superstar horse. He's something special," said Brown. "He's in the best of hands with Ciaran Maher."
Maher had a record seven horses in this year's cup, including the second and first place runners, Zahrann and Juja Kibo.
Brown, who grew up in Alice Springs, said he never dreamed as a kid that he would be riding the Melbourne Cup, but he had been given "a lot of great support" in his career.
Brown said he was "inches from losing my life" after a fall from his horse in a 2023 race sent him to hospital and kept him out of racing for six months.
Tens of thousands of people enjoyed sunny weather at Flemington on Tuesday, where they were also entertained by Robbie Williams. Organisers said the UK pop star's appearance, which included a 10-piece band, backup dancers and pyrotechnics, was the biggest pre-cup performance ever staged at Flemington.
The day was not without controversy. One horse, Asterix, was scratched from the race earlier on Tuesday, after it was discovered a stable worker had administered it the medication penetrene earlier that morning.
The medication is used to treat inflammation and muscle soreness, but no treatments of any kind are permitted on race day. Race stewards said the medication was applied in error but still constituted a "serious breach", the Age reported. Trainer Chris Waller was reportedly fined $50,000 for what he described as a simple mistake by a staff member under pressure.
Outside Flemington, crowds from the Australia-wide "Nup to the Cup" movement also gathered to protest against horse racing on the industry's most high profile day. Some held signs with slogans including "horse racing kills", "don't bet on cruelty" and "no more whips".
Interest in the race among Australians has been declining, according to a Guardian Essential poll, which this year found just 9% of people said they had high interest in the race, and 23% had moderate interest. However more than 60% said it was a unique part of Australia's national identity.
Last year the Melbourne Cup drew a record $382.5 million in bets.

Every fast bowler has a run-up that begins long before the first stride. Mohammed Siraj’s began in Hyderabad, took him to his India debut against New Zealand in November 2017, and has now carried him, nine years later, to that country again.
Siraj, 32, is now a senior statesman. As if to remind himself of the road travelled, he stopped at the start of it: two Ranji Trophy matches as Hyderabad captain, two emphatic wins over Tripura and Andhra, and a final tune-up at the Gymkhana under the watchful eyes of T. Dilip, the former India fielding coach.
“I am very excited to play in New Zealand because a fast bowler needs grass and bounce. It will be very challenging because there will be a lot of swing. My plan will be simple: enjoy the experience,” Siraj told Sportstar.

If there is one thing he is wary of before a big assignment, it is idleness. His body, he has made it clear, does not take kindly to rest. The two back-to-back games for Hyderabad, tiring as they were, felt more like a gift than a burden.
“The first few sessions were about making him realise that he doesn’t need to do anything different as he has been successful at the international level. But when you have a long graph, there will be ups and downs. How you pick yourself up mentally is the most important,” Dilip told Sportstar.
Dilip, now Mumbai Indians’ fielding coach, revealed he had nudged Siraj to look back on what he is capable of.
“Siraj is generally someone who can bowl at 140kmph and has the ability to bowl long spells. We all know that he is a fighter where one odd error on the field or one odd bad over doesn’t affect him because he always comes back harder. I just made him realise those aspects as a quick recap is necessary. We just went through some of his spells from before and videos of a few previous performances to revisit what he had done and where he was mentally then. Besides that, we made little tweaks to his run-up and adjustments that will help him get back rhythm,” Dilip said.
When Siraj was asked about personal goals, he said: “I’m not a believer in milestones. It’s all about collecting wins and memories as a team.
“I had nothing at the beginning and I have everything now. I have a fan following. I thank the almighty who has brought me here. My only thought is to keep myself grounded, keep working hard and keep winning matches for my country,” said Siraj, who has 233 international wickets across three formats.
In the Shaky Isles, where the grass runs green and the ball sings through the air, Siraj has wasted no time in making his presence felt by scalping four wickets for India-A in the second ‘Test’ against New Zealand-A. It augurs well for the pacer as well as India.

Flying across several time zones often causes jet lag, a feeling when the body insists it’s the middle of the night while the clock says it’s lunchtime. Now it turns out this nuisance is not exclusive to humans.
A new Science study on Manx shearwaters, seabirds that can fly hundreds of kilometers a day over the North Atlantic, shows they jet-lag themselves during their excursions. And because these birds navigate by the Sun, that jet lag leaves a measurable mark—it skews their compass.
Clockwork compass
Patrick Lewin is a behavioral and sensory ecologist at the University of Oxford and lead author of the study. “Manx shearwaters are medium-sized birds, about the same size as a pigeon,” Lewin said. “They are white underneath and black on top, but they have very long wings, and they are closely related to albatross.” Manx shearwaters nest in burrows on coastal islands around the North Atlantic. Most breed around the UK and Ireland, with about half of their population living in Wales.
From there, they head out to feed anywhere from a few dozen to more than 1,000 kilometers into the Atlantic. To get back, shearwaters are thought to work out where they are located using a map sense, possibly based on smells, and then use the Sun as a compass to set their direction.
The trouble with navigating by the Sun, though, is that it moves across the sky. “You can imagine an animal or a human that wants to travel south all day. At sunrise, when the Sun’s in the east, it needs to be traveling 90 degrees clockwise of the Sun, but by midday it needs to be traveling straight towards the Sun, and by sunset it needs to be traveling 90 degrees anticlockwise of the Sun,” Lewin said. Effective navigation by the Sun requires a clock that tells you what time of day it is. Birds, like nearly all animals, have such a clock built in. But the clock in Manx shearwaters is not perfect.

The disgraced best-selling author Craig Silvey has claimed he experienced trauma as a child in a 9,000-word apology published after he was jailed for child exploitation offences.
The young adult novelist was sentenced on Monday to seven months’ imprisonment, after being charged in January and subsequently pleading guilty to distributing and possessing depraved child exploitation material.
The 44-year-old writer posted an article on his Substack titled “My Apology”.
He said that throughout his life he had always been able to find the right words, “but articulating the depth of my contrition and the enormity of my remorse feels beyond my aptitude for language”.
“I am guilty of these offences. I am appalled and mortified by my conduct, and I am deeply, profoundly sorry,” he wrote.
“I want to acknowledge that my engagement with this material is reprehensible and indefensible.
“It is re-traumatising to victims, and perpetuates a cycle of harm.”
Silvey, a father of three, said he betrayed the trust of thousands of people across the country, including those who had read his books, many of whom reacted to his offending with “shock, dismay, disgust, concern and disappointment”.
“I am painfully aware of the possible assumption that my offence must have been informed by a horrible and inappropriate attraction, and that my behaviour must then be connected to sinister and ulterior motivations,” he wrote.
“I assure you this is not the case at all.”
Silvey said he had carried a history of “trauma, shame and anxiety” through most of his life.
Silvey said he suffered a “crisis of mental health and a destructive, despairing breakdown” before he offended.
He was found with numerous sexually explicit photos and videos of children and adults on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his home in Fremantle.
He also engaged in an online conversation with a person he believed shared his interest in child exploitation material, telling them he preferred boys older than five before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.
“I haven’t had any experience, I’m sad to say.
“I’m a bit obsessed.”
Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin literary award and the International Dublin literary award, is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, which had been considered a modern Australian classic and was adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb, Honeybee – which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 – and the children’s novel Runt, which was also made into a film.

UN's peacekeeping mission in disputed Western Sahara ends after 35 years
CASABLANCA, Morocco — The U.N.'s long-running peacekeeping mission for the disputed Western Sahara ceased operations Sunday after 35 years, as a result of a U.S.-Russia standoff at U.N. headquarters over the territory's future.
The end of the mission raises concerns about stability in the region. Rich in minerals and fisheries, Western Sahara is a vast desert territory roughly the size of Colorado along Africa's northwestern Atlantic coast. Once ruled by Spain, it is claimed by both Morocco and the pro-independence Polisario Front.
"This 1 November 2026 marks the start of the liquidation period," Stéphane Dujarric, spokesperson for the U.N. secretary general, said in a statement. "A smaller team reporting to the United Nations' Department of Operational Support will oversee the orderly transportation of assets belonging to troop-contributing countries to their respective nations, and the appropriate disposal of equipment belonging to the United Nations.''
The mission had been repeatedly extended since it was established in 1991. In the U.N. Security Council on Friday, Russia vetoed a draft U.S. resolution that would have supported Morocco's demand for sovereignty over Western Sahara and ended the peacekeeping mission next year.
Then a rival Russian resolution to extend the mission was voted down. The disagreement led to an abrupt end of the force's mandate.
Morocco's royal palace welcomed the non-renewal of the mission. It called it an "instrument to internationalize the dispute.''
The Polisario Front, backed by Algeria, called it "an unacceptable decision.'' The Algerian foreign ministry said it profoundly regrets the non-renewal of the mandate and criticized what it called the ''excessive bias'' of the U.S. draft resolution.
Western Sahara is Africa's longest territorial dispute
The U.N. classifies Western Sahara as a "non-self-governing territory," while critics of Morocco's control describe it as Africa's last colony. Morocco administers nearly all of the disputed territory, except for a narrow strip known as the "free zone" that lies east of a Moroccan-built sand wall.
After Morocco annexed it in 1975, the dispute escalated into an armed conflict that lasted more than 15 years and claimed more than 16,000 lives on both sides, according to the French Senate.
Bringing Western Sahara under its full sovereignty has been a central objective of Morocco's foreign policy for decades. Rabat, which has secured the backing of a growing number of Western capitals, including Washington, Paris and London, refers to the territory as its southern provinces. The dispute has become a defining feature of Morocco's diplomacy, with the kingdom often measuring its relations with other countries by their position on the issue.
The Polisario Front seeks independence for the territory, which it considers the homeland of the Indigenous Sahrawi people. Operating from refugee camps in the Algerian city of Tindouf, the movement aims to establish an independent Sahrawi Republic. Mainly backed by Algeria, Russia and South Africa, the Polisario has seen its international support dwindle in recent years.
The expired mission was established to monitor a referendum
A U.N.-brokered cease-fire took effect in 1991. The agreement also paved the way for the creation of the U.N. Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara, known as MINURSO.
The settlement plan provided for a referendum on self-determination, with independence among the options. But the vote never materialized. Morocco wanted the voter list to include Sahrawis living in the territory it controls, while the Polisario objected, arguing that their inclusion would tilt the outcome toward integration with Morocco. The movement insisted on using Spain's colonial census to determine voter eligibility.
Twenty MINURSO personnel lost their lives in the mission. The U.N. force was authorized to have 534 personnel, and its 2026-2027 budget was more than $62 million. The top military contributors to the force were Egypt, Ghana and Pakistan.
As the mission ends, the U.N. secretary-general ''calls upon all parties to respect and promote the rights of the people of Western Sahara,'' Dujarric said, and "remains concerned about the security situation throughout the Territory and the risk of escalation of hostilities. He calls on all concerned to exercise maximum restraint."
The Polisario withdrew from the ceasefire in 2020 after clashes and the territory has since remained the scene of tensions and low-intensity hostilities, the U.N. said last month.
Western Sahara is the major flashpoint in the rivalry between regional heavyweights Morocco and Algeria. Algiers, which arms, funds and hosts the Polisario Front, sees full Moroccan sovereignty over the territory as a major diplomatic defeat. The two countries severed diplomatic relations in 2021, and the end of the mission risks further straining ties and fueling an arms race.

“If the public is drifting away from government hospitals and being pushed into the clutches of the corporate healthcare system, it is undeniably because politicians and governments lack genuine sincerity,” said 115 citizens and activists in an open letter to Telangana Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy and Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha.
The letter accused successive governments of failing to strengthen public healthcare, alleging that the lack of basic amenities in government hospitals is driving patients towards private healthcare.
Gaps in basic facilities
The letter highlights concerns over drinking water facilities, toilets, sanitation and the maintenance of infrastructure at major government hospitals in Hyderabad, including Osmania General Hospital, Gandhi Hospital, Nizam’s Institute of Medical Sciences (NIMS), Niloufer Hospital and Petlaburj Maternity Hospital.
The signatories — comprising social activists, academics, writers, journalists, teachers and other citizens — questioned whether the government’s promises to improve public healthcare translated into better conditions for patients.
Is the problem a lack of medical expertise or basic facilities?
The signatories argued that the challenges confronting government hospitals cannot be viewed solely through the lens of shortages of doctors and other medical personnel. The signatories acknowledged that healthcare workers were already working under considerable pressure, but said the absence of basic amenities was adding to the difficulties faced by patients.
“Government hospitals have experienced doctors, medical staff and research capabilities, but inadequate facilities are undermining the healthcare experience,” they added.
Referring to Osmania, Gandhi, NIMS, Niloufer and Petlaburj hospitals, the signatories questioned why patients should have to endure difficult conditions to access treatment when the institutions were expected to provide essential public healthcare services.
When basic amenities become a question of dignity
They have identified clean drinking water, functional toilets and proper sanitation as among the most pressing requirements in public hospitals. Questioning the government’s responsibility for maintaining these facilities, the signatories asked whether patients should be held responsible for unhygienic conditions and unpleasant odours in hospital toilets, arguing that the responsibility for maintenance rested with the authorities.
They said patients who could afford private healthcare might choose to seek treatment elsewhere, but those unable to bear the additional expense were left with fewer options.
Should hospital maintenance be handed over to private entities?
The signatories also cautioned the government against transferring responsibility for maintaining basic hospital amenities to corporate entities under the banner of public participation as doing so would impose an additional financial burden on patients. They called for the government to take responsibility for improving existing infrastructure and ensuring that essential facilities were properly maintained.
They further questioned the emphasis placed on changing photographs on walls and ambulances after a government assumes office, arguing that the same attention should be directed towards providing basic amenities in hospitals.
A call for a Right to Health law
Beyond immediate improvements to hospital infrastructure, the signatories urged the Telangana government to introduce a strong Right to Health law through consultations with people’s organisations and public. They called for a broader effort to strengthen the public health and medical system so that ordinary citizens would not be compelled to abandon government hospitals because of inadequate facilities.

The people of Iraq are in urgent need of better health care and their situation is deteriorating by the day. The UN has today appealed for at least $325 million in emergency funds to meet the immediate health, nutrition, water and sanitation needs of the most vulnerable populations. Out of this amount, the World Health Organization urgently appeals for $185 million.
This request is part of the wider United Nations humanitarian appeal for $2.1 billion to provide assistance to the people of Iraq over the next six months. This appeal is being launched jointly by all the UN humanitarian agencies in New York and Geneva.
WHO is already working in Iraq to provide badly needed medical assistance. The health status of the Iraqi people has been seriously affected by more than two decades of war and economic sanctions. Child death rates today are more than twice as high as they were in 1990: one in eight children dies before the age of five, one in three children is malnourished and one in four begins life as an underweight baby.
"Overall, the health of people in Iraq is poor and likely to get worse," said Dr Gro Harlem Brundtland, Director General of the World Health Organization. "This appeal is not an optional extra. It is the only way of stabilising the situation, and indeed improving it."
The three biggest child killers in Iraq are acute respiratory infection, diarrhoeal diseases and measles. Almost half of the country's 24.5 million people are children whose future depends on a massive and rapid improvement in the country's health and infrastructure.
Conflict is already adding to the strains on the health of the population and on the infrastructure on which they depend. For example, damage to the electricity and water supply in the southern city of Basra is expected to lead to additional health problems, particularly for children and other vulnerable groups. People elsewhere may soon face similar or worse emergencies.
A substantial investment is needed to provide essential care to people who are either injured in the conflict or whose health suffers as a result of damage to the infrastructure. In the months to come, more will be needed to begin rebuilding the most critical and most badly effected parts of the public health system.
That means building up the capacities of hospitals and health centres; it means providing some $60 million of medicines, medical supplies and equipment; it means repairing and rehabilitating vital hospitals and health centres.
There must be substantial investment in the ability to detect and respond to outbreaks of disease, in the training and equipment of health workers and in the health information which is vital to prioritise health work.
WHO today has more than 300 staff working hard in Iraq to support the health system and to bring badly needed medical assistance to people across the country. During the current conflict, WHO has successfully sent teams to help with an outbreak of diarrhoeal disease in northern Iraq and to assess the health needs of people who have left their homes. WHO is ready to do much more work across the whole country in support of the health system.
In the weeks and months to come, Iraq's health system will almost inevitably come under unprecedented pressure. Health is a crucial part of the economic and social system.

The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century.
NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope’s orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction.
The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies’ current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope’s performance through, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry.
“The requirement includes that the boost and/or servicing mission must not harm the HST and that this mission is expected to occur by 2032,” NASA wrote in the RFI. The contractor would be responsible for providing the launch vehicle, servicing spacecraft, mission operations, and “crew if applicable.”
No commitments yet
NASA is not committing to buying a Hubble rescue mission, but officials want to know who might be interested in mounting such a mission, how much it would cost, and which companies would have a realistic shot at reaching Hubble before it falls out of orbit and burns up on reentry. Orbital dynamicists currently predict that it will likely happen in 2033 or 2034 without intervention, but reentry forecasts can change based on solar activity.
It took 24 years for Hubble, which lacks onboard propulsion, to glide from its 2002 altitude of 362 miles (583 km) to its current orbit some 292 miles (470 km) above Earth. A reboost to NASA’s requirement of 373 miles (600 km) would likely keep Hubble in orbit for at least 25 more years.

Shopping for a PC gamer is a perilous endeavor. What might look like a great sale on a GPU or gaming keyboard can turn out to be a bad deal because of an arcane spec only the most die-hard forum-dwellers understand. If you're shopping for the gamer in your life who lives that nerd life, we have a simple, accessible guide to what they might like.
Updated November 2026: We've added the Razer Viper V4 Pro, SteelSeries Rival 3 Gen 2, Smartish Cord Holders, Razer Kraken Kitty V3 Pro, Branch Ergonomic Chair SEGA Edition, and Creative Pebble V3 Speakers.
Shopping Tips
AccordionItemContainerButton
The best advice I can give when shopping for a PC gaming enthusiast is simple: If you're unsure, just ask. Find out if they have a favorite mouse, keyboard, or headset brand they've been eyeing, or anything else they've been thinking about picking up for themselves. If you're still not sure and don't want to get them the wrong thing, another one-size-fits-all gift any PC gamer will like is a Steam gift card. This lets them pick a game from a vast online store. Most popular titles are around $60, so use that as a baseline for how much to add to the card.
Dedicated gaming headsets can get very expensive, especially if you want something higher quality with the latest features. But the SteelSeries Arctis Nova 3 Wireless (9/10, WIRED Recommends) delivers the goods at half the price of the competition without sacrificing sound quality or comfort. Reviewer Brad Bourque even called it the “most comfortable gaming headset" he'd ever tested. Check out our Best Gaming Headsets guide for other options.
There are more powerful computer speakers out there, but none are as giftable as the Creative Pebble V3. These tiny little speakers are shockingly small, so they don't dominate your desk. However, they are angled up toward your ears to deliver clear, loud sound that brings your games to life. WIRED reviewer Nena Farell has often recommended these, noting the impressive sound quality for the price.
Not everyone needs a mouse that costs over $100. If you want to spend a bit less, I'd recommend the SteelSeries Rival 3 Gen 2. It doesn't have some of the bells and whistles that higher-end mice have, but the average PC gamer will find everything they need here. It's light, has a grippy scroll wheel, and comes in either a cheaper wired model or a wireless option. It's the rare PC gaming accessory that comes in at a perfectly giftable price.
Asus' compact ROG Falchion Ace HFX (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is a great example of why small keyboards are all the rage. It removes the number pad, function keys, and navigation keys in favor of a smaller footprint (also known as 65 percent layout) than even the tenkeyless (TKL) layout. It won't get in the way of your mouse hand, especially when turned sideways or on a smaller desk. Meanwhile, the Hall effect switches feel snappy, and the software makes it easy to customize everything. The keyboard doesn't cut as much as a 60% layout, which removes the arrow keys, making it more usable for work and school.
For the gamer who has it all, lighting can be an aesthetic upgrade that enhances the PC gaming experience. It doesn't take much to toss in a splash of color to a wall or desk. This Govee light strip is a great option, since the light is already diffused, so it won't blind you when it's in full view. Whether you curve it into a shape on a wall or line your desk with it, these light strips are a simple way to enhance a gaming station.
If your giftee takes their multiplayer gaming seriously, they need a mouse that is fast, lightweight, and highly customizable—and that's exactly what the Razer Viper V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is. New this year, the Viper V4 Pro replaced its already popular predecessor (our gift recommendation last year), making it even lighter and adding some pro-level features. Our resident mouse enthusiast, Henri Robbins, calls it “perfectly balanced” and notes that the added agility gave him “the ability to contend with multiple enemies at once” in Helldivers 2.
Here's a great stocking stuffer if the PC gamer in your life doesn't already have a mousepad. It's basic, yes—but that's the point. While we typically recommend desk-sized mats like the Wool Felt Desk Pad from Grovemade, this smaller SteelSeries mousepad is a whole lot cheaper and more practical for smaller desks. Most importantly, the smooth surface ensures the mouse is responsive, regardless of what kind of surface the gaming is happening on. Even better, you can choose from a variety of sizes and colors.
Razer’s most adorable wireless headset is best recognized for its iconic kitty ears. They feature RGB lights you can customize in the Razer Chroma app, including the lights scattered across the earcups. The cute design is eye-catching, with comfortable memory foam ear cushions and a squishy lining on the headband. Sound quality is strong, and the retractable mic sounds great when in use and tucks away neatly when it isn’t. It's compatible with PC, Mac, PlayStation, and smartphones, so it’s an easy gift recommendation for any gamer. (It connects to Xbox via Bluetooth.) I prefer the light pink color scheme, but it’s also available in black or white. —Louryn Strampe
The HyperX Quadcast 2 S improves on its predecessor, the USB mic that almost every Twitch streamer seemed to own, in every way. It has even more of its trademark vibrant LEDs, allowing for complex patterns and designs that look great for anyone streaming online. Audio recording has been upgraded to 32-bit/192 kHz, which is handy if you plan to edit your audio later, and its shock-mount design makes it easy to pull it from its stand and use it elsewhere. If your gift recipient plans to be on camera while playing games for an audience (or likes accessories that glow), this is one of the best USB mics you can get.
The Elgato Stream Deck+ feels a bit like having a piece of a space shuttle on your desk. It packs eight full-color LCD buttons that can be customized with macros and shortcuts to easily launch apps, mute a mic, or run scripts with a single press. A second, wider color touchscreen provides a heads-up display for different system stats; paired with the four prominent dials along the bottom, it's a handy tool for anything from running sound to video editing. It's designed for streamers who need to handle complex technical tasks while broadcasting, but it's also helpful for anyone who wants to record gameplay, adjust music or chat while they're playing, or fine-tune their setup to their exact preferences.
Even with the proliferation of wireless accessories, it's far too easy to let a desk get disorganized and descend into chaos. WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu stands by these small cable-tidying accessories. They keep your cables together where they should be, but not in a more permanent way that other solutions use. They magnetically stick to the base when not in use, ensuring that you disconnected cables don't clutter up your desk.
I have been using BenQ's ScreenBar lights for years, and they are fantastic. It essentially hangs off the top of a monitor, illuminating the keyboard and desktop. You can angle it just right so it doesn't cast light onto your monitor screen. The ScreenBar Pro has a motion sensor, so your giftee can have their setup automatically light up when they sit down. There are touch controls to adjust the color temperature and brightness, with a toggle for auto brightness. This is a must-have desk accessory for any gamer. —Julian Chokkattu
Intense gaming sessions can get physically taxing when you sit in the wrong chair for too long. This is actually our favorite office chair, but the Sega collaboration makes it perfect for any gaming setup. You can dial in the perfect fit with several ergonomic adjustments, from the back to the seat tilt to the armrests. I regularly work in this chair for eight hours, followed by several sweaty hours of League of Legends gaming, and I never feel sore or unsupported. Except for my teammates, of course. If your giftee is still sitting in an uncomfortable chair, this upgrade will make a world of difference. Assembly is easy too. —Louryn Strampe
Even games that are better with a controller can have disadvantages compared to a keyboard and mouse. That's where highly customizable options like the Xbox Elite Wireless Controller Series 2 can help. It lets you tweak the resistance of its control sticks, swap out paddles and D-pads, and even add extra rear buttons to customize your game. This is not the same controller that comes with the Xbox, but an upgraded version.

Smriti Irani cites 10 SIR exercises under Congress, slams Opposition over EC protests
Addressing a press conference in Kolkata as part of the BJP's 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' campaign, Smriti Irani questioned the Opposition's objections to SIR, pointing out that 10 of the 12 such exercises conducted in India had taken place when the Congress was in power.
Former Union Minister and BJP leader Smriti Irani on Tuesday launched a sharp attack on Congress leader Rahul Gandhi, calling him a "prince in perpetual waiting", and accused the Opposition of undermining constitutional institutions by questioning the Election Commission over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.
Addressing a press conference in Kolkata as part of the BJP's 'Save Democracy, Remove Anarchy' campaign, Irani questioned the Congress's opposition to the exercise, pointing out that 10 of the 12 SIR exercises conducted in India since 1952 took place when the party was in power.
Irani also challenged the Opposition to acknowledge the work of Booth Level Agents (BLAs), claiming that around 20 lakh agents belonging to opposition parties had gone door to door to verify electoral details.
"Nobody can deny that Booth Level Agents went door to door to verify the facts. Out of those, 20 lakh BLAs belonged to opposition parties. I want to ask the Opposition whether it wants to deny the work done by its own BLAs," she said.
   
    
  
The BJP leader's remarks come amid an escalating political confrontation over SIR, with the Congress, the Trinamool Congress (TMC) and other opposition parties accusing the Election Commission of facilitating "vote chori" and demanding the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
'CONGRESS LOST 56 ASSEMBLY ELECTIONS SINCE 2014'
Irani accused the Congress of blaming the Election Commission for its electoral defeats instead of examining its leadership and organisational failures.
She claimed that the party had lost 56 Assembly elections between 2014 and 2025, before the current SIR exercise, and questioned how the poll panel could be held responsible for its electoral setbacks.
"The Congress has been losing elections since 2014. Gyanesh Kumar was not even the Chief Election Commissioner then," she said.
She also cited the Congress's prolonged absence from power in several states, including Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, to question its electoral strategy.
Irani further alleged that the Congress was refusing to accept the removal of duplicate and ineligible voters from electoral rolls. "Why does the Congress want duplicate and fake voters to remain on the electoral rolls?" she asked.
ACCUSES TMC OF PROTECTING INFILTRATORS
Targeting the Mamata Banerjee-led TMC, Irani alleged that the party had facilitated the presence of infiltrators in West Bengal for electoral gains.
"Why does the TMC want duplicate and fake voters in the electoral list? Because it accommodated infiltrators for its own benefit," she alleged.
She also took a swipe at the Opposition's joint protest against the Election Commission at Delhi's Ramlila Maidan, challenging the Congress, TMC and CPI(M) to organise a similar demonstration in West Bengal.
"In Delhi, Adhir da (Congress leader Adhir Ranjan Chowdhury) and Mamata didi are joining hands. Why are they not doing so in West Bengal?" she asked.
Irani also referred to Mamata Banerjee's remarks, alleging that the West Bengal Chief Minister had inadvertently admitted during her speech that those who had looted Bengal now wanted to loot Delhi.
'PRINCE IN WAITING' ATTACKS INDIAN STATE
In a series of allegations against Rahul Gandhi, Irani said the Congress leader had targeted the Supreme Court, the Indian state and now the electoral system.
She also questioned Gandhi's remarks during overseas visits and alleged that Congress leaders had sought foreign assistance to undermine the Narendra Modi government.
"Mani Shankar Aiyar goes to Pakistan and makes comments against the country. Rahul Gandhi goes to London and says he wants to defeat Modi. Is it right for the Leader of Opposition to make such remarks on foreign soil?" she asked.
Irani also referred to allegations of foreign interference, questioning why Congress leaders had sought help from billionaire investor George Soros.
She further accused the Opposition of joining hands with forces that, she alleged, had celebrated the Pulwama terror attack and called for a change of government in India.

The Delhi Police had posted a video on their X handle on October 25, which urged citizens to not burn crackers this Diwali. Along with a meme video, the post was captioned: “This festive season, let tails wag, not tuck. Say NO to crackers, YES to a greener Diwali.”
Soon after the post was made, social media users had predicted that it would be removed soon. Incidentally, just within a few hours of the post being made, the Delhi Police removed it from X.
While Delhi Police did not issue any clarification as to why the post was taken down, several X users wondered whether the reason behind the post being taken down was perhaps the purported pressure from the BJP-led central government.
Alt News co-founder Mohammad Zubair had also remarked on Delhi Police’s post, before it was taken down, with the caption: “This tweet will soon be deleted due to political pressure.”
Another X user, Jeevansh Arya, shared a screen grab of the Delhi Police’s post and questioned whether it would be deleted.
@zoo_bear @DelhiPolice Tweet Deleted Now ?
Daro Mat 😂😂 https://t.co/q51PIYEFZG
— 𝐉𝐄𝐄𝐕𝐀𝐍𝐒𝐇 𝐀𝐑𝐘𝐀 🇮🇳 (@jeevansharya) October 25, 2026
After the post was deleted, many social media users posted that they expected something like this to happen.
Like most of us predicted, tweet deleted by @DelhiPolice
— Piyush Rai (@Benarasiyaa) October 25, 2026
The official handle of Indian Youth Congress also questioned the logic behind the retreat of the Delhi Police.
Administrative Indecision in The Past
This is, however, not the first time that the Delhi administration retracted its position during Diwali regarding firecrackers. Over the past two years, Delhi’s authorities and the courts have attempted to take a strong stance against firecrackers due to the city’s severe air pollution, but they have often backtracked on their decisions.
Ahead of Diwali 2024, the Delhi government imposed a complete ban on the manufacture, sale, storage and bursting of all firecrackers until January 1, 2025. The Supreme Court later criticised the poor enforcement of the ban and suggested that the government consider making it permanent. In December 2024, the Delhi government told the court that it had imposed a year-round ban on firecrackers.
However, the position changed soon. In April 2025, the Supreme Court refused to relax the ban, but in October it allowed green crackers to be sold and used in Delhi-NCR for a limited period during Diwali. The court said these crackers had to meet standards set by the National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI), and allowed their use only during specified hours. The Delhi government and the Centre supported the relaxation.
In effect, the authorities moved from a complete ban on firecrackers to allowing a limited category of green crackers, despite earlier court observations that even green crackers could not be considered a comprehensive solution to Delhi’s pollution problem.
Delhi Pays The Price
Delhi’s air quality worsened sharply during Diwali 2025, with the city’s AQI (Air Quality Index) reaching almost 500, falling under the hazardous category. Firecracker bursting was followed by a dramatic rise in PM2.5 and PM10 levels.
According to a Times of India report, between 9 pm and 10 pm on Diwali 2025, the PM 2.5 concentration of Delhi’s Nehru Nagar region saw a spike from 679 micrograms per cubic metre to 1,763µg/m³. The report also mentioned that the peak PM2.5 concentration was more than 29 times the national daily limit of 60 µg/m³ and around 118 times the World Health Organization’s recommended daily guideline.
Pollution Concerns Framed as Anti-Hindu
Following Diwali last year, Alt News had written about the Right-wing supporters in the country interpreting complaints on the detrimental environmental effects of bursting firecrackers as an “attack against Hindutva” itself.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee had posted a video on his X page asking his audience to desist from burning firecrackers. Right-wing social media users immediately began sharing images of firecrackers that they had apparently hoarded. While some questioned Rathee’s stake in it, others indulged in whataboutery and asked whether he had shown environmental concerns on Bakrid. Certain users went to the extent of mockingly comparing the extreme pollution levels in India to the genocide in Gaza.
Similarly, when BJP leader Subramaniam Swamy wrote on X, “Exploding fire crackers after 10 pm today is a criminal offence. Police should crackdown on them”, Right-wing influencer Chandan Sharma (Hindutva Knight/@HPhobiaWatch) targeted Swamy’s daughter, The Hindu’s Diplomatic Editor, Suhasini Haidar, using obscene language for being married to a Muslim man.
Several Right-wing accounts, such as @NamitaBalyan, @AchAnkurArya, and @JaipurDialogues, posted photos showing the firecrackers and the knight sky shrouded in smog, ultimately dismissing grave environmental concerns under the garb of protecting Hindu festivals.

Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing side effects of cancer treatment in children. Preventing them is essential not only to improve quality of life, but also to help patients complete treatment. Yet the medicines used to prevent vomiting can themselves cause adverse effects, making the search for safe alternatives an important challenge in paediatric oncology.
An Indian multicentre clinical trial suggests that olanzapine may offer an alternative to dexamethasone, a corticosteroid routinely used to prevent chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting in children receiving highly emetogenic chemotherapy — treatment with a high risk of inducing vomiting. The current regimen using dexamethasone is a guideline that is used regularly, but dexamethasone is a corticosteroid. The study was aimed at finding a comparable, non-corticosteroid option.

Bangladeshi author Taslima Nasrin, who is currently living in Kolkata, on October 20, Tuesday, wrote on Facebook that although Leftists in West Bengal organise bookstalls during Durga Puja, such stalls are absent during other ‘religious’ festivals such as Christmas and Eid. She questioned why Leftists choose not to sell books promoting ‘atheism’ during other religious festivals, but instead promote them only during a Hindu festival.
In her post, she wrote (translated from Bengali), “Someone asked, “Have you ever seen Leftists selling books on atheism to Muslims near an Eidgah on Eid? Have you ever seen them selling books by Richard Dawkins or Christopher Hitchens to people attending Christmas prayers on Christmas Day? Then, quite naturally, the question arises: why do they want to sell books on atheism specifically at Hindu Durga Puja pandals?” What answer do the Leftists of Kolkata have to this question?”
This post has garnered over 7,000 likes and 1,300 reshares, and garnered significant traction, although she had disabled the comment section of the Facebook post.
Nasrin, who has been in exile since leaving Bangladesh in 1994 amid death threats and protests over her writings critical of the ‘dogmas’ of Islam, was forced to leave Kolkata in 2007 following violent protests against her autobiography ‘Dwikhandito’ and pressure on the then CPI(M)-led Left Front government.
She remained unable to return to West Bengal for nearly 19 years, with successive CPI(M) and Trinamool Congress (TMC) governments in power. However, in July 2026, following the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) coming to power in the state, Nasrin returned to Kolkata and was publicly welcomed and celebrated by sections of the Right-wing BJP-RSS ecosystem.
Against this backdrop, her recent Facebook post questioned what she portrayed as the Left’s selective promotion of atheism. Moreover, her statement comes on the heels of state authorities demolishing and damaging certain bookstalls set up by Left parties near Jadavpur’s 8b bus stand on October 17.
Fact Check
Alt News found several social media posts and news reports that refute Nasrin’s claim that the bookstalls are exclusively set up during Durga Puja.
The Students’ Federation of India (SFI) and the Democratic Youth Federation of India (DYFI) have been organising a bookstall near Park Street, where Christmas is celebrated in Kolkata, for at least 10 years. Prominent Left leader Biman Bose has also visited the stall. The bookstall has been featured on the social media handles of SFI, DYFI, CPI(M) and other affliated organisations, and has also been covered by the media. The Telegraph reported the setting up of the bookstall at Park Street for the first time in 2016, Alt News also founds images of stalls from 2017, 2022, 2024.
Below are images of a bookstall set up by SFI-DYFI during Christmas in 2017:
Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2022:
Below are images of a bookstall set up during Christmas in 2024:
Similarly, the SFI-DYFI local committee in the Khidderpore area of Kolkata organised a bookstall during Eid this year. Khidderpore has historically been home to a significant Muslim population. The bookstall was organised for two days and was featured on the Facebook page of the CPI(M) Kolkata Port Assembly Committee.
Below are glimpses of the stall set up on Eid at Khidderpore:
Further, Nasrin claimed that the Leftist bookstalls only sell books promoting atheism. However, the images on social media, posted by people who bought books from hundreds of these stalls, clearly show a vast array of books from across genres being sold in these stalls.
An Alt News correspondent visited the CPI(M) bookstall set up near Jadavpur 8B bus stand and encountered a diverse section of books, ranging from Bengali classics, poetry, history among others. Books on Ramkrishna and Vivekananda were also available at the stall.
CPI(M) leader Shatarup Ghosh made a video, interviewing a woman who visited the stall and described herself as a devotee of spiritual leader Lalon Fakir. In the video, she shared her book haul which comprised books on Lalon Fakir, and other Hindu spiritual leaders like Nityananda Mahaprabhu, and even a cook book.
CPI(M) leader Sudip Sengupta, who is in charge of the 8B bookstall regularly posted pictures of the stall on his Facebook page. In one such image, physician Dr. Arjun Dasgupta was seen holding a book on Swami Vivekananda, along with a book on the Second World War.
According to Dasgupta, apart from Leftist books, the stall also contains books such as Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s Anandamath. “I was looking at some old pictures my family took at the Jadavpur 8B stall, and I could see Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay’s books behind me. His books include ‘Anandamath’, which has the song ‘Vande Mataram’. So it is simply not true that these stalls only sell books promoting atheism. These stalls are part of Bengal’s culture, and anyone who loves books should stand against efforts to shut them down,” said Dasgupta.
“We Bengalis feel that a book is a book, whether it is sold at an ISKCON stall or a CPI(M) stall. We love books and naturally gather around any stall that sells them. When we were children, these stalls introduced many of us to great books from around the world. I vividly remember my father buying me a copy of ‘Ispat’, the Bengali translation of Nikolai Ostrovsky’s ‘How the Steel Was Tempered’. I think thousands of people like me have similar memories,” he added.
Similarly, the Rashbehari-1 area committee of the CPI(M) set up a book stall near the Kalighat temple during Durga Puja. Images of the stall show stacks of books ranging from Bengali children’s classics such as Thakurmar Jhuli to literary works including ‘Ichhamati’ by Bibhutibhushan Bandyopadhyay, ‘Kapalkundala’ by Bankim Chandra Chatterjee, ‘Grihadaha’ and ‘Devdas’ by Sarat Chandra Chattopadhyay, among others. Books on Maa Sarada, and books written by Rabindranath Tagore were also visible at the stall.
Thus, the findings above show that Nasrin’s claim that Leftists organise bookstalls only during Hindu festivals such as Durga Puja is false, as there is documented evidence of Left organisations organising bookstalls during both Eid and Christmas. Her claim that books exclusively on atheism are sold at the stalls is also false, as there is documented evidence of books of various genres being sold across Left bookstalls.

As Americans go to the polls today, many will have had their decision about who to vote for informed by an artificial intelligence-powered chatbot.
Around 50 percent of recently surveyed US adults have at one time used an AI chatbot, and 8 percent say they have used these tools ahead of the midterms to find information on candidates and policies, according to Pew Research.
But a lot of information from these chatbots is out of date and has been hallucinated or sourced from partisan websites.
Even supposedly non-partisan chatbots like OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, and Google’s Gemini have been found wanting when it comes to questions about the midterms.
Just last week, Google’s AI Mode refused to provide the results of the 2020 elections and the company’s Gemini chatbot said the deadline to request a mail-in ballot in Pennsylvania was November 3, rather than the real deadline of October 27, according to research by Forum AI.
According to the Forum AI research, almost 40 percent of election answers given by all the mainstream chatbots contained at least one factual error. In August, when Forum AI’s researchers asked why someone should vote for North Carolina congressman Don Davis, Claude gave a response that confused the lawmaker with a “former school superintendent” of the same name.
Google and Anthropic did not respond to requests for comment. Open AI directed WIRED to a blog outlining the company’s approach to elections in 2026.
Part of the problem is that chatbots are reliant on an increasingly problematic pool of online information. Research by NewsGuard found that mainstream chatbots cite so-called “pink slime” websites nearly 50 percent of the time when asked about candidates and policies related to the midterms. “Pink slime” sites present as mainstream news websites, but are in fact funded by political or ideological groups and individuals.
Ahead of the midterms, many more of these sites have sprung up, and chatbots are paying attention. The worst offender, according to NewsGuard, was OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which cited the “pink slime” sites in more than 70 percent of searches, while xAI’s Grok chatbot performed best, citing “pink slime” sites in 30 percent of cases.
“I don't think that most Americans are prepared to navigate an election in the age of consumer AI,” Nina Jankowicz, executive director of the American Sunlight Project and a former disinformation czar during the Biden administration, tells WIRED. “One of the problems is that executives and companies have really overpromised on what AI is capable of. It has to ingest this information from somewhere, and often those sources are not very good. And it's predictive, so if it doesn't know the answer, it does frequently make things up.”

In October, a screenshot spread purportedly showing a social media post by U.S. President Donald Trump, in which he appeared to say the state of Montana should be renamed to "Mountain."
Trump allegedly questioned why the United States is using a Spanish word, Montana, to name one of its states, and supposedly suggested a rebrand would drive up property prices for Montanans. The text reads, in full (archived):
Montana should immediately change its name to MOUNTAIN. Many people don't know this, but Montana is a SPANISH word. It means MOUNTAIN! Why are we using Spanish words to name our GREAT AMERICAN STATES? We speak ENGLISH in America, not Spanish! The name MOUNTAIN would bring tremendous VALUE and PRESTIGE to the State. Property Values would SKYROCKET, wages would go UP, and the people would be even PROUDER to live in the most BEAUTIFUL State in the Country! The Radical Left doesn't want you to know this. They love Spanish Mountains. I love AMERICAN MOUNTAINS! Nobody loves Mountains more than me. The biggest, most beautiful Mountains. We're going to make Montana AMERICAN AGAIN! Thank you for your attention to this matter. President DONALD J. TRUMP
The screenshot spread on X and Threads, while Snopes readers contacted us to ask if the president really demanded the name change.
In short, the post in question is fake. It was not possible to find a trace of it on Trump's official X or Truth Social accounts. Searching for sentences from the alleged post on Trump's Truth, an archive of the president's Truth Social posts, also returned no results.
The screenshot features a mixture of emblems and profile photos from Trump's various social media profiles. It contains his current Truth Social profile photo but the gray, verified checkmark from his X account. Trump also styles his account name as "@realDonaldTrump" on both platforms. In the fake post, his username features a capital "R" at the start of "Real." Additionally, the format in the screengrab is also incorrect when compared to authentic posts on both platforms.
It is possible the fake post has a satirical origin. The earliest version of the screenshot appears to be an Oct. 20 Instagram post (archived) from an account called @whatthehelena_, which describes itself as, "Satire about life in Helena, Montana and Montana in general."
Snopes contacted the @whatthehelena_ page to ask whether a manager of the account created the fake screenshot. We await a response to our inquiry.
Though the post in question is fake, Montana's name does stem from a non-English language. According to Montana Historical Society on an official state government website, the name is a "Latin and Spanish word for a mountainous region," first applied to the territory at its creation in 1864. Montana became a U.S. state in 1889.
For further reading, Snopes has previously investigated other rumors about Trump wanting to rename things.

The AI race has largely revolved around frontier labs and models that can write, code, analyse documents and reason through prompts. But as companies move from chatbots to AI agents, another part of the stack is gaining attention: models that make a specific decision and return an answer that another system can act on. Decision models gained momentum with the arrival of Jev, the first public model from TypeSafe AI, founded by Diogo Almeida, who helped develop research behind ChatGPT at OpenAI. Released in September, Jev focuses on decision-oriented outputs, including scores and yes-or-no probabilities, rather than conventional text generation. Other companies have since explored similar capabilities, though their products differ in architecture and intended use. Cloudflare has introduced Clef and Clef-flash, while Microsoft has released Decision-1, a model based on Alibaba’s Qwen family that has been post-trained for decision tasks. AWS has introduced Strands Decider 2B for agent workflows, and OpenAI has launched a Decisions API. Perplexity has also explored decision-oriented APIs. Under this approach, an agent handling a customer complaint, for instance, may need to decide whether to escalate it, route it to a particular team or resolve it automatically. It does not necessarily need a long, generated response to make that decision. The same applies to systems classifying transactions, checking whether an action should proceed or routing requests across software tools. These decisions can be handled by general-purpose large language models (LLMs), but using them for every step can add latency, cost and complexity. Decision models are designed to handle narrower tasks, returning a label, score, probability or confidence level instead of a paragraph of text. The idea is to give software a more direct way to make a bounded judgement without requiring a general-purpose model to generate a full response at every stage. In agentic systems, where multiple tools and models work together, this could make routine decisions easier to integrate into a workflow. They are not necessarily replacements for LLMs. Rather, they can become specialised components within larger AI systems, handling defined decisions while general-purpose models take on tasks that require broader reasoning or language generation. Enterprises Seek Reliability For enterprises, the opportunity extends beyond reducing token consumption and cost savings. Companies need AI systems that can work with internal data, understand domain-specific context and make decisions that can be reviewed and governed. General purpose models are probabilistic by design. Their responses can vary, even when prompts appear similar. That flexibility is useful for open-ended tasks, but enterprise workflows in sectors such as manufacturing, energy, finance and aerospace often require defined outputs, traceability and tighter controls. Articul8 AI, an enterprise AI company spun out of Intel in 2024, is building a platform around what it calls a “correctness stack”. According to Ananthanarayanan S, the company’s managing director for India, enterprises need more than access to a capable model. They need a system that connects their data and domain knowledge with models that can deliver outputs suited to specific workflows. The platform is designed to work across cloud environments, on-premises deployments and air-gapped systems. Its data perception layer brings information from different enterprise sources into a unified view, helping AI systems work with the context and relationships within an organisation’s data. Articul8 has developed around 28 domain models spanning areas such as energy, finance, aerospace and manufacturing. Its platform can select models depending on the task and combine specialised models with customers’ preferred frontier or reasoning models. The company says its approach can reduce token usage by more than 50% in relevant workflows, although the savings will depend on the application and deployment. In October, Articul8 announced Bivia, a multimodal decision model designed to process inputs such as text, images, video frames, tables and charts, and return structured decisions. Ananthanarayanan said the differentiation lies less in any single model than in the platform’s ability to connect models and solve difficult customer problems. He cited an engineering company with around 10,000 documents that were ingested in roughly 10 hours before an application was made available for use. Articul8 has also said the American Society of Mechanical Engineers selected it for work related to standards. These examples point to the company’s focus on applying AI within existing enterprise workflows rather than selling a standalone model alone. PurpleTalk is approaching the opportunity through Sthānika, its applied AI research lab, and the Sieve family of decision models. Sieve-31Bv3 is designed to be called by AI agents as one component in a larger system. It returns a defined answer with a confidence score, allowing the agent to decide what to do next. The company claimed at the time of launch that Sieve-31Bv3 ranked first on the full Jev Decision Index, a collection of 43 private and public benchmarks hosted on Hugging Face. The company reported a score of 71.1 on the full index and 71.7 on the public test, where it ranked third. Sieve builds on earlier compact, confidence-aware decision models used within PurpleTalk products Ello and Mina. The company sees potential applications in voice, customer experience and robotics, where routine decisions need to be made quickly and predictably. “Sieve-31B shows that a focused model fine-tuned in India can perform among the best in the world at this work. The private tests matter most to us. They come from domains outside the public suite, and Sieve generalised better than most of the field. It learned the task, not the test,” said Sridhar Muppidi, cofounder of PurpleTalk. Bharat Lingam, CEO of PurpleTalk, believes decision models will open up a new category of agentic systems: more reliable, more controllable, and fast enough for voice, customer experience and robotics. “We are publishing everything needed to reproduce our results, and we invite the research community to test it, challenge it and build on it,” Lingam added. The approaches illustrate two sides of the enterprise opportunity. Articul8 is building a broader platform around enterprise data, models and governance, while PurpleTalk’s Sthānika is a specialised model that agents can call for particular decisions. In both cases, the commercial test will be whether these systems improve real workflows, not simply whether their models perform well on benchmarks. A Decision Model For Every Workflow The decision model opportunity is not limited to enterprise platforms in India. Smaller AI startups and researchers are also exploring models that can be adapted, deployed locally and used by developers building their own applications. Kerala-based ConvAI Innovations has developed Laya, an open-weight decision model intended to run locally on devices such as laptops and mobile phones and be adapted by developers. Founder Nandakishore Mukkunnoth said the initial focus was on building small, fast models that did not always require cloud access. Interest in a general-purpose, open-source decision model grew after Jev’s release. The startup has discussed plans for Laya Max, with image and audio capabilities, alongside APIs, software development kits and a commercial enterprise offering. It has also suggested that Laya could deliver substantial cost savings compared with Jev. These claims will need to be tested against comparable workloads, as performance and cost depend on the task, model configuration and deployment. Laya’s significance lies in the possibility of giving developers an adaptable model that can run closer to where decisions need to be made. Local execution could be useful where latency, connectivity, data control or inference costs matter. But open weights alone will not establish a durable advantage. The model will still need to perform reliably on real tasks and be straightforward to integrate into applications. For investors, the opportunity may be less about backing another general-purpose model and more about identifying where decision-making can become a product in its own right. “Decision models are one of the most important shifts in AI this year. What can’t be copied is a company’s own record of decisions and outcomes. For startups, the real test is how fast the model improves on a specific, high-volume workflow,” said Shubham Gupta, founding general partner at Together Fund. That points to a potential advantage for startups that can pair models with proprietary data, feedback from actual outcomes and a clearly defined customer problem. A model may be accessible to competitors, but the data and workflow knowledge used to improve its decisions can be harder to replicate. In the Indian context, this creates several possible entry points: developing specialised models, building infrastructure that routes tasks to the right model, and creating applications around high-volume enterprise workflows. The challenge is to demonstrate measurable improvements in accuracy, cost or speed, rather than compete on benchmark scores alone. As the global industry moves towards more specialised AI systems, the question is whether Indian builders can turn their models into products that enterprises repeatedly use. The next advantage may not belong to the model that can do the most things, but to the system that can make a particular decision reliably, cheaply and at scale.

South African police arrest 5 after farmer is shot, ears cut off in violent robbery
Police in South Africa have arrested five suspects connected to a violent farm robbery
JOHANNESBURG -- Police in South Africa have arrested five suspects in connection with a violent farm robbery in the North West province in which a 50-year-old farmer was shot and had his ears cut off.
The suspects, aged 26 to 56, are expected to appear before the Ventersdorp magistrates’ court on Tuesday on charges of house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition, Col. Adele Mybrugh said Monday.
Police initially arrested two suspects before detaining three more on Sunday near Potchefstroom, about 120 kilometers (74 miles) west-southwest of Johannesburg. Officers seized four firearms, two of which were linked to the attack, along with clothing and jewelry.
The attack occurred Oct. 28 on a farm in Syferfontein, near Ventersdorp, in North West province. Three armed men wearing balaclavas confronted a farmworker mowing the lawn, demanded to know where the owner was, and bound his hands and feet with cable ties, police said.
When the farmer arrived, the attackers shot him in the upper body, dragged him inside, bound him and stabbed and assaulted him. They stole three firearms from a safe and fled in his pickup truck, police said.
The worker freed himself and called for help. The farmer was hospitalized in serious condition.
The Moral Regeneration Movement, a civil society organization, identified the farmer as Donovan Marx and said Monday that he was recovering in the hospital.
Farm attacks affect both Black and white farmers, workers and residents. Research by the Institute for Security Studies points to robbery as the predominant motive and has found no evidence of an organized campaign against white farmers or a “ white genocide ” as the Trump administration has claimed.
“Any attack on farmers represents a serious threat to food security,” said the movement’s provincial convenor, Pastor Lesiba Kgwele.
Kgwele called for increased police visibility in farming communities and cautioned against using crime to fuel racial hatred and division.
